# Part 3 source records: framing records (how each paper states its problem, challenge, objective, solution and gain), one per work of the store and of the deck list, 2026-09-30

**Date:** 2026-09-30 · generated by `tools/evidence-check/build_part3_files.py` from the verified store; not edited by hand.

Each work was saved as full text and read by one agent, which locked every item to a line of the saved text with a short verbatim anchor. A script checked that each anchor occurs in the saved text and that the numbers of the item stand within three lines of it. A second agent, which did not write the record, then tried to refute each item against the text. Items shown here passed both checks. Where the auditor corrected an item, the corrected wording is shown and the Audit column says so. The verbatim anchors and the saved texts are kept outside the repository; this file gives the location of every item instead. Only works that are eligible under the source rule (2026-09-29, D313; citation priority restated on 2026-09-30) are listed; the others are in the evidence ledger, section 1b.

Columns: # = item index (the reference is <record id>#<index>); Field = what the item is about; Line = line in the saved text of the version read. Full references: evidence ledger, References.

## f002 — Towards Reliable LLM Evaluation: Correcting the Winner's Curse in Adaptive Benchmarking

- Source: https://arxiv.org/html/2605.05973v1 · version read: v1 (arXiv HTML; PDF text of v1 also saved and cross-checked for pool sizes and limitations) · v1: 2026-05-07
- Source class: institutional supplement · no formal publication confirmed
- Audit: usable; 6 items kept, 0 dropped

| # | Field | Claim | Figure | Measurement definition | Location | Line | Label | Audit |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 0 | framing_problem | When adaptive prompt and program search reuses benchmark items inside tuning, the reported score of the winning artifact need not estimate the fresh-data performance of the full tune-then-deploy procedure; the paper studies inference for this procedure-level target under explicit tuning budgets. | - | Framing statement (how the paper states its problem, challenge, objective, solution or gain); not a measurement. | line 86 of the saved text | 86 | primary | corrected by the auditor |
| 1 | framing_challenge | Once benchmark examples are reused inside the tuning loop the reported artifact is itself data dependent, so the retrospective question (which candidate looked best on the searched sample) and the operational question (expected fresh-data performance of rerunning the budget-B tuner) diverge; the paper calls this gap the winner's curse in adaptive benchmarking. Prior work on prompt variation and statistically principled evaluation targets different statistical objects (robustness to prompt choice, efficient evaluation over a pre-specified prompt pool, stochastic evaluation under meaning-preserving perturbations, prompt choice under controlled risk guarantees) rather than inference after budgeted adaptive search (line 90). Technically, the reporting error is not a simple sample-mean error, because each benchmark item affects the estimate both through held-out scores and through scoring-subset scores that change the selection weights (line 159); a discontinuous hard argmax selector requires smoothing or an additional margin condition (line 177). | - | Framing statement (how the paper states its problem, challenge, objective, solution or gain); not a measurement. | line 89 of the saved text | 89 | primary | corrected by the auditor |
| 2 | framing_objective | Procedure-level target theta_j(B) = E[ mu_j(W^new, a_hat_j(B; D)) ] (eq. 3), where mu_j(w,a) = E_xi[ Z_j(W,a,xi) / W=w ] (eq. 1) is the item-conditional mean score of artifact a for system j, Z_j in [0,1] is the per-item score, xi is execution randomness, a_hat_j(B;D) = T_{j,B}(D,U_j) (eq. 2) is the artifact returned by the budget-B tuner from development sample D with internal randomness U_j, W^new ~ P is a fresh task instance independent of D, and B records the cost of the tuner; the goal is to estimate theta_j(B) on a finite pre-specified budget grid. SIREN's point estimator is theta_tilde_{j,R}(B) = sum_r omega_r Y_hat_{r,j}(B) (eq. 6), with Y_hat_{r,j}(B) = q_hat_{r,j}(B)^T T_hat_{r,j}(B), where q_hat = g_{j,B}(S_hat) are selector weights computed from scoring-subset scores S_hat (eq. 4) and T_hat are held-out scores (eq. 5); the theorems and bootstrap cover the finite-sample reporting target theta^{RS/G}_{j,M}(B) = E[theta_tilde_{j,R}(B) / G_M] (eq. 7), conditional on the frozen shortlist and split design. Reported experimental metrics: 'bias' = theta_hat_A - theta*_A in percentage points and 'dir' = number of cells where sign(theta_hat_A - theta*_B) = sign(theta*_A - theta*_B), with theta* a 10,000-redraw Monte Carlo approximation of eq. 7 (lines 218-220). | - | Framing statement (how the paper states its problem, challenge, objective, solution or gain); not a measurement. | line 121 of the saved text | 121 | primary | corrected by the auditor |
| 3 | framing_solution | SIREN freezes the post-search shortlist, repeatedly splits a separate evaluation pool into a scoring part (which sets stabilized selection weights) and a held-out part (which evaluates the selected output), so aggregation keeps the selection step but separates selection evidence from performance evaluation; an item-level Gaussian multiplier bootstrap gives confidence intervals and simultaneous bands over budgets without rerunning the tuner. | - | Framing statement (how the paper states its problem, challenge, objective, solution or gain); not a measurement. | line 91 of the saved text | 91 | primary | corrected by the auditor |
| 4 | framing_gain | Point-estimation accuracy against theta*, a 10,000-redraw Monte Carlo approximation of the finite-sample reporting target of eq. 7 (line 218): on MMLU-Pro Math/Law with random search and DSPy over 11 open-weight models and a 4-point token-budget grid, SIREN's mean signed error is between -0.20 and +0.08 percentage points in the four aggregate rows, whereas winner-based reporting (M1 naive max) is optimistic in all four (+1.37, +1.43, +1.90, +1.01 pp). Directional accuracy: SIREN 42/44, 43/44, 42/44 vs M1 37/44, 34/44, 15/44 on Math-random search, Math-DSPy and Law-random search; on Law-DSPy SIREN ties M1 and M4 at 40/44, and M4's bias there (+0.08) is smaller in magnitude than SIREN's (-0.20) (Tables 1-2, lines 221-500). | - | Framing statement (how the paper states its problem, challenge, objective, solution or gain); not a measurement. | line 502 of the saved text | 502 | primary | corrected by the auditor |
| 5 | framing_classification | Classification by the extractor, checked by the auditor: efficiency in the stated problem = secondary; efficiency terms = tuning budget B ('B records the cost of the tuner', line 115), token-budget grid {500K, 1.5M, 3M, 6.5M} (line 208), limited evaluation budgets (of prior prompt-optimization work, line 90), computational payoff: bootstrap without rerunning the tuner (lines 92, 198-199), wall-clock: multiplier bootstrap 7.5 ms vs 281 ms for a nonparametric item bootstrap (37.6x speedup at M=500, K=10, R=5, B_boot=1000; line 2363); about 35x over a paired bootstrap and ~10^5x over PromptEval at MMLU-Pro scale (line 2364), repeated splits buy efficiency: CI width -22% from R=1 to R=5, only -4% more to R=10 (line 2352), hardware: all models served via vLLM on a single NVIDIA RTX 4090 (line 218); agent kind = LLM systems (a base model plus fixed pipeline components) whose prompts, demonstrations or language-model programs are tuned by adaptive search (random search, DSPy); the paper is an evaluation/statistical-inference method, not about agents; position = evaluation/measurement. | - | Reader classification (not a statement of the paper). | whole abstract and introduction |  | secondary | corrected by the auditor |

|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 0 | framing_problem | Fixed-size benchmarks are an inefficient tool for model evaluation: because evaluation objectives (ranking, selection, testing during development) need different statistical power, fixed sample sizes lead to either excessive computational cost or compromised reliability. | - | Framing statement (how the paper states its problem, challenge, objective, solution or gain); not a measurement. | line 60 of the saved text | 60 | primary | corrected by the auditor |
| 1 | framing_challenge | Evaluation costs have grown (high-resolution images, large contexts, many datasets, LLM-as-Judge metrics), yet fixed-size evaluation continues to the predetermined sample size even when the outcome is already statistically clear, while ad-hoc subsampling lacks guarantees; and naively checking results during data collection ('peeking') invalidates standard p-values and confidence intervals. | - | Framing statement (how the paper states its problem, challenge, objective, solution or gain); not a measurement. | line 64 of the saved text | 64 | primary | corrected by the auditor |
| 2 | framing_objective | Provide statistical guarantees while minimizing sample usage: stop evaluating once user-defined stopping rules are met - efficacy (significance reached), equivalence margin, precision-based (CI narrow enough for the minimum detectable effect size), threshold crossing, futility, and diminishing returns (Sec. 5.3) - using group sequential testing with the Pocock spending function, which applies a constant critical value c across stages so that the overall Type I error equals alpha under repeated looks. Measured quantity: benchmark score S_A(D) = (1/n) sum_{i=1..n} ( (1/m_i) sum_{j=1..m_i} S_i^A(e_ij) ) (eq. 1), a mean-of-means over n datasets D_i with m_i examples e_ij and scoring function S_i in [0,1] applied to model A's outputs; comparisons use delta_hat_{A,B}(D) = S_A(D) - S_B(D) (eq. 2) tested as H0: delta=0 vs H1: delta>0 (eqs. 3-4). Stages k=1..t add batches of size b so N_k = kb (eq. 5), with test statistic Z_k^{AB} = (S_k^A(D) - S_k^B(D)) / sqrt(sigma_hat_k^2 / N_k) (eq. 6), sigma_hat_k^2 the pooled variance. Reported metrics: percentage of benchmark samples used, 95% CI half-width, and share of model pairs distinguished at 95% confidence. | - | Framing statement (how the paper states its problem, challenge, objective, solution or gain); not a measurement. | line 94 of the saved text | 94 | primary | corrected by the auditor |
| 3 | framing_solution | Replace the fixed sample size with adaptive evaluation based on sequential testing: evaluate in batches, apply stopping criteria tailored to the evaluation need, and use group sequential testing so interim looks do not inflate error rates; evaluation stops as soon as the practical and statistical needs are met. | - | Framing statement (how the paper states its problem, challenge, objective, solution or gain); not a measurement. | line 68 of the saved text | 68 | primary | corrected by the auditor |
| 4 | framing_gain | Fewer evaluated samples than fixed-size evaluation at the stated reliability, with 'cost' measured as the fraction of benchmark samples run; the results are computed on the leaderboard's released prediction records, scored by the authors with a Llama 3.1 8B LLM-as-a-Judge (lines 181-183), not on live model runs: on the Open VLM Leaderboard (206 VLMs, 31 datasets) an 80% reduction in computational cost with a 2.5-point CI width allowance while maintaining statistical significance (abstract; Fig. 1: stopping at +/-2.5); about 15% of samples for a +/-3-point CI and about 30% for +/-2 points; 44% cost reduction with diminishing-returns stopping at a 0.132-point precision loss; in 1K pairwise comparisons 76% of pairs distinguished at 95% confidence vs 55% for a fixed 1.2K-sample bootstrap baseline; ranking five top-15 models (equivalence margin +/-2, alpha=0.05) used 60% of examples, though 2.4 of 20 comparisons per run were indistinguishable and required the full benchmark (line 238); the 2-point meaningful-change test used 63% of examples; model selection with a 60-point filter used 30% of the total sample budget (50% without the filter). | - | Framing statement (how the paper states its problem, challenge, objective, solution or gain); not a measurement. | line 62 of the saved text | 62 | primary | corrected by the auditor |

| # | Field | Claim | Figure | Measurement definition | Location | Line | Label | Audit |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 0 | framing_problem | Reliable agent evaluation is complicated by automatic harness optimization that repeatedly uses a released benchmark to guide a Proposer editing the harness around a fixed model; task holdout varies tasks but leaves the benchmark protocol fixed, so a 'bad genius' Proposer can produce a harness whose improvement depends on a benchmark-wide shortcut. | - | Framing statement (how the paper states its problem, challenge, objective, solution or gain); not a measurement. | line 16 of the saved text | 16 | primary | corrected by the auditor |
| 1 | framing_challenge | The 'bad genius' Proposer is optimized for benchmark score, not for preserving what that score is intended to measure, and harness evolution adds an executable route: the Proposer can write the shortcut into the harness. Existing methods (banning task identifiers, filenames and per-task recipes, then evaluating on held-out tasks) limit task-specific shortcuts but not benchmark-wide shortcuts (protocol correlations shared across tasks), which persist on held-out tasks; in realistic benchmarks such shortcuts can arise from many parts of the protocol and remain hidden from both manual inspection and automated checks, making them difficult to pre-specify with fixed rules. | - | Framing statement (how the paper states its problem, challenge, objective, solution or gain); not a measurement. | line 47 of the saved text | 47 | primary | corrected by the auditor |
| 2 | framing_objective | Goal: achieve a substantial positive released gain G_rel(H;H0) while keeping Delta_BS(H;H0) below a small tolerance. Definitions: R_B(A,H) = E_{U~P} E_{tau~p_A(./H,B,U)} [ r_B(tau,U) ] is the population score of foundation model A with harness H on benchmark B, r_B in [0,1] the score of trajectory tau on task U; G_rel(H;H0) = R_rel(A,H) - R_rel(A,H0) the gain over initial harness H0 on the released benchmark; G_0 the same gain on the ideal shortcut-neutralized benchmark B0; Delta_BS = G_rel - G_0 the gain attributable to a benchmark-wide shortcut. Operational form (eq. 2): H_t in arg max_H G_rel(H;H0) s.t. Delta_b(H;H0) <= epsilon for all B_b in the archive A_{t-1}, where Delta_b = G_rel - G_b is the released gain destroyed by counterfactual benchmark B_b and epsilon >= 0 the tolerated gain loss; the Challenger solves B_bt in arg max_{B_b in B_val} Delta_b(H_t;H0) (eq. 3); the final harness is selected by eq. 4 under all archive constraints. Reported metrics: on OfficeQA certification (76 questions, 3 rollouts) R_rel, the archive-average R_avg,A3 = /A/^-1 sum_{Bb in A} R_Bb,Dcert(A,H) and archive-worst-case R_min,A3 = min_{Bb in A} R_Bb,Dcert(A,H) (lines 436-449), plus R_ProV2 on the 90-question Pro V2 release; on Syn-Ledger (208 certification tasks) R_rel, R_0, G_rel, G_0 and Delta_BS (lines 458-464). | - | Framing statement (how the paper states its problem, challenge, objective, solution or gain); not a measurement. | line 227 of the saved text | 227 | primary | corrected by the auditor |
| 3 | framing_solution | CHASE casts harness evolution as constraint generation over valid counterfactual benchmarks: after each Proposer update a Challenger searches for an executable protocol transformation with large gain destruction, a validity firewall checks task semantics are preserved, and counterfactuals confirmed on held-out tasks enter a finite archive that constrains later harness updates and final selection. | - | Framing statement (how the paper states its problem, challenge, objective, solution or gain); not a measurement. | line 108 of the saved text | 108 | primary | corrected by the auditor |
| 4 | framing_gain | Robustness of harness gains to valid protocol transformations, not the highest released score: on Syn-Ledger CHASE has the highest shortcut-neutralized score and gain (R0 38.30%, G0 +23.08%, Delta_BS -17.79%) versus e.g. Meta-Harness (G0 +4.65%) and HarnessEvolve (G0 +3.04%, Delta_BS +8.65%), while trailing HarnessEvolve on the released benchmark (R_rel 87.18% vs 93.59%). On OfficeQA Full certification CHASE has a competitive released score (68.86% vs 69.30% for HarnessEvolve and 67.98% for the unchanged harness) and the highest archive-average and worst-case scores (68.42%, 67.98% vs 68.20%, 67.11% for HarnessEvolve and 66.23%, 64.47% for the unchanged harness), where the archive is the final CHASE archive A3, i.e. the counterfactuals found by CHASE's own Challenger and used as constraints in CHASE's optimization on disjoint question sets (lines 297-298, 436-438, 954-958), and 30.37% on Pro V2 vs 27.04% for the unchanged harness (Tables 1-2, lines 481-485, 536-541). | - | Framing statement (how the paper states its problem, challenge, objective, solution or gain); not a measurement. | line 468 of the saved text | 468 | primary | corrected by the auditor |

| 0 | framing_problem | Existing GUI agents use sequential episodes of multi-step operations across pages as prior GUI knowledge, which fails to capture the complex transition relationships between pages, making it hard for agents to deeply perceive the GUI environment and generalize to new scenarios. The paper poses the question of how to explicitly model the semantic relationships among pages and enhance GUI agents' perception in new scenarios. | - | Framing statement (how the paper states its problem, challenge, objective, solution or gain); not a measurement. | line 81 of the saved text | 81 | primary | corrected by the auditor |
| 1 | framing_challenge | Knowledge collected from devices is treated as independent, linear episodes; such linear knowledge restricts the agent to consecutive steps and it lacks perception of possible actions leading to other pages, so the semantic association between pages is not integrated and a single sequential episode may not instruct the agent to finish a new task at deployment. Prior RAG for GUI agents retrieves discrete items (widget descriptions, reference trajectories) without graph structure. | - | Framing statement (how the paper states its problem, challenge, objective, solution or gain); not a measurement. | line 98 of the saved text | 98 | primary | corrected by the auditor |
| 2 | framing_objective | none stated as an optimisation objective. The paper reports benchmark metrics: the AITW action matching score, element accuracy (Ele.Acc), operation F1 (Op.F1) and step success rate (Step SR) on Mind2Web, and the original GUI Odyssey metric setting. Its equations (1)-(16) define the graph-construction and agent functions (e.g. R_d = D_agent(I_t, R_o, R_s, G_{I_t}, tau_{<t}), where I_t is the current screenshot, R_o the observation, R_s the sub-task plan with candidate actions, G_{I_t} the retrieved guidelines and tau_{<t} the interaction history), not an objective. | - | Framing statement (how the paper states its problem, challenge, objective, solution or gain); not a measurement. | line 406 of the saved text | 406 | primary | corrected by the auditor |
| 3 | framing_solution | Because pages are naturally connected by actions and an episode is a path sampled on that graph, the method reconstructs episodes into a page graph (unique pages as nodes, merged in-page action queues as edges) via page-jump determination, node similarity check and graph update; at run time it locates similar nodes from a screen summary, runs BFS over outgoing edges to collect (action queue, achievable tasks) guidelines, and injects them via RAG into the sub-task planning and decision agents without any parameter modification. | - | Framing statement (how the paper states its problem, challenge, objective, solution or gain); not a measurement. | line 103 of the saved text | 103 | primary | corrected by the auditor |
| 4 | framing_gain | On AITW, PG-Agent yields the best average (overall) action matching score among the API-based agents compared (Table 3: 59.5 overall), and the paper states that its GoogleApps action accuracy 'exceeds state-of-art result by 13.4%'; on Mind2Web it achieves the best Ele.Acc and Step SR and the second-best Op.F1; on GUI Odyssey it produces the best results in most scenarios and is suboptimal only in Multi-Apps. The paper reports that the effectiveness holds even with limited (randomly sampled) episodes for page-graph construction, with full episodes better only in specific scenarios. | - | Framing statement (how the paper states its problem, challenge, objective, solution or gain); not a measurement. | line 355 of the saved text | 355 | primary | corrected by the auditor |

|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 0 | framing_problem | The behavioral structure of LLM-based agents is opaque: long unstructured traces resist the safety auditing and runtime monitoring that deployment requires. The paper frames behavioral recovery as an inverse problem: given a corpus of execution traces, reconstruct an FSM that explains the observed behavior, to support next-step and failure prediction. | - | Framing statement (how the paper states its problem, challenge, objective, solution or gain); not a measurement. | line 161 of the saved text | 161 | primary | corrected by the auditor |
| 1 | framing_challenge | Existing approaches operate per trace or on successful traces only (requiring task descriptions, manual specification or success filters), so they miss the cross-run topology that links next-step and failure prediction; the structure emerges from system prompt, tools and task distribution but is nowhere specified, and because traces are positive examples only, identifying the target language is impossible in the limit. | - | Framing statement (how the paper states its problem, challenge, objective, solution or gain); not a measurement. | line 162 of the saved text | 162 | primary | corrected by the auditor |
| 2 | framing_objective | Replay fitness (Definition 1): fit(sigma, M) = k/T, where sigma = (a_1,...,a_T) is an activity sequence, M the FSM (Q, A, delta, q_0, Q) with states Q, finite activity alphabet A, deterministic partial transition function delta and initial state q_0, and k the number of symbols consumed when replaying sigma from q_0 (steps where delta(q, a_t) is defined); corpus fitness Fit(D, M) = (1//D/) * sum over tau in D of fit(sigma(tau), M), D = {tau_1,...,tau_N} the trace corpus (Eq. 1). Next-step prediction is scored by cross-entropy CE = -(1/T) * sum_t log2 P_hat(a_t / context) (Eq. 5); failure prediction by held-out AUROC; additional axes are precision (fraction of random/permuted invalid traces rejected), compression /Q_baseline///Q_ours/ and stability across splits (Sec. 3.6). The next-step estimator is P_hat(a / q) = (C(q,a) + alpha) / (sum over a' in A of C(q,a') + alpha/A/), where C(q,a) counts how often activity a follows state q in training data and alpha is a smoothing parameter (Eq. 4). The runtime monitor is scored by rank-AUROC at the 25% trace checkpoint and by precision, recall, F1, 'Latency' (mean % of trace at intervention) and 'Saved' (mean % of remaining computation avoided) (Table 40, App. H.13). | - | Framing statement (how the paper states its problem, challenge, objective, solution or gain); not a measurement. | line 227 of the saved text | 227 | primary | corrected by the auditor |
| 3 | framing_solution | Since agent behavior is generated by a bounded set of tools and actions, traces have small activity alphabets (6-42 symbols), which makes the problem tractable: an entire trace corpus is collapsed into one compact, deterministic FSM built from a prefix tree merged by last activity (plus rare-transition filtering) in linear time without learning hyperparameters; the FSM state is then used as context for next-step prediction and its per-state features for failure prediction and an online monitor. | - | Framing statement (how the paper states its problem, challenge, objective, solution or gain); not a measurement. | line 163 of the saved text | 163 | primary | corrected by the auditor |
| 4 | framing_gain | Per-state behavioral features reach held-out AUROC up to 0.94 for failure prediction; FSM-state context outperforms Agent Workflow Memory on 8/8 datasets (abstract: on every ground-truth-matched dataset) and FSM state conditioning improves next-step cross-entropy by 0.155 bits (21%) over identical methods without state; an online monitor ranks failing SWE-agent runs above passing ones at the 25% checkpoint (rank-AUROC 0.66 vs 0.5 for flag-everything) and, in a simulated deployment that replays recorded traces, triggers early stopping at 32% mean trace completion on SWE-agent (precision 85.9%, recall 95.5%, reported as 'saving 68% of remaining compute'; in Table 40 this 'Saved' value equals 100% minus the 32% intervention point, calc.) and at 56% on tau2-bench airline; the FSMs have 15-3,036x fewer states than RPNI at >= 0.997 test fitness and build in milliseconds. | - | Framing statement (how the paper states its problem, challenge, objective, solution or gain); not a measurement. | line 167 of the saved text | 167 | primary | corrected by the auditor |
| 5 | framing_classification | Classification by the extractor, checked by the auditor: efficiency in the stated problem = secondary; efficiency terms = build in milliseconds, linear time, early stopping well before completion, Runtime, speedup, per-trace replay latency, ms/step, saving 68% of remaining compute, Steps saved, sample efficiency; agent kind = LLM-based agents executing multi-step tasks (coding agents resolving GitHub issues, web navigation, desktop, customer-service and multi-agent pipelines); the paper models their execution traces as a finite-state machine (FSM); position = evaluation/measurement. | - | Reader classification (not a statement of the paper). | whole abstract and introduction |  | secondary | corrected by the auditor |

| 0 | framing_problem | Dynamic specification mining extracts candidate specifications from logs of execution traces, and the common challenge is faithfulness: how can one be confident the extracted specifications faithfully characterize the program? Since producing and analyzing traces is costly, how would one know enough traces have been seen, and that resources were not wasted on too many? | - | Framing statement (how the paper states its problem, challenge, objective, solution or gain); not a measurement. | line 41 of the saved text | 41 | primary | corrected by the auditor |
| 1 | framing_challenge | Producing and analyzing traces is costly, and in dynamic specification mining the system and its full set of system traces is unknown, so whether a log is complete (adding any new system trace would not change the algorithm's output) cannot be established from the log and must be estimated as a probability. | - | Framing statement (how the paper states its problem, challenge, objective, solution or gain); not a measurement. | line 46 of the saved text | 46 | primary | corrected by the auditor |
| 2 | framing_objective | Log confidence: the estimated probability that a log l is complete with regard to an algorithm A. A log l is complete w.r.t. a log-property LP = <LP_tr, LP_log> if the information extractable about LP from l equals that from any log containing l (Def. 2); l is complete w.r.t. A iff it is complete w.r.t. every LP in LP(A), the set of log properties representing A (Def. 3); confidence w.r.t. A is the minimum over the LPs in LP(A): conf_A(l) = min{ P[Y^n_LP = f_LP(pi)] / LP in LP(A) } (Def. 4), where Y^n_LP is the property value manifested by the n traces of the log and f_LP(pi) the value manifested by all traces T(M) of the unknown model M. Evaluation measures: reliability rel(l) = 1 if l is complete w.r.t. A and 0 otherwise (Def. 7), and redundancy red(l) = 1 - i_min(l)//l/, where i_min(l) is the minimal index such that the first i_min traces are complete w.r.t. A and /l/ is the number of traces (Def. 8). | - | Framing statement (how the paper states its problem, challenge, objective, solution or gain); not a measurement. | line 156 of the saved text | 156 | primary | corrected by the auditor |
| 3 | framing_solution | A black-box probabilistic framework based on log completeness: each mining algorithm is represented by a set of log properties, traces are treated as random independent samples, and the probability that the log already manifests all property values is estimated without running the mining algorithm, so an engineer can stop adding traces once a confidence threshold is reached. | - | Framing statement (how the paper states its problem, challenge, objective, solution or gain); not a measurement. | line 52 of the saved text | 52 | primary | corrected by the auditor |
| 4 | framing_gain | Evaluated against true log completeness (checked with a model checker) on 24 models from 9 sources, reliability is always greater than or equal to the confidence threshold and is very high with low variance at threshold 0.95; Spearman correlation between confidence and reliability is .68, .70 and .52 (p < .05) for k-Tails, Synoptic and triggers/effects; confidence computation never exceeded 15 milliseconds; at threshold .95 the maximal redundancy is about .74 and the maximal median redundancy about .63 (worst case a log about 4 times longer than its minimal complete sublog). | - | Framing statement (how the paper states its problem, challenge, objective, solution or gain); not a measurement. | line 530 of the saved text | 530 | primary | corrected by the auditor |

| 0 | framing_problem | Tool-using language-model agents repeatedly pay to rediscover procedures they have already executed: a recurring intent is issued again and again and each time the agent re-derives the same tool sequence. The paper formulates recurring agent-trace reuse as a compilation problem over workflow structure, parameter provenance and residual LLM decisions, under partial observability (line 170-171). | - | Framing statement (how the paper states its problem, challenge, objective, solution or gain); not a measurement. | line 121 of the saved text | 121 | primary | corrected by the auditor |
| 1 | framing_challenge | On each occurrence the agent re-resolves stable identity and configuration, retries equivalent calls, re-reads tool documentation and carries an expanding reasoning history; most of this is not intrinsic to the task but the cost of treating every request as new. Reuse is hard because traces mix reusable procedure with accidental history, event order alone does not establish dependency, and exported traces may record arguments but not outputs (line 132-149, 199-205). | - | Framing statement (how the paper states its problem, challenge, objective, solution or gain); not a measurement. | line 127 of the saved text | 127 | primary | corrected by the auditor |
| 2 | framing_objective | none stated as an objective function: the paper says the design priorities trade runtime LLM nodes, tool-call cost, structural complexity and replay error against fitness and validation thresholds, but no weights are fitted and no reported number is the value of such an expression (line 241-248). What it quantifies: minimality (observed versus runtime calls), determinism (residual LLM nodes), generalization (execution on withheld instances) and auditability (line 236-239). Formal objects: a trace tau=(c,u,e_1...e_n,y,z) = system context, user request, execution events, final output, metadata (line 194-195); an intent cluster C={tau_1...tau_m} (line 207); the output workflow W=(V,E,B,G,I,O) = typed nodes, control-flow edges, parameter bindings, guards, and input/output schemas (line 216-217). | - | Framing statement (how the paper states its problem, challenge, objective, solution or gain); not a measurement. | line 243 of the saved text | 243 | primary | corrected by the auditor |
| 3 | framing_solution | Instead of replaying traces or summarising them as textual guidance that an LLM must reinterpret at runtime, repeated traces are compiled into an executable workflow in which decisions supported by evidence leave the model's runtime responsibility: intents are discovered by clustering, retries/schema lookups/unused reads are denoised, an edge a->b is kept only when an argument of b consumes a value attributable uniquely to a, and only genuinely open choices remain as LLM nodes; at runtime a router dispatches matching requests to the workflow and falls back to the general agent otherwise (line 348-352). | - | Framing statement (how the paper states its problem, challenge, objective, solution or gain); not a measurement. | line 139 of the saved text | 139 | primary | corrected by the auditor |
| 4 | framing_gain | For the one AppWorld intent compiled to an executable graph (Venmo money request, three instances of released ReAct-agent trajectories), the 34 API calls observed across the three instances compile to 11 runtime calls (3, 3, 5 per instance, counted under a warm authenticated session) with 1 residual LLM node (lines 112-113, 456, 471-472, 563-564); under leave-one-out execution against the benchmark's state tests the workflow passes 15 of 21, the failing fold escalating rather than acting (lines 113-115, 576), a score that includes hand-written argument parsing at the residual node (lines 608-612). | 1 | framing_challenge | Crawlers use state abstraction functions (a similarity function plus a threshold over URLs, text, DOM or screenshots) as a proxy for page similarity, but minimal DOM changes can create duplicate states even when not reflected visually (lines 10-14), and the amount of change in the DOM tree, text or visuals is not always directly proportional to the change in app functionality (lines 109-114); there is no generally accepted definition of near-duplicate states and no unified standard against which a technique can be assessed, and similarity thresholds are usually educated guesses because no systematic means to estimate them automatically exists (lines 29-39). | - | Framing statement (how the paper states its problem, challenge, objective, solution or gain); not a measurement. | line 29 of the saved text | 29 | primary | corrected by the auditor |
| 2 | framing_objective | Model quality is measured by F1, the harmonic mean of Pr and Re, where Pr = unique states (bins) covered by the model / total number of states in the model (lower Pr denotes greater redundancy) and Re = bins covered by the model / total bins identified by humans in the ground truth (line 487-495). For crawling, threshold selection is framed as maximizing the F1 score of a state abstraction function's distinct-pair detection (line 502-504). A state abstraction function is A = (dist, t): A(dist, p1, p2, t) = true if dist(p1, p2) < t, false otherwise (Definition 1, line 93-106). State-pair classification uses Gamma(p1, p2, f, tc, tn) = Cl if f(p1,p2) < tc, D if f(p1,p2) > tn, Nd otherwise (lines 336-360), scored by macro-averaged F1 over the three classes (lines 444-452). Thresholds: statistical pair Stc = 3rd quartile of distances on clone pairs, Stn = median distance on near-duplicate pairs (Definition 8, lines 376-379); optimal pair (Oc, On) found by Bayesian optimization maximizing the average F1 of Gamma over all three classes (Definition 9, lines 381-385); Stn3 = median distance of labelled Nd1 or Nd2 near-duplicates, i.e. Stn excluding Nd3 (Definition 10, lines 507-509). | 0 | framing_problem | The SWE-Bench Verified leaderboard appears near saturation (top system 78.80%), but the performance is inflated: about one in five 'solved' patches from the top-30 agents are semantically incorrect and pass only because weak test suites fail to expose their errors. | - | Framing statement (how the paper states its problem, challenge, objective, solution or gain); not a measurement. | line 150 of the saved text | 150 | primary | corrected by the auditor |
| 1 | framing_challenge | A mismatch in objectives: SWE-Bench tests come from development pull requests designed to verify that a specific patch passes predefined tests, not to discriminate between all correct and incorrect solutions, which creates coverage gaps (tests miss patch-affected code) and semantic blind spots (tests accept superficially correct behavior) (line 172). | - | Framing statement (how the paper states its problem, challenge, objective, solution or gain); not a measurement. | line 171 of the saved text | 171 | primary | corrected by the auditor |
| 2 | framing_objective | Goal: construct an augmented test suite T_aug that rejects incorrect patches while accepting correct alternative implementations. Each instance has issue I, gold patch P_gold and original suite T_ori = T_base ∪ T_patch (repository's existing tests and tests added in the PR). Stage I: T_cov = T_td ∪ LLM_cov(L_rel \ ∪_{t∈T_td} Cov(t)), where T_td are decoupled tests the gold patch passes, L_rel the patch-relevant lines from program slicing, Cov(t) the lines exercised by t, LLM_cov a generator for uncovered lines. Stage II: from issue-relevant mutants P_rel, P_adv^FN = {p ∈ P_rel / equiv(p) ∧ p ⊭ T_cov} and P_adv^FP = {p ∈ P_rel / ¬equiv(p) ∧ p ⊨ T_cov}; T_fn are the tests rejecting FN mutants, T'_fn = LLM_fix(T_fn, P_adv^FN), T_mut(p) = LLM_aug(p, T_cov); final T_aug = (T_cov \ T_fn) ∪ T'_fn ∪ ∪_{p∈P_adv^FP} T_mut(p). Reported metrics: Strengthened (instances where at least one previously passing patch fails), Drop (decrease in resolve rate, percentage points), Patch Kill (patches rejected), Spearman ρ between original and augmented leaderboard rankings (lines 418-422). | - | Framing statement (how the paper states its problem, challenge, objective, solution or gain); not a measurement. | line 223 of the saved text | 223 | primary | corrected by the auditor |
| 3 | framing_solution | A two-stage adversarial framework: Stage I targets coverage gaps by using program slicing to identify patch-relevant code and generating LLM tests that exercise it, decoupled from gold-patch-specific behaviors to avoid overfitting; Stage II targets semantic blind spots by synthesizing plausible-but-incorrect mutant patches with an LLM and generating adversarial tests that reject them (while generalizing tests that wrongly reject semantically equivalent mutants), mirroring red-team/blue-team dynamics (lines 182-185, 219-221, 294-308). | - | Framing statement (how the paper states its problem, challenge, objective, solution or gain); not a measurement. | line 219 of the saved text | 219 | primary | corrected by the auditor |
| 4 | framing_gain | On SWE-Bench Verified, SWE-ABS strengthens 50.2% of instances (251/500), a 25.1x improvement over the prior test-augmentation method UTBoost (10/500); relative to the original SWE-Bench Verified tests, it rejects 2,184 of 11,041 previously passing patches from the top-30 agents (19.78%), lowers the top agent from 78.80% to 62.20% (1st to 5th place), and gives an average resolve-rate drop of 14.56 percentage points with 30 rank changes. Appendix A.8 reports $4.98 vs $80.00 per strengthened instance against UTBoost (16x better cost efficiency), while cost per instance is higher ($2.50 vs $1.60). | - | Framing statement (how the paper states its problem, challenge, objective, solution or gain); not a measurement. | line 153 of the saved text | 153 | primary | corrected by the auditor |

| 1 | framing_challenge | The paper traces the three limitations to one cause: current methods give the meta-agent broad freedom to change the harness while feeding it only external outcomes and letting it revise everything at once (unrestricted edits invite overfitting, outcome-only evidence invites misattribution, simultaneous edits invite interference); it names the core challenge as the lack of structure and discipline governing the evolution process, not harness evolution itself. Alongside Pass@1 the paper reports the number of evolution Turns, 'since each turn entails evaluation of the evolved harness' (line 232). | - | Framing statement (how the paper states its problem, challenge, objective, solution or gain); not a measurement. | line 189 of the saved text | 189 | primary | corrected by the auditor |

| 1 | framing_challenge | The paper gives as a central reason for the regressions seen with distilled skills (on SkillsBench 16 of 84 tasks regress, line 109) that existing distillation pipelines treat a skill as a single unit and partition trajectories into successes and failures, which conflates repairing a bug (adding a missing step) with compressing waste (removing an expensive but inessential step); the second operation requires per-step cost, and standard observability stacks expose per-span tokens and cost only as dashboard analytics for human operators, not as a compact summary a distillation pipeline can ingest. | - | Framing statement (how the paper states its problem, challenge, objective, solution or gain); not a measurement. | line 110 of the saved text | 110 | primary | corrected by the auditor |
| 2 | framing_objective | No single optimised objective; per task the paper reports quality Q in [0,1], the fraction of rubric items satisfied (Q=1.0 every cell matches, Q=0 no scorable file), and cost, the cache-aware USD total from ClawTrace. Per-step cost (Appendix B.11, line 631/635) is cost = r_in*t_in + r_out*t_out + r_cacheRead*t_cacheRead + r_cacheWrite*t_cacheWrite, where r_* are per-token USD rates and t_* are provider-reported token counts. A held-out task regresses when Q_skill < Q_baseline - 0.01 and wins in the reverse case (line 245); regression count and quality-preservation rate are the main comparison quantities. On the SkillsBench transfer each task is graded by a Docker-contained pytest verifier with binary pass/fail; wins/regressions/ties are counted on 74 quality-gradeable pairs and the cost-decrease direction on 79 paired tasks with nonzero baseline cost (line 263). Figure 4 reports a 'quality preservation rate' per ablation condition (83.3% Full CostCraft, 53.3% No-prune) without a separate formula in the text. | - | Framing statement (how the paper states its problem, challenge, objective, solution or gain); not a measurement. | line 240 of the saved text | 240 | primary | corrected by the auditor |
| 3 | framing_solution | ClawTrace records cost-attributed traces via eight event hooks (LLM calls, tool use, sub-agent spawns; cached tokens billed at their actual rate) and compiles each session into a ~1.5 kB TraceCard listing per-step USD cost, typed token counts, redundant tool-call clusters and failed-or-repaired steps; CostCraft reads TraceCards and emits three patch types, replacing Trace2Skill's success-versus-error split with a correctness-versus-efficiency split: preserve (keep what worked), prune (drop unnecessary cost; must name a specific high-cost step and give a counterfactual) and repair (fix specific failures). | - | Framing statement (how the paper states its problem, challenge, objective, solution or gain); not a measurement. | line 112 of the saved text | 112 | primary | corrected by the auditor |
| 4 | framing_gain | On 30 held-out SpreadsheetBench tasks across two seeds, removing prune patches (No-prune ablation vs Full CostCraft) roughly tripled the quality-regression count (pooled 5 vs 14, 2.8x; seed 0: 4 vs 13, line 246/248) without lowering median cost; quality preservation is 83.3% for Full CostCraft vs 53.3% for No-prune (Figure 4). On the full 84-task SkillsBench transfer CostCraft saves no aggregate cost (median $0.143 baseline vs $0.144), with cost decreasing on 41 of 79 paired tasks; all three quality regressions trace to the preserve lane and both quality wins to the prune lane, which the paper reads as prune patches acting as quality guardrails while preserve patches drive regressions. | - | Framing statement (how the paper states its problem, challenge, objective, solution or gain); not a measurement. | line 101 of the saved text | 101 | primary | corrected by the auditor |

| 0 | framing_problem | Agent capability increasingly depends on model-external execution infrastructure (the agent harness), and changing the harness while holding weights fixed can substantially alter task performance; yet most agent evaluations select a harness and report downstream task performance, treating the harness as part of the experimental configuration rather than as an artifact to be developed, so it remains underexplored whether models can both create and continually improve runnable, persistent harnesses. | - | Framing statement (how the paper states its problem, challenge, objective, solution or gain); not a measurement. | line 150 of the saved text | 150 | primary | corrected by the auditor |
| 1 | framing_challenge | Harness engineering differs from ordinary code editing: when a model modifies its own harness it edits the execution substrate through which it observes, plans and recovers in all future tasks, so it must recognise its own behavioural limitations from execution traces, diagnose structural bottlenecks and commit changes that accumulate; evaluating a generated harness is also harder because it can overfit to the model that wrote it, memorise development examples, silently regress, or improve the feedback-set score through non-transferable changes. | - | Framing statement (how the paper states its problem, challenge, objective, solution or gain); not a measurement. | line 160 of the saved text | 160 | primary | corrected by the auditor |

For each frozen harness the paper reports two quantities (Sec. 3.5): downstream task performance under the benchmark's native metric (capability) and executor-model tokens consumed during evaluation, as total and mean per task, excluding the creator's tokens (efficiency); Evolution reports the performance change from the initial harness H_0 under the same executor and scorer. | 2 | framing_objective | J(p) = E_{x~P_X}[R(pi_theta(p), x)], the expected task reward of the target agent pi_theta(p) with fixed model parameters theta under system prompt p over tasks x drawn from P_X; prompt optimization seeks a prompt maximizing J(p). General update form p_{t+1} = Pi[p_t (+) rho(p_t, phi_t)], where rho proposes a modification from execution feedback phi_t, (+) applies it and Pi decides acceptance; search methods use phi_t = (sampled rollout batch B_t with rewards, validation estimate r_val(p) = (1//D_val/) sum_{x in D_val} R(pi_theta(p), x)), while CASD uses phi = (Phi(D), {tau_i}_{i in I(Phi)}), corpus statistics Phi over the rollout corpus D = {tau_i}_{i=1}^N and an index set I of representative trajectories; p* = CASD(D, p_0). Reported metrics: ALFWorld win rate, tau^2 pass@1, SSB modified accuracy, and optimizer cost in USD; in the ablation (Table 4, lines 334-337) 'Rec.' = fraction of the no-think -> think accuracy gap recovered by the skill and 'tok' = mean output tokens per episode. | 1 | framing_challenge | Current research relies on manually designed, task-specific agentic systems that depend on expert insight and intensive human labor and struggle to adapt to novel tasks; prior automatic approaches (LLM prompt rewriting such as OPRO/Promptbreeder, and ADAS search of whole agentic systems in code space) are limited in their ability to explicitly recombine the strengths of agentic modules discovered by different researches and located in separate codebases. Solving MoLAS has three named challenges: (1) the search space, the Cartesian product of four orthogonal modules, is vast and hard to explore; (2) the module sets encompass any code with standard IO interfaces, making module selection open-ended; (3) the high costs of agent evaluation during the search process constrain the overall search scale, since many agent tasks require multiple steps and substantial input and output tokens (evaluating a simple CoT agent based on GPT-4o in ALFWorld requires around $60, making agent search economically unsustainable at scale). | - | Framing statement (how the paper states its problem, challenge, objective, solution or gain); not a measurement. | line 135 of the saved text | 135 | primary | corrected by the auditor |

| 0 | framing_problem | Adaptive reuse of a held-out benchmark should in principle invite overfitting, yet benchmark-driven ML shows surprisingly little; the paper asks what keeps ordinary ML research (here, an LLM research agent's iterative loop) from this worst-case overfitting, i.e. what keeps the gap between population and validation risk small, and how to test it directly, via the hypothesis that successful ML strategies are highly compressible. | - | Framing statement (how the paper states its problem, challenge, objective, solution or gain); not a measurement. | line 93 of the saved text | 93 | primary | corrected by the auditor |
| 1 | framing_challenge | In the research loop the explorer queries the validation set T times and chooses what to try next from the responses, so its final model depends adaptively on D_val; it may achieve low validation loss by tuning, implicitly or explicitly, to the specific samples in D_val rather than by finding a model that generalizes (the pathology known as data dredging or p-hacking). | - | Framing statement (how the paper states its problem, challenge, objective, solution or gain); not a measurement. | line 112 of the saved text | 112 | primary | corrected by the auditor |
| 2 | framing_objective | The quantity studied is the gap R(ĥ) - R̂_Dval(ĥ), where R(h) = E_(x,y)~P[ℓ(h(x),y)] is the true risk (population loss) of hypothesis h, R̂_Dval is the validation risk and ĥ is the best model reported after T adaptive queries (line 108-110). Bounds: Theorem 1, with probability at least 1-δ over D_val, sup over m in M of /R̂_Dval(h_m) - R(h_m)/ <= sqrt(log(2/M//δ)/(2n)) for a finite description set M fixed before seeing D_val, fixed decoder Φ, loss ℓ in [0,1], n validation samples (line 159); Corollary 2 (output compression, message m of at most B tokens from vocabulary V, bound on the reproducer's hypothesis h_m): <= sqrt(((B+1) ln/V/ + ln(2/δ))/(2n)) (line 167); Corollary 3 (ladder, bound on the explorer's running-best model at each improvement checkpoint j): ε_j = sqrt(ln(2N_j/δ_j)/(2n)) = O(sqrt((j log T_max + log(1/δ_j))/n)) with N_j = C(T_max - 1, j - 1) and sum_j δ_j <= δ (lines 174-180); with K_max=7, T_max=50, n=5,000, δ=0.05, ε_1 ≈ 2.4 pp and ε_7 ≈ 4.7 pp (line 182). Empirical metrics per dataset (Table 1, lines 187-238): accuracy, MSE, log-loss or bits per byte on validation and a post hoc holdout. Output compression compares the reproducer's validation metric with the explorer's (lines 243, 254); a compression certificate fails when the explorer's validation metric beats the reproducer's by more than 5% relative, and a checkpoint is labelled overfitting when the explorer's validation metric beats its holdout metric by more than 10% relative (line 939). The ladder explorer is compared with the score-based explorer on holdout performance (line 257). | - | Framing statement (how the paper states its problem, challenge, objective, solution or gain); not a measurement. | line 108 of the saved text | 108 | primary | corrected by the auditor |
| 3 | framing_solution | Compressible hypotheses generalize: the paper places an explicit bottleneck on the validation-set channel, either on the output side (a compressor distils the explorer's strategy into a short prompt m of at most B tokens, and a fresh, reset reproducer receives only m and the training data) or on the input side (the explorer receives only one-bit 'improved / not improved' ladder feedback), so the final model depends on D_val only through a short description and a Hoeffding-plus-union-bound guarantee applies (Theorem 1). The output-compression bound constrains only the reproducer's hypothesis, while the ladder bound constrains the explorer's own running-best models (lines 169, 182, 271); the bottlenecks serve as an empirical probe of why benchmark reuse generalizes and as a falsifiable test for validation-set exploitation (line 104). | - | Framing statement (how the paper states its problem, challenge, objective, solution or gain); not a measurement. | line 97 of the saved text | 97 | primary | corrected by the auditor |
| 4 | framing_gain | Against the uncompressed, score-based explorer across 8 datasets, both bottlenecks preserve performance: 32-token prompts largely reproduce the explorer's adaptively optimized performance (32-token reproducers match or exceed the explorer under a one-sided 5% relative-gap criterion on 38 of 41 improvement checkpoints, 92.7%; line 254), and one-bit ladder feedback matches or slightly exceeds full numerical score feedback on holdout performance on all 8 datasets (lines 100, 257). When overfitting is deliberately induced (aggressive prompting and sample-level validation access; 38 of 102 checkpoints with a validation metric more than 10% better than holdout), failure to reproduce from a 128-token prompt flags all 38 overfitting checkpoints and 6 of the 64 others, i.e. 100% sensitivity and 91% specificity (lines 102, 263-264). | - | Framing statement (how the paper states its problem, challenge, objective, solution or gain); not a measurement. | line 100 of the saved text | 100 | primary | corrected by the auditor |

| 1 | framing_challenge | The estimation problem is sequential and adaptive: as participants repeatedly evaluate submissions on the leaderboard they may begin to overfit to the holdout data, because feedback from the leaderboard incorporated into classifier design creates a dependence between classifier and evaluation data, in which case the holdout no longer gives an unbiased estimate of true performance; few theoretical results give actionable advice, existing approaches resort to poorly understood heuristics (limiting the bit precision of answers and the rate of re-submission), and recent results suggest that accurate estimates on a sequence of many adaptively chosen classifiers may be computationally intractable. | - | Framing statement (how the paper states its problem, challenge, objective, solution or gain); not a measurement. | line 46 of the saved text | 46 | primary | corrected by the auditor |
| 2 | framing_objective | Minimise the leaderboard error (Definition 2.1, eq. 3): lberr(R_1,...,R_k) = max_{1<=t<=k} / min_{1<=i<=t} R_D(f_i) - R_t /, where f_1,...,f_k is an adaptively chosen sequence of submitted classifiers (f_t = A(f_1,R_1,...,f_{t-1},R_{t-1}) for an analyst A), R_t is the estimate released at step t, and R_D(f) = E_{(x,y)~D}[l(f(x),y)] is the true loss of f under the unknown distribution D with a bounded loss l: Y x Y -> [0,1]. The goal is that at each step the leaderboard reflects the minimum true loss of any classifier submitted so far. Theorem 3.1 gives lberr <= O(log^{1/3}(kn)/n^{1/3}) with high probability for step size eta = O(n^{-1/3} log^{1/3}(kn)), where n is the size of the holdout sample S. | - | Framing statement (how the paper states its problem, challenge, objective, solution or gain); not a measurement. | line 298 of the saved text | 298 | primary | corrected by the auditor |
| 3 | framing_solution | The Ladder mechanism compares each submission's empirical loss with the previous best and releases a new estimate (rounded to the nearest multiple of eta) only if it is below the previous best by a margin eta; otherwise it releases the previous best loss. It thus only releases a score if it presents a statistically significant improvement over the participant's previous best, which intuitively prevents exploiting or overfitting to minor fluctuations in observed scores. A parameter-free variant sets the margin adaptively via a one-sided paired t-test against the loss vector of the previous best submission (threshold s/sqrt(n)), needing no tuning; the authors call this use of the test primarily heuristic. | - | Framing statement (how the paper states its problem, challenge, objective, solution or gain); not a measurement. | line 165 of the saved text | 165 | primary | corrected by the auditor |
| 4 | framing_gain | Theoretical: in a fully adaptive model with no limit on submissions, the Ladder's maximum error on any estimate is never worse than O((log(k)/n)^{1/3}) (k submissions, n holdout size), whereas the error of the Kaggle mechanism (and similar solutions) scales with the number of submissions as sqrt(k), i.e. an exponential improvement in k; a lower bound shows no estimator can beat Omega((log(k)/n)^{1/2}). Empirical: under a boosting attack the Kaggle mechanism's accuracy diminishes rapidly with the number of submissions while the Ladder encounters only a small bias; on 1,785 real submissions from Kaggle's Photo Quality Prediction challenge the parameter-free Ladder produces a leaderboard very close to Kaggle's, with differences the authors assess as not statistically significant. | - | Framing statement (how the paper states its problem, challenge, objective, solution or gain); not a measurement. | line 133 of the saved text | 133 | primary | corrected by the auditor |

| 1 | framing_challenge | LLMs confidently answer any question and readily provide palatable natural-language explanations without guarantees of correctness or faithfulness (lines 61, 64); reasoning traces are often interpreted as provenance explanations despite evidence that they are neither faithful representations of the model's computations nor necessarily semantically meaningful (lines 54, 65); and in typical studies users who can verify the answer themselves are not dependent on the explanation, making it extremely difficult to isolate the explanation's effect on trust (lines 68, 89). | - | Framing statement (how the paper states its problem, challenge, objective, solution or gain); not a measurement. | line 64 of the saved text | 64 | primary | corrected by the auditor |

| 1 | framing_challenge | Grader prompts are unintuitively sensitive to seemingly minor changes in wording or structure (line 92), and a human cannot completely validate an LLM evaluator: the point of LLM evaluators is to reduce developer effort, and the only way to fully align one would be to ask the user to label all outputs, which defeats the purpose (line 133); the user study further finds 'criteria drift' (users need criteria to grade outputs, but grading outputs helps them define criteria), which implies it is impossible to completely determine evaluation criteria prior to human judging of LLM outputs (line 95). | - | Framing statement (how the paper states its problem, challenge, objective, solution or gain); not a measurement. | line 133 of the saved text | 133 | primary | corrected by the auditor |
| 2 | framing_objective | Per criterion, EvalGen selects the candidate assertion with the highest alignment with user grades. - Source: https://web.archive.org/web/20260324203141id_/https://dl.acm.org/doi/pdf/10.1145/3613904.3641960 · version read: ACM Digital Library PDF (version of record, 21 paper pages plus the ACM cover page stamped 'PDF Download ... 24 March 2026'), retrieved from the Wayback Machin… · v1: 2024-05-11

| 0 | framing_problem | LLM-generated annotations are cheaper and faster to obtain but often erroneous for complex or domain-specific tasks and may introduce bias, so LLMs cannot fully replace human annotators; the paper seeks a human-LLM collaborative annotation process that ensures accuracy and reliability of labels while keeping the cost advantage. | - | Framing statement (how the paper states its problem, challenge, objective, solution or gain); not a measurement. | line 73 of the saved text | 73 | primary | corrected by the auditor |
| 1 | framing_challenge | Having humans examine all LLM-generated labels would sacrifice the scalability and cost reduction of using LLMs for annotation, so a subset of potentially erroneous labels must be identified for human re-annotation (lines 282-290); the two common LLM uncertainty measures (self-evaluation / verbal certainty, and consistency across prompt formats) may not work well in this setting because LLMs tend to be over-confident and the predicted label is pretty consistent for classification tasks (lines 293-299); and training a verifier needs gold labels, while using thousands of them would be contrary to the goal of generating annotations cheaper and faster (lines 275-278). | - | Framing statement (how the paper states its problem, challenge, objective, solution or gain); not a measurement. | line 284 of the saved text | 284 | primary | corrected by the auditor |
| 2 | framing_objective | The verifier is a binary classifier P_theta(v / x, y_hat, e_hat), where x is the text input, y_hat the LLM label, e_hat the LLM explanation, and v = 1(y_hat = y*) is 1 when the LLM label equals the gold label y*; examples are ranked by P_theta and the bottom instances (by threshold or fixed count) are sent to humans. Reported targets: verifier 'accuracy' on the bottom 100/200/300 (and bottom-quantile) instances, overall dataset accuracy after re-annotation vs percentage re-annotated, and accuracy vs total annotation cost, where verifier cost = $1.1 x number of gold labels for training (+ LLM inference cost for a transfer dataset) and human re-annotation cost = $1.1 x number of re-annotations (LLM inference cost is identical across verifiers and ignored). | - | Framing statement (how the paper states its problem, challenge, objective, solution or gain); not a measurement. | line 319 of the saved text | 319 | primary | corrected by the auditor |
| 3 | framing_solution | A three-step framework: the LLM labels and explains each instance, a cheaply trained verifier (random forest, SVM or BERT on features of the input, the LLM label and the LLM explanation, trained on a few hundred gold labels or a related dataset) scores label quality, and only the lowest-scored labels go to human re-annotation, which avoids wasting human effort on already-correct labels; a crowdsourced study tests whether showing LLM labels and explanations helps re-annotators. | - | Framing statement (how the paper states its problem, challenge, objective, solution or gain); not a measurement. | line 307 of the saved text | 307 | primary | corrected by the auditor |
| 4 | framing_gain | Trained verifiers identify wrong LLM labels more accurately than baseline verifiers that use GPT's first-token logit or entropy, 'especially for the worst annotations in the bottom 5% or 10%' (lines 525-528; e.g. SNLI bottom-100 accuracy 0.85 Combined vs 0.44 BV-l, Table 4 line 511), although Trans does poorly on hate speech (HateXplain bottom-100 0.32 vs 0.50 BV-l) and the SBIC margin is small (Self 0.59 vs 0.54). Assuming oracle re-annotation, the verifiers 'can potentially' improve overall accuracy on all test examples by at least 10% while re-annotating only 15% of labels, a large margin over the baseline verifier in 4 of 6 datasets (lines 544-548). | 1 | framing_challenge | Test suites are generally too weak to fully specify correct behaviour, so a patch passing all tests may still be incorrect (overfitting); researchers therefore fall back on manual assessment, which has three major problems: difficulty (analysts may not understand the program), bias (analysts are often the authors of the repair system) and scale (dozens of patches per bug; e.g. 66,596 test-suite adequate patches cannot be assessed manually in a reasonable amount of time). | - | Framing statement (how the paper states its problem, challenge, objective, solution or gain); not a measurement. | line 93 of the saved text | 93 | primary | corrected by the auditor |
| 2 | framing_objective | None stated as a formula. RGT decision rule: if a ground truth patch passes all RGT tests but an APR patch fails any of them, the APR patch is assessed as overfitting, otherwise correct (Algorithm 1: machine patch set P, ground truth patch set G, RGT test set T; FT_i = failing tests of machine patch p_mi). Reported targets: number/share of patches in D_overfitting (patches manually labelled overfitting in prior work) that RGT identifies as overfitting, false positive rate on D_correct (patches claimed correct by their authors), and time cost split into TCGen (test case generation), SC (sanity check) and EXEC (executing tests over APR patches) (lines 497-499). | - | Framing statement (how the paper states its problem, challenge, objective, solution or gain); not a measurement. | line 366 of the saved text | 366 | primary | corrected by the auditor |
| 3 | framing_solution | Generate regression tests (Evosuite, Randoop) on the human-written patched program so that its runtime behaviour becomes the oracle; any generated test that fails on a machine patch witnesses a behavioural difference and marks the patch overfitting. The oracle is improved by also counting exception-related differences (not only assertion value differences as in DiffTGen), and flaky tests are removed by a sanity check run three times on the ground-truth program. | - | Framing statement (how the paper states its problem, challenge, objective, solution or gain); not a measurement. | line 111 of the saved text | 111 | primary | corrected by the auditor |
| 4 | framing_gain | On the 381 D_overfitting patches (manually labelled overfitting in prior work), RGT (Evosuite + Randoop together) identifies 274 as overfitting versus 143 for the state-of-the-art DiffTGen, reported as '190%' improvement (274/143 = 1.92x, calc.); on the 257 D_correct patches (claimed correct by their authors) RGT finds 10 (out of the 97 assessed as semantically equivalent) that are actually overfitting, confirmed by the original authors, with a false positive rate of 6/257 = 2.3%. On time, over 87% of RGT time is test generation; newly generated tests need 14.5 (Evosuite) and 11.76 (Randoop) minutes per patch, versus 2.4 minutes per patch on average when reusing previously generated RGT tests, which however identify 219/381 overfitting patches (80% of the 274 found with new tests). | - | Framing statement (how the paper states its problem, challenge, objective, solution or gain); not a measurement. | line 1279 of the saved text | 1279 | primary | corrected by the auditor |

| 1 | framing_challenge | Agents have amnesia because most LLMs are stateless; they lack systematic mechanisms to learn from their execution experiences (line 74). Extracting actionable learnings from trajectories is non-trivial: valuable patterns exist across clean successes, inefficient successes, failure-then-recovery sequences and complete failures; causality is often non-obvious from raw logs (a failure at step 15 may stem from a decision at step 3); and learnings must be contextually retrieved, actionable and specific, and traceable to their source (lines 92-97). Existing approaches fall short (lines 107-111): rule-based systems cannot adapt to unforeseen situations and need constant manual maintenance; prompt engineering is generic and has no mechanism for automatic improvement from observed outcomes; generic memory systems (Mem0, Letta) lack understanding of execution patterns, causal analysis, structured learning extraction and provenance; RL needs extensive training data, is computationally expensive to train and update, and offers limited interpretability. | - | Framing statement (how the paper states its problem, challenge, objective, solution or gain); not a measurement. | line 74 of the saved text | 74 | primary | corrected by the auditor |

Delayed credit measures an action's association with downstream progress but does not establish whether the action produces a state fact required later; across episodic, reflective, workflow and graph memories, the paper names the common missing element as a fact-grounded criterion that separates historical association with success from procedural necessity. | - | Framing statement (how the paper states its problem, challenge, objective, solution or gain); not a measurement. | line 73 of the saved text | 73 | primary | corrected by the auditor |

| 0 | framing_problem | Software systems that depend on commercial LLM APIs must migrate to successor versions when vendors deprecate older models, and migration decisions typically rely on aggregate benchmark scores that compress heterogeneous item-level behaviour into a single net figure; the paper asks whether aggregate benchmark scores reliably reflect the backward compatibility of commercial LLM API upgrades and measures what that compression conceals. | - | Framing statement (how the paper states its problem, challenge, objective, solution or gain); not a measurement. | line 91 of the saved text | 91 | primary | corrected by the auditor |
| 1 | framing_challenge | Standard benchmark reporting compresses item-level behaviour into aggregate scores, so a net gain (e.g. two points) may consist of items answered more reliably and items answered less reliably; in addition, because LLM outputs are stochastic, a single correct-to-incorrect flip between two model versions may reflect sampling noise alone. The paper cites Ma et al. for non-determinism as one of three obstacles to applying regression testing to LLM APIs, alongside vendor-controlled updates and prompt sensitivity (related work). | - | Framing statement (how the paper states its problem, challenge, objective, solution or gain); not a measurement. | line 68 of the saved text | 68 | primary | corrected by the auditor |
| 2 | framing_objective | Per migration edge (source model s to target t) and benchmark: aggregate change Δ = mean_i(p̂_{t,i}) − mean_i(p̂_{s,i}), where p̂_{m,i} is the fraction of the K=50 trials of item i under model m scored correct under the strict rule; reliable-improvement share P^+, reliable-regression share P^−, reliable-change share P^chg = P^+ + P^−. An item is reliably improved or regressed (by sign) when a Fisher exact test on the 2×K correct/incorrect counts is significant under Benjamini–Hochberg FDR control at 5% within each migration–benchmark cell and /p̂_{t,i} − p̂_{s,i}/ ≥ ε with ε = 0.2; items whose 95% confidence interval for the difference lies entirely within (−ε, ε) are practically equivalent and the rest inconclusive; shares are compared against the 95th percentile of a 1,000-replication label-permutation null. | 1 | framing_challenge | The execution of a complete task requires the collaborative operation of multiple models (Planner 4B, Decider 7B, Grounder 3B), and experiences recorded at different levels trade off: lower-level experiences (Grounder actions) can be executed with higher efficiency but typically generalize weakly, while higher-level ones (Planner plans) generalize better but are less efficient to execute because they still require model inference; a key challenge when accelerating with AgentRR is determining how many prefix actions can be reused. For evaluation, variable environmental factors, multiple correct trajectories and the lack of deterministic verification make it hard for current benchmark frameworks to give accurate assessments. | - | Framing statement (how the paper states its problem, challenge, objective, solution or gain); not a measurement. | line 150 of the saved text | 150 | primary | corrected by the auditor |
| 2 | framing_objective | No explicit end-to-end acceleration objective; the reported targets are MobiFlow task completion scores (a task that completes all DAG milestone events gets the full score, a subset may get partial credit by user-defined criteria, and a termination penalty is imposed on tasks the agent cannot complete or exit), and for AgentRR the action replay rate, replay correctness and speedup, with the acceleration ratio stated to be positively correlated with the proportion of ActTree nodes that can be reused. Written formulas for the acceleration component: reuse decisions Embed-Reuse^(l)(T_i,T_j) = True iff S(v_i^(l), v_j^(l)) ≥ τ1, where v_i^(l) = f(T_i,l) is an instruction-aware task embedding for ActTree layer l and S is cosine similarity; candidate set C = {T ∈ T_hist / Embed-Reuse^(l)(T,T_c)} over historical tasks on the current node's outgoing edges; Rerank-Reuse^(l) = True iff some T_i ∈ C has reranker score g(T_i,T_c,l) ≥ τ2. The embedding model is trained with InfoNCE L = E_v[−ln(e^{S(v,v+)/τ} / (e^{S(v,v+)/τ} + Σ_{j=1}^{M} e^{S(v,v_j^−)/τ}))], positives sharing an action prefix of length ≥ l (pre(T_s,T_i) ≥ l) and negatives < l; the reranker is trained with SFT on yes/no labels. Training rewards: grounder GRPO reward R = R_iou + R_center, where R_iou = α if IoU(b_pred, b_gt) > β else 0 and R_center = 1 − α if Center(b_pred) is inside b_gt else 0 (b_pred, b_gt predicted and ground-truth bounding boxes, α, β hyperparameters); decider reward R = R_content = 1 if a_pred = a_gt else 0 for non-click actions, and R = R_center (grounder as reward model) for clicks. | - | Framing statement (how the paper states its problem, challenge, objective, solution or gain); not a measurement. | line 338 of the saved text | 338 | primary | corrected by the auditor |
| 3 | framing_solution | AgentRR exploits prefix reusability of GUI tasks (similar tasks share identical trajectory prefixes, predictable from task-description similarity): trajectories are cached in an ActTree, a lightweight latent memory model (task embedding and reranking) decides whether a cached action can be reused, and on a cache hit the action is replayed without invoking the agent model, reducing end-to-end latency. | - | Framing statement (how the paper states its problem, challenge, objective, solution or gain); not a measurement. | line 163 of the saved text | 163 | primary | corrected by the auditor |

| 1 | framing_challenge | The paper names four causes: LLM agents often hallucinate because of the probabilistic nature of LLMs (reliability); cloud-hosted agents require sending personal or sensitive data to remote servers (privacy); sophisticated tasks typically demand multiple turns of interaction between the agent and the LLM, with vision-language model calls costlier than text (cost); and complex multi-step tasks are often bottlenecked by the LLM's inference speed and the overhead of iterative prompt exchanges (performance). Distilled or pruned lightweight models cannot adapt when tasks or requirements change, and in record-and-replay, precise replay lowers success rate and generalization when environments and tasks change, while generalized experiences bring reliability problems (an experience that is too abstract can lead the replaying agent to instantiate incorrect details, one that is too concrete is hard to reuse). | - | Framing statement (how the paper states its problem, challenge, objective, solution or gain); not a measurement. | line 96 of the saved text | 96 | primary | corrected by the auditor |
