- Source: https://arxiv.org/html/2110.14043v2 · version read: v2 · v1: 2021-10-26
- Source class: top venue · formal venue (confirmed at the official source): IEEE Transactions on Software Engineering, vol. 49, no. 3, pp. 1086-1101, March 2023 (journal article; early access 2022; also presented in the ICSE 2023 Journal-First Papers track)
- Audit: usable-after-fixes; 6 items kept, 0 dropped

| # | Field | Claim | Figure | Measurement definition | Location | Line | Label | Audit |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 0 | framing_problem | Model-based test generation is proposed as an alternative to costly manual regression test creation for web apps, but existing model inference techniques rely on threshold-based whole-page comparison to decide state equivalence, which cannot reliably identify near-duplicate pages; they therefore infer inadequate models of dynamic web apps and fragile test oracles, making the generated regression suites ineffective. | - | Framing statement (how the paper states its problem, challenge, objective, solution or gain); not a measurement. | line 61 of the saved text | 61 | primary | corrected by the auditor |
| 1 | framing_challenge | The main challenge named is the presence of a large number of near-duplicate web pages that whole-page state abstraction functions (a distance function plus a manually chosen threshold) cannot identify: a high threshold drops distinct states (incomplete model), a low one keeps near-duplicates (imprecise model); near-duplicates cause redundant test cases and wasted exploration effort on already-seen functionality, and whole-page oracles break on minor non-functional changes (false-positive failures). The root cause identified is duplicated functionality within a page (Nd3-struct near-duplicates). | - | Framing statement (how the paper states its problem, challenge, objective, solution or gain); not a measurement. | line 168 of the saved text | 168 | primary | corrected by the auditor |
| 2 | framing_objective | No single optimisation objective; evaluation targets are (RQ1) the multi-class classification F1 averaged over clone, near-duplicate and distinct classes plus the number of detected near-duplicates; (RQ2) model quality against a ground-truth model, with Pr = covered ground-truth states / total states in the inferred model and Re = covered ground-truth states / total ground-truth states (and F1); (RQ3) test breakages / successful test actions and mutation-analysis detection of changes. Exploration itself is driven by Eq. 2-3: score(alpha) = -1 if alpha is explored, 0 if an equivalent actionable alpha_eq is explored, otherwise c_0 * size({alpha_eq ...}) with 0 < c_0 <= 1 (default 1); score(S) = sum of score(alpha) over the actionables of state S, and the next state/actionable with the highest score is explored. | - | Framing statement (how the paper states its problem, challenge, objective, solution or gain); not a measurement. | line 758 of the saved text | 758 | primary | corrected by the auditor |
| 3 | framing_solution | Treat a web page not as a single functional entity but as a hierarchy of fragments (VIPS segmentation); classify state pairs by comparing fragments structurally (APTED on pruned DOM subtrees) and visually (colour histogram) without thresholds, discard clone/Nd2-data states, de-prioritise actionables equivalent to already explored ones so exploration is diversified toward unique fragments, and generate fragment-level assertions with memoised data-fluid fragments so oracles tolerate non-functional changes. | - | Framing statement (how the paper states its problem, challenge, objective, solution or gain); not a measurement. | line 273 of the saved text | 273 | primary | corrected by the auditor |
| 4 | framing_gain | Against whole-page structural and visual state-comparison techniques: on 86,165 labelled state pairs FragGen detects 123% more near-duplicates on average; its crawl models have higher precision and recall (abstract: 62% more precision, 70% more recall; results: 79% precision, 83% recall, F1 0.80 vs 0.47 and 0.46); its test actions succeed nearly 100% on the same app version (introduction: existing techniques' suites have nearly 17% of test actions failing on the same version; results: whole-page techniques' test actions succeed 86.2% on average) and its oracles detect 98.7% of visible changes while ignoring 90.6% of equivalent mutants. | - | Framing statement (how the paper states its problem, challenge, objective, solution or gain); not a measurement. | line 67 of the saved text | 67 | primary | corrected by the auditor |
| 5 | framing_classification | Classification by the extractor, checked by the auditor: efficiency in the stated problem = secondary; efficiency terms = costly manual test creation and test maintenance cost (motivation; an Accenture study is cited for $120 million per year of test repair), wasted / redundant exploration effort, discover unique states faster, exploration time limit as stopping criterion (maximum exploration time of 1 hour; 60 minute crawls), memoization to improve the performance of the recursive Classify function, costly manual analysis of false-positive test failures (line 262); fewer false positives reduce the manual effort needed to identify app changes (lines 887, 917); agent kind = automated model-based test generation for web apps: a crawler (FragGen, built on Crawljax) that triggers events on actionables to infer a graph-based state-transition model of the web app and derives regression test cases with assertions from its paths; no LLM or learned agent is involved; position = other (state abstraction and exploration strategy inside a web-app crawler that infers an app model for regression test generation). | - | Reader classification (not a statement of the paper). | whole abstract and introduction |  | secondary | corrected by the auditor |

The natural-language routines of AWM and ICAL pose challenges for formal verification and precise composition, and both methods rely on test queries (online) or high-quality annotated demonstrations (offline). | - | Framing statement (how the paper states its problem, challenge, objective, solution or gain); not a measurement. | line 122 of the saved text | 122 | primary | corrected by the auditor |

| 0 | framing_problem | Automated agent design improves agent harnesses through iterative revision, evaluation and feedback summarization, but existing methods are candidate-centric, leaving repair progress implicit; this causes inefficient repair targeting, slow consolidation of partial progress, and propagation of ineffective interventions across rounds. | - | Framing statement (how the paper states its problem, challenge, objective, solution or gain); not a measurement. | line 67 of the saved text | 67 | primary | corrected by the auditor |
| 1 | framing_challenge | Organizing cross-round experience around candidates makes repair progress implicit: evidence about each issue is scattered across candidate records, so the optimizer must reconstruct the repair context before each revision; because each candidate is evaluated as a whole, the outcome of a particular intervention is difficult to isolate; and beneficial and harmful changes remain entangled. Realizing issue-centric optimization raises two key challenges: reliable issue-state maintenance (turning heterogeneous trajectories and sparse outcomes into stable, evidence-grounded issue identities and tracking their repair progress) and actionable, attributable revision (turning a multi-issue descriptive state into a focused code modification). Appendix A adds that interactive settings have a larger, task-dependent design space, sparse, delayed and hard-to-attribute feedback, and expensive evaluation, since each candidate needs environment rollouts that may require extensive model calls and interaction steps. | - | Framing statement (how the paper states its problem, challenge, objective, solution or gain); not a measurement. | line 78 of the saved text | 78 | primary | corrected by the auditor |
| 2 | framing_objective | For a fixed task environment, evaluator and backbone, with an optimization budget of T rounds, the system proposes candidates A_t, evaluates validation performance M_val(A_t), selects the best-validation candidate among A_0..A_T, and 'the objective is to achieve high test performance M_test'. Candidate-centric methods use A_{t+1} = argmax_{A∈Propose(H_t)} J_cand(A), where H_t holds candidates, trajectories, metrics M and diagnostic reports D, and J_cand estimates aggregate candidate quality; ADIAS uses A_{t+1} = argmax_{A∈Propose(H_t,E_t)} J_issue(A;E_t), with E_t the persistent issue state and J_issue the expected repair progress on unresolved issues, and E_{t+1} = UpdateIssueState(E_t, H_{t+1}). Reported: Score (success rate, or mean normalized native score r_i for WebShop/ScienceWorld; Eq. 15), interaction efficiency Eff. = Score / L̄ with L̄ the average number of environment interaction steps (Eq. 16), optimization efficiency as the best-so-far validation score B_t = max_{1≤j≤t} V_j (Eq. 17), and optimization stability as the cumulative average validation score V̄_t (Eq. 18). | - | Framing statement (how the paper states its problem, challenge, objective, solution or gain); not a measurement. | line 101 of the saved text | 101 | primary | corrected by the auditor |

| 2 | framing_objective | Multi-step KL-regularized RL objective E_{pi_theta, env}[ sum_t r(a_t, h_t) ] - beta D_KL[ pi_theta(a_t/h_t) // pi_ref(a_t/h_t) ] (Eq. 3), where pi_theta is the LLM policy, a_t the composite step action (plan/thought/environment/explanation), h_t the agent history (actions so far plus current browser state), r the reward (sparse 1/0 success/failure, discount gamma = 1), env the external environment, pi_ref a reference policy (usually the initial model) and beta the KL weight. It is optimized with step-level DPO (Eq. 5) on preference pairs from MCTS whose action values are Q = alpha * Q_tilde + (1 - alpha) * Q_hat (Eq. 10), Q_tilde being the empirical MCTS value and Q_hat the value from the AI critic's ranking; pairs are kept when /Q(h_t,a_w) - Q(h_t,a_l)/ >= theta_threshold. The DPO loss (Eq. 5) is L_DPO(pi_theta; D) = -E_{(h, a^w, a^l) ~ D}[log sigma(beta log(pi_theta(a^w/h^w)/pi_ref(a^w/h^w)) - beta log(pi_theta(a^l/h^l)/pi_ref(a^l/h^l)))], with a^w preferred over a^l; Theorem 1 states that under preferences p(a^w > a^l / h_t) proportional to sigma(Q(h_t,a^w) - Q(h_t,a^l)) the DPO optimum equals the optimal RL policy pi*(a/h_t) proportional to pi_ref(a/h_t) exp(Q(h_t,a)/beta) (Eq. 9). | 0 | framing_problem | Self-improving agents rely on self-authored tests or metrics to accept their own edits while controlling both the optimised object and its verifier, so self-assigned scores can stay near perfect while real deployment performance degrades or stays low; the paper studies this as the verifier-deployment gap. | - | Framing statement (how the paper states its problem, challenge, objective, solution or gain); not a measurement. | line 44 of the saved text | 44 | primary | corrected by the auditor |
| 1 | framing_challenge | A structural conflict of interest: the agent can alter both the policy being optimised and the measuring instrument used to judge it, so passing verification may reflect an easier sample distribution, a more local metric or tests sharing the policy's mistaken assumption; formally, no endogenous-only gate can make both false-acceptance and false-rejection small when agent-visible evidence cannot distinguish regressing from non-regressing candidates. | - | Framing statement (how the paper states its problem, challenge, objective, solution or gain); not a measurement. | line 62 of the saved text | 62 | primary | corrected by the auditor |
| 2 | framing_objective | Primary outcome is deployment truth of the accepted policy after round 10: Y_D(pi) = E[Score(Rollout(pi; D))], the true performance under target distribution D measured by an agent-hidden evaluation; the verifier-deployment gap is present when the self-report r_t = V_{T'_t}(pi'_t) (score of candidate tests T'_t on candidate policy pi'_t) stays high while Y_D(pi_t) is low, decreasing or unable to recover. SEAL's acceptance rule accepts a candidate iff c_t >= b_t - delta_t, with b_t = A(pi_t), c_t = A(pi'_t) the sealed audit scores of incumbent and candidate and delta_t = max(delta_min, rho/b_t/) the slack (rho relative slack ratio, delta_min minimum absolute slack). | - | Framing statement (how the paper states its problem, challenge, objective, solution or gain); not a measurement. | line 136 of the saved text | 136 | primary | corrected by the auditor |
| 3 | framing_solution | SEAL keeps the agent's self-authored tests but places a fixed harness-side audit on hidden instances outside the agent's control before deployment: the agent cannot author or inspect it, receives only an accept/reject bit, and the whole incumbent policy-test state is retained after a clear regression, supplying the external acceptance boundary that endogenous verification lacks. | - | Framing statement (how the paper states its problem, challenge, objective, solution or gain); not a measurement. | line 47 of the saved text | 47 | primary | corrected by the auditor |
| 4 | framing_gain | Final deployment truth (and retention of discovered behaviour) versus unprotected self-authored verification: SEAL outperforms unprotected baselines across six models and three seeds; at equal proposal count on Breakout it improves mean final truth by 7.7 and cuts mean peak-to-final loss from 6.9 to 0.4, and across 12 model-game comparisons it is equal or better in 11. | - | Framing statement (how the paper states its problem, challenge, objective, solution or gain); not a measurement. | line 50 of the saved text | 50 | primary | corrected by the auditor |

| 1 | framing_challenge | Failures cluster at a small slice of mutating (environment-changing) steps: deviations in mutating actions are the decisive predictors of failure while non-mutating deviations matter little, yet current frameworks treat all decision steps uniformly; errors also grow with context length as agents drift from role and over-trust stale tokens ('lost-in-the-middle'). Separately, τ-Bench annotation errors and under-specified instructions cap attainable performance. | - | Framing statement (how the paper states its problem, challenge, objective, solution or gain); not a measurement. | line 1061 of the saved text | 1061 | primary | corrected by the auditor |
| 2 | framing_objective | Reduce the probability of decisive deviations Pr[Δ_t^+ = 1]. Definitions: trajectory τ = (s_0, a_0, s_1, a_1, …, s_T) in system M = ⟨S, A, P⟩ with transition law P(s_{t+1} / s_t, a_t); Z(τ) ∈ {0,1} is the failure indicator (1 = failure); τ* is a successful reference trajectory, τ′ a candidate diverging first at index t with extra action ã_t; Δ_t^+(τ′, τ*) = 1 if Z(τ*) = 0 and Z(τ′) = 1, else 0. Hypothesis (Eq. 3): P(Δ_t^+ = 1 / ã_t ∈ A^mut) ≫ P(Δ_t^+ = 1 / ã_t ∈ A^non), with A^mut the actions that change the external environment or user-visible state and A^non = A \ A^mut. Dataset-level test: M(τ) and N(τ) count mutating and non-mutating actions; d_mut = /M(τ′) − M(τ*)/, d_non = /N(τ′) − N(τ*)/, regressed (logistic) against success. | 3 | framing_solution | SABER is a model-agnostic, gradient-free, test-time safeguard that concentrates scrutiny where failures arise: an auxiliary model gates only mutating actions for user confirmation, injects a targeted reflection of constraints before mutating steps, and cleans context by keeping only the most relevant summarised blocks, so most turns stay autonomous and overhead stays low. | - | Framing statement (how the paper states its problem, challenge, objective, solution or gain); not a measurement. | line 1054 of the saved text | 1054 | primary | corrected by the auditor |

## f175 — InferCept: Efficient Intercept Support for Augmented Large Language Model Inference

- Source: https://arxiv.org/html/2402.01869v2 · version read: v2 · v1: Fri, 2 Feb 2024 19:47:57 UTC
- Source class: top venue · formal venue (confirmed at the official source): Proceedings of the 41st International Conference on Machine Learning (ICML 2024)
- Audit: None; 6 items kept, 0 dropped

| # | Field | Claim | Figure | Measurement definition | Location | Line | Label | Audit |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 0 | framing_problem | LLMs are increasingly integrated with external tools, environments and agents, but today's LLM inference systems are designed for standalone LLMs: they treat each external interaction (an 'interception') as the end of generation and form a new request when it finishes. The paper asks how an LLM inference system should efficiently support interceptions. | - | Framing statement (how the paper states its problem, challenge, objective, solution or gain); not a measurement. | line 55 of the saved text | 55 | primary | corrected by the auditor |
| 1 | framing_challenge | Existing inference systems treat an interception as the end of a request, so for each interception the initial prompt and all tokens generated before it are formed as a new request, causing substantial recomputation of the KV cache for all previously processed tokens; this recomputation wastes GPU resources that could serve new requests (37-40% of total model forwarding time with the mixed six-augmentation workload, lines 55, 207). The alternatives have their own costs: Preserve avoids recomputation but occupies GPU memory during the entire interception; Swap avoids recomputation, but with limited GPU-CPU link bandwidth foreground forwarding could be bottlenecked waiting for swapping to finish (lines 75-76). Interception time varies drastically across augmentation types and requests, which complicates request scheduling, and context length and interception time also vary highly across requests (lines 69-70). | - | Framing statement (how the paper states its problem, challenge, objective, solution or gain); not a measurement. | line 73 of the saved text | 73 | primary | corrected by the auditor |
| 2 | framing_objective | Minimize GPU memory waste caused by interceptions ('min-waste interception'; 'minimizing GPU memory waste as a unified objective', line 325). Per-interception waste equations: Eq.1 WasteDiscard_i^j = T_fwd(C_i^j)×C_i^j×M + T_fwd(C_i^j)×C_other×M; Eq.2 WastePreserve_i^j = T_INT^j×C_i×M; Eq.3 WasteSwap_i^j = 2×T_swap(C_i^j)×C_batch×M; Eq.4 WasteChunkD_i^j = T_fwd(C_i^j)×C_i^j×M/2 + n×T_fwd(C_i^j/n)×C_other×M; Eq.5 Waste_i^j = min(WastePreserve_i^j, WasteChunkD_i^j), used to rank intercepted requests. Symbols (from the text): i = request, j = interception; C_i^j = context tokens of request i when interception j occurs; C_i in Eq.2 = the request's context held in GPU memory (line 209); M = KV-cache memory per token; T_fwd = mapping from number of scheduled tokens in a batch to that iteration's execution time; C_other = sum of the contexts of other requests; T_INT^j = duration of interception j (for highly variable or not offline-profiled interceptions estimated as T̂_INT = t_now - t_call, line 282); T_swap = mapping from number of tokens to swap to swapping latency; C_batch appears in Eq.3 without a separate definition; n = number of iterations to finish recomputing the request. Swap limit per iteration: T_swap(N_i) = T_fwd(B_i), where N_i = number of tokens that can be swapped for free (hidden behind forwarding) at iteration i with batch size B_i (line 234); recomputation chunk size = S minus the running group size, S = GPU saturation point in query tokens (lines 247-248). Swap-in/out budgets are set by maximizing inference throughput (tokens added to an iteration) under three memory/bandwidth constraints (lines 238-241). Reported evaluation metrics: normalized latency vs request rate (intercepted time removed from end-to-end latency), completed requests per second, TTFT. | - | Framing statement (how the paper states its problem, challenge, objective, solution or gain); not a measurement. | line 80 of the saved text | 80 | primary | corrected by the auditor |
| 3 | framing_solution | InferCept derives waste equations for Discard, Preserve and Swap; reduces the waste of Swap (layer-by-layer swap pipelining overlapped with model forwarding, and swap chunking across iterations so each iteration stays within a swap budget the GPU-CPU link can sustain) and of Discard (recomputation split into chunks small enough to fit the GPU processing capacity left unused by decoding); and sorts intercepted requests in descending order of potential memory waste (Eq. 5), swaps out context from them in that order until the swap-out budget (determined at every iteration, lines 236-241) runs out, and preserves or discards the remaining requests according to the Eq. 5 decision; for resumption, it assigns the swap-in budget to swapped-out requests with the earliest original arrival times and schedules discarded, preserved and non-intercepted waiting requests in FCFS order until the GPU's processing capacity (saturation point) is reached, FCFS ensuring fairness (lines 82-93, 268-278). | - | Framing statement (how the paper states its problem, challenge, objective, solution or gain); not a measurement. | line 89 of the saved text | 89 | primary | corrected by the auditor |
| 4 | framing_gain | Compared with state-of-the-art LLM inference systems, InferCept improves overall serving throughput by 1.6x-2x and completes 2x more requests per second (abstract, line 57); the introduction states this as 1.6x-2x higher serving load than vLLM while maintaining similar latency per token generation and over 2x more completed requests per second (line 95), evaluated on GPT-J-6B, Vicuna-13B and Llama3-70B on A100 GPUs with a mixed workload of six augmentations. The conclusion states 1.6x-2x higher request arrival rates and 1.3x-12x lower normalized latency compared to state-of-the-art inference systems (line 325); in the 6B technique breakdown at 2 requests/s the full InferCept has 0.69% GPU memory waste (line 322). | - | Framing statement (how the paper states its problem, challenge, objective, solution or gain); not a measurement. | line 57 of the saved text | 57 | primary | corrected by the auditor |
| 5 | framing_classification | Classification by the extractor, checked by the auditor: efficiency in the stated problem = central; efficiency terms = GPU memory waste / GPU resource wastage (GB*min), recomputation (share of total model forwarding time), serving throughput, serving load / request arrival rate (requests per second), completed requests per second, normalized latency (median end-to-end latency divided by output length), latency per token generation, time-to-first-token (TTFT), swap latency / GPU-CPU link bandwidth (swap budget), GPU processing capacity (GPU saturation point), interception time (tool / human response duration), iteration time (added by recomputation or swapping), GPU core utilization; agent kind = LLM inference (serving) system for 'augmented LLMs': LLMs whose generation is intercepted by external tools, non-LLM models, humans or environments (e.g. ChatGPT plugins, calculators, QA retrieval, ALFWorld virtual environment, chatbot, image generation, TTS); the introduction cites Ng's remark on 'AI agent workflows' (line 65) and views tool use and interaction with humans or environments generally as interceptions (line 66); position = model inference/serving. | - | Reader classification (not a statement of the paper). | whole abstract and introduction |  | secondary | corrected by the auditor |

## f176 — OSWorld-Human: Benchmarking the Efficiency of Computer-Use Agents

- Source: https://arxiv.org/html/2506.16042v2 · version read: v2 · v1: Thu, 19 Jun 2025 05:26:40 UTC

| 0 | framing_problem | State-of-the-art computer-use systems have focused solely on improving accuracy on leading benchmarks and are practically unusable due to extremely high end-to-end latency (e.g. tens of minutes) for tasks that typically take humans a few minutes (line 63); as far as the authors know, no existing work has properly studied the latency aspect of CUAs (line 105), so the paper studies where the latency comes from and benchmarks agents' temporal efficiency. | - | Framing statement (how the paper states its problem, challenge, objective, solution or gain); not a measurement. | line 63 of the saved text | 63 | primary | corrected by the auditor |
| 1 | framing_challenge | Most computer tasks involve a sequence of discrete steps and total latency accumulates across them; LLMs/VLMs are called for planning, judging and reflection at each step and often involve long prompts; and, unlike a human expert following a direct path, CUAs may engage in trial-and-error, explore irrelevant parts of the interface, spend time recovering from errors or perform a correct but less efficient sequence of actions (line 104). Because the prompt at each step includes the history of all previous steps, later model calls take longer and have longer prompts (line 152); each successive step can take 3x longer than steps at the beginning of a task (abstract, line 63). In the GTA1 failure analysis, grounding errors cause repeated steps (23% of failures, line 236). | - | Framing statement (how the paper states its problem, challenge, objective, solution or gain); not a measurement. | line 104 of the saved text | 104 | primary | corrected by the auditor |
| 2 | framing_objective | Weighted Efficiency Score, intended to approximate end-to-end latency by comparing agent step counts with human trajectories: WES^+ = (1/n) Σ_t^n r_t · t_human/t_agent and WES = WES^+ · (1 - t̄_fail/S). Symbols (from the text): r_t = 1 if task t was completed successfully, 0 otherwise; t_human = minimum expected, human-performed number of steps (OSWorld-Human single-action or grouped-action trajectory); t_agent = actual agent-generated number of steps; n = number of tasks; t̄_fail = average number of steps across all failed tasks; S = maximum steps allowed (each agent's own value). Reported alongside the OSWorld success rate; the latency study additionally reports per-stage share of task latency, prompt/completion tokens per call and dollar cost per task. | - | Framing statement (how the paper states its problem, challenge, objective, solution or gain); not a measurement. | line 380 of the saved text | 380 | primary | corrected by the auditor |
| 3 | framing_solution | After profiling Agent S2 and GTA1 to locate the bottlenecks, the paper builds OSWorld-Human with the minimal human-perceived steps for all 369 tasks, including grouped-action trajectories of actions that can be executed from the same screenshot, so that one observation and model call could serve a group of actions and future agents could use fewer LLM calls; WES then penalizes inefficient successful and failed trajectories. | - | Framing statement (how the paper states its problem, challenge, objective, solution or gain); not a measurement. | line 284 of the saved text | 284 | primary | corrected by the auditor |
| 4 | framing_gain | No method gain is claimed. Benchmark finding: the best agent with publicly released trajectories (Agent S2 w/ Gemini 2.5) reaches 41.4% OSWorld success but only 15.6% single-action WES (9.6% grouped-action) (lines 74, 395); the abstract, intro and conclusion state this as leading agents taking 2.7x-4.3x more steps than necessary, while Sec. 5.2 derives 2.7x and 4.3x as the reduction from the 41.4% success score to the 15.6% and 9.6% WES scores (line 395). Latency study (39-task OSWorld subset): planning accounts for more than half, sometimes close to 75%, of total task latency (Table 1 averages 53.5% S2, 74.6% GTA1), judging (GTA1) and reflection (S2) for 22.5% and 33.6% (line 69); GTA1 costs $2.43 per task on average at TogetherAI unit prices (line 204, Table 3). | - | Framing statement (how the paper states its problem, challenge, objective, solution or gain); not a measurement. | line 74 of the saved text | 74 | primary | corrected by the auditor |
| 5 | framing_classification | Classification by the extractor, checked by the auditor: efficiency in the stated problem = central; efficiency terms = end-to-end latency / request latency / task latency, temporal performance / temporal efficiency, per-step latency, number of steps, number of LLM calls, prompt tokens and completion tokens, dollar cost per task, wall-clock time, prefill vs decoding stage time, Weighted Efficiency Score (WES), maximum step budget S (step limit), wasted steps (loops from grounding errors), accessibility-tree generation time / observation-type effect on task latency; agent kind = computer-use agents (CUAs) that control desktop applications through GUI and CLI on OSWorld (studied: Agent S2 and GTA1; evaluated: 16 leaderboard agents); the paper is a latency study plus a benchmark (OSWorld-Human) and an efficiency metric (WES), not a new agent; position = evaluation/measurement. | - | Reader classification (not a statement of the paper). | whole abstract and introduction |  | secondary | corrected by the auditor |

## f178 — SPORK: Self-Speculative Forking to Accelerate Agentic LLM Inference

- Source: https://arxiv.org/html/2607.03333v1 · version read: v1 · v1: Fri, 3 Jul 2026 13:51:32 UTC
- Source class: institutional supplement · no formal publication confirmed
- Audit: None; 6 items kept, 0 dropped

| # | Field | Claim | Figure | Measurement definition | Location | Line | Label | Audit |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 0 | framing_problem | The agent's Thought-Action-Observation loop is often serial: the model reasons, emits a tool call, then idles the GPU until the result returns, and this tool wait consumes 16-37% of wall time in the authors' workloads (35-61% in prior reports); speculative tool execution can hide it, but existing systems need auxiliary predictors, historical traces or static workflow graphs, leaving a gap for training-free, day-one deployment. | - | Framing statement (how the paper states its problem, challenge, objective, solution or gain); not a measurement. | line 84 of the saved text | 84 | primary | corrected by the auditor |
| 1 | framing_challenge | Each tool result conditions all subsequent tokens, so the cycle enforces a strict serial dependency: the tool call cannot be dispatched until decoding completes and the next decode cannot begin until the result arrives; tool wait is bounded by network round-trips, container cold-starts and database I/O, and as model inference gets faster its share of wall time grows. Token-level speculative decoding and serving systems do not dispatch tools earlier, and agents generate tool calls online, so there is no static graph to prefetch. | - | Framing statement (how the paper states its problem, challenge, objective, solution or gain); not a measurement. | line 240 of the saved text | 240 | primary | corrected by the auditor |
| 2 | framing_objective | Latency ratio (EQ1): Ratio = T_base / (T*_base - α·t_overlap + T_oh); speculation helps when Ratio >= 1, approximately α·t_overlap >= T_oh, with ceiling Ratio = 1/(1 - f_tool) at α = 1, T_oh = 0 (1.58x on BrowseComp, f_tool = 0.366). Symbols (from the text): α = fraction of tool-call turns where speculation is accepted (gate rate, per turn); t_overlap = mean realized time overlap per accepted turn; T*_base = realized main-stream decode cost on the speculative path, equal to T_base unless prefix recovery lowers it; T_oh = per-turn overhead from probe computation and wasted speculative execution on rejected turns; T_base = T_dec + T_tool, the serial baseline per-turn cost (Appendix A), with T_dec main generation wall time and T_tool tool execution wall time; f_tool = T_tool/T_base. Exact form (Appendix A, lines 1199-1223): T_hit = T_base - t_overlap (accepted, p = α); T_miss = T*_base + T_oh (rejected, p = 1-α) with T*_base = T_base - T_D3; S = T_base / (T_base - α·t_overlap + (1-α)(T*_base - T_base + T_oh)); break-even α·t_overlap >= (1-α)(T*_base - T_base + T_oh), reducing without D3 to α·t_overlap >= (1-α)·T_oh; ceiling S_max = (T_dec + T_tool)/T_dec = 1/(1 - f_tool) when α = 1 and t_overlap = T_tool (perfect overlap of all tool time; line 1225). Evaluation metrics: latency = per-query end-to-end wall-clock time; quality = exact match (GAIA/HotpotQA) and F1 (HotpotQA); speedup = P95 ratio (baseline/Spork). | - | Framing statement (how the paper states its problem, challenge, objective, solution or gain); not a measurement. | line 289 of the saved text | 289 | primary | corrected by the auditor |
| 3 | framing_solution | The running model is used as its own predictor: a probe forked at the main generation's first token (sharing the KV-cache prefix, with a forced tool-call prefix) predicts the next tool call, which is dispatched early so its execution overlaps the remaining chain-of-thought decode; each component improves one term of the cost model (prefix-cache fork lowers probe cost, a logprob confidence gate filters mispredictions, partial-token accept turns rejected probes into speculative-decoding drafts), and on a mismatch the agent falls back to serial execution. | - | Framing statement (how the paper states its problem, challenge, objective, solution or gain); not a measurement. | line 95 of the saved text | 95 | primary | corrected by the auditor |

| 0 | framing_problem | Users can query a growing number of LLMs for a fee, the fees are heterogeneous and can differ by two orders of magnitude, and using LLMs on large collections of queries and text can be expensive; the paper asks how to use LLMs affordably and accurately. | - | Framing statement (how the paper states its problem, challenge, objective, solution or gain); not a measurement. | line 49 of the saved text | 49 | primary | corrected by the auditor |
| 1 | framing_challenge | LLM APIs differ in cost (prompt cost, generation cost and sometimes a fixed per-query cost) and in quality: the largest models are expensive for high-throughput use, cheaper models such as GPT-J can be much worse on difficult tasks, relying on one provider is unreliable, and existing ensemble or cascade methods were built for predictive tasks with a known label set; the strategy search space (prompts, APIs, aggregation) is vast. | - | Framing statement (how the paper states its problem, challenge, objective, solution or gain); not a measurement. | line 60 of the saved text | 60 | primary | corrected by the auditor |
| 2 | framing_objective | Budget-aware LLM API usage: maximize E_{(q,a)∈Q×A}[r(a, â(s,q))] subject to E_{(q,a)∈Q×A}[c(s,q)] ≤ b, where q is a query from the query distribution Q, a its correct answer, â(s,q) the answer generated by strategy s, c(s,q) the cost of processing q with s, b a user-defined bound on average cost, and r(·,·) a reward measuring how closely the generated answer matches the correct one. Per-API cost: c_i(p) ≜ c̃_{i,2}//f_i(p)// + c̃_{i,1}//p// + c̃_{i,0}, with f_i the i-th of K LLM APIs mapping a prompt p to an answer and c̃_{i,j} constants. For the cascade: max_{L,τ} E[r(a, f_{L_z}(q))] s.t. E[Σ_{i=1}^{z} c̃_{L_i,2}//f_{L_i}(q)// + c̃_{L_i,1}//q// + c̃_{L_i,0}] ≤ b, z = argmin_i g(q, f_{L_i}(q)) ≥ τ_i, where L ∈ [K]^m are the indexes of the m APIs selected by the router, τ the threshold vector, g(·,·): Q×A→[0,1] the generation scoring function giving a reliability score, and z the API at which the router stops and returns the answer. Empirical metrics: accuracy on each dataset and cost in USD (Table 3: 'Cost to reach the same accuracy' of the best individual LLM and its cost savings in %; Figure 5 accuracy-cost trade-off curves). A diagnostic metric, maximum performance improvement (MPI) of LLM A with respect to LLM B, is defined as the probability that A answers correctly while B answers incorrectly (line 219). | - | Framing statement (how the paper states its problem, challenge, objective, solution or gain); not a measurement. | line 94 of the saved text | 94 | primary | corrected by the auditor |
| 3 | framing_solution | Because different LLM APIs have different strengths and even an inexpensive LLM can sometimes correctly answer queries on which a more expensive LLM fails (line 219), an LLM cascade sends each query to a list of LLM APIs sequentially, returns an API's answer as soon as its reliability score from a generation scoring function (e.g. a trained regression model) is higher than that API's threshold, and queries the remaining APIs only if the previous APIs' generations are deemed insufficiently reliable; query cost is reduced when the first APIs are relatively inexpensive and produce reliable generations (line 106). The API list and thresholds are learned as a budget-constrained optimization problem by a specialized optimizer that prunes lists with small answer disagreement and interpolates the objective from a few samples (line 114). | - | Framing statement (how the paper states its problem, challenge, objective, solution or gain); not a measurement. | line 106 of the saved text | 106 | primary | corrected by the auditor |
| 4 | framing_gain | Against the best individual LLM API, FrugalGPT matches its performance with up to 98% cost reduction (HEADLINES: 33.1 vs 0.6 to reach GPT-4's accuracy, 98.3%; OVERRULING 73.3%; COQA 59.2% against GPT-3) or improves accuracy over GPT-4 by 4% at the same cost. | - | Framing statement (how the paper states its problem, challenge, objective, solution or gain); not a measurement. | line 49 of the saved text | 49 | primary | corrected by the auditor |

|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 0 | framing_problem | Tool calls and environment interactions leave the agent idle while waiting for observations; existing works treat this idle time as unavoidable overhead or use restricted solutions that utilize it poorly, so the paper asks how to exploit idle time from agentic interactions robustly and generally to improve agent performance on complex tasks. | - | Framing statement (how the paper states its problem, challenge, objective, solution or gain); not a measurement. | line 105 of the saved text | 105 | primary | corrected by the auditor |
| 1 | framing_challenge | Observation uncertainty: during idle periods the observation is not yet available, so plans generated then may become invalid or suboptimal when it arrives; in addition, the reasoning budget available during idle time varies strongly across tool calls, and the prior idle-time method (Sleep-time Compute) ignores this variation (the introduction says it uses only 13.7% of total idle time on GAIA, line 103; Appendix B.1 gives 13.2%, line 832) and assumes predictable future queries. | - | Framing statement (how the paper states its problem, challenge, objective, solution or gain); not a measurement. | line 114 of the saved text | 114 | primary | corrected by the auditor |
| 2 | framing_objective | None stated as a formula for the task objective. The stated aim is to improve agent performance while minimizing latency overhead; the reported targets are accuracy (%) on GAIA (Levels 1-3) and FRAMES, and submission, valid-submission, above-median and medal rates (Bronze/Silver/Gold, Any Medal total) on MLE-Bench Lite within a 24-hour wall-clock budget per task. Efficiency metrics: end-to-end latency (Figure 3), per-task wall-clock latency in seconds (Appendix Table 8), idle-time and test-time output tokens (Table 3), and idle-time utilization, Eq. (5): ITU_task = Σ_{k=1}^{K} t^{(k)}_{LLM-on-idle} / Σ_{k=1}^{K} t^{(k)}_{idle} ∈ [0,1], where t^{(k)}_{idle} is the tool execution duration of step k and t^{(k)}_{LLM-on-idle} ≤ t^{(k)}_{idle} the part of it spent on LLM computation, averaged over tasks (and seeds). The method's own equations define the candidate set D_final = D_prog ∪ D_rec (Eq. 1), p = Pr(ℓ = Prog) with p ~ Beta(α,β) (Eqs. 2-3), where ℓ ∈ {Prog, Rec} is the forecast signal and α, β count past Prog and Rec signals (initialized to 1), the posterior update (α,β) ← (α+1,β) if ℓ = Prog, (α,β+1) if ℓ = Rec (Eq. 4), and the sampling rule: draw p̂ ~ Beta(α,β), choose Prog if p̂ > 0.5, else Rec. | - | Framing statement (how the paper states its problem, challenge, objective, solution or gain); not a measurement. | line 86 of the saved text | 86 | primary | corrected by the auditor |
| 3 | framing_solution | While a tool executes, the agent iteratively drafts plan candidates until the observation arrives, sampling between complementary progressive drafts (assuming a favorable observation) and recovery drafts (assuming no progress) so as to cover plausible future observations; the drafts are then aggregated as non-binding guidance for the next reasoning step, and the strategy distribution is updated from a forecast signal by Thompson sampling. | - | Framing statement (how the paper states its problem, challenge, objective, solution or gain); not a measurement. | line 116 of the saved text | 116 | primary | corrected by the auditor |
| 4 | framing_gain | Against a vanilla baseline that does no computation during idle time, IdleSpec raises average accuracy over GAIA Levels 1-3 and FRAMES to 55.6% with Gemini-2.5-Flash (+5.1 from 50.5; +4.6 on Gemma4-E4B, 30.9 to 35.5; +6.8 on Qwen3.5-4B, 33.2 to 40.0) and the MLE-Bench Lite medal rate by 9.1 points (36.4% to 45.5%, Gemini-2.5-Flash, single seed). On latency, the efficiency analysis (Figure 3, vLLM on an NVIDIA A6000) says IdleSpec keeps latency close to vanilla while Sequential Revision and Planning are about 1.30x and 1.33x slower; Appendix Table 8 (full GAIA, Gemini-2.5-Flash, single fixed seed) gives per-task wall-clock latency of 107 vs 99 s (Level 1), 191 vs 196 s (Level 2) and 374 vs 376 s (Level 3) for vanilla vs IdleSpec. | - | Framing statement (how the paper states its problem, challenge, objective, solution or gain); not a measurement. | line 91 of the saved text | 91 | primary | corrected by the auditor |

| 0 | framing_problem | LLM-based agents incur high end-to-end latency on edge devices; on-device AI agents still suffer from suboptimal latency even for simple tasks (one TinyAgent task takes 35.4 s on average on a Mac mini M4 Pro), and the paper sets out to systematically characterize and eliminate these latency bottlenecks without accuracy loss. | - | Framing statement (how the paper states its problem, challenge, objective, solution or gain); not a measurement. | line 61 of the saved text | 61 | primary | corrected by the auditor |
| 1 | framing_challenge | Unlike server-based, conversation-oriented LLM workloads whose latency is dominated by decode, on-device agents spend significant time in both prefill and decode: agents process much longer inputs than they generate, and on-device accelerators offer limited compute throughput and memory bandwidth, rendering prefill disproportionately expensive; dynamically retrieved tool descriptions and guidelines inserted early in the Planner prompt limit KV cache reuse by prefix caching; decode output is highly correlated with the provided examples and user prompt (96% of Planner and 87% of Arbiter output tokens overlap with their input prompt), so a large portion of decode time is spent generating straightforward, formulaic sequences that do not require the LLM's reasoning capabilities; and speculative decoding is hindered on-device by draft-LLM latency and the 'multi-token tax' of multi-token verification. | - | Framing statement (how the paper states its problem, challenge, objective, solution or gain); not a measurement. | line 76 of the saved text | 76 | primary | corrected by the auditor |
| 2 | framing_objective | No overall closed-form objective. The stated objective of PromptWeaver and ExSpec is to speed up their target stages (prefill and decode) without compromising task accuracy or introducing substantial overhead in the resource-constrained on-device environment. Reported targets: end-to-end task latency and speedup, and Planner accuracy (the output plan is turned into a DAG of function calls with dependency edges and compared against the ground-truth DAG; the paper says it translates directly to end-to-end task accuracy). Explicit selection metric in Algorithm 1: under a KV cache budget of N clusters, greedily add the cluster prefix p^ = argmax_{p in options}[coverage(D, C U {p}) - coverage(D, C)], where coverage(D, C) is the sum, over the activated cluster sequences of the Planner training dataset D, of the number of leading clusters whose KV cache is in C (longest cached prefix). Draft token accuracy = fraction of draft tokens ultimately accepted during verification. | - | Framing statement (how the paper states its problem, challenge, objective, solution or gain); not a measurement. | line 219 of the saved text | 219 | primary | corrected by the auditor |
| 3 | framing_solution | PromptWeaver reconstructs the input prompt so that most of it forms a cacheable static prefix - all-inclusive static tool descriptions and guidelines, then tool-use examples clustered by tool co-activation in a fixed theme-based order whose KV caches are precomputed offline and stored on SSD, then a few uncacheable dynamic examples - to accelerate prefill; ExSpec uses an n-gram lookup table built on the fly from the few-shot examples and the user query as an LLM-free draft model for speculative decoding, which incurs no draft-token generation overhead, and falls back to standard autoregressive decoding when the table has no entry for the current context, so the multi-token tax is avoided when no speedup is expected. | - | Framing statement (how the paper states its problem, challenge, objective, solution or gain); not a measurement. | line 77 of the saved text | 77 | primary | corrected by the auditor |
| 4 | framing_gain | Average end-to-end task latency improves 1.61x over the baseline TinyAgent pipeline (TinyAgent-7B backend on a Mac mini M4 Pro; the text labels it only 'baseline'), with the prefill and decode stages sped up 1.97x and 1.73x; PromptWeaver alone gives 1.16x and ExSpec alone 1.43x end-to-end; the paper reports no accuracy loss. | - | Framing statement (how the paper states its problem, challenge, objective, solution or gain); not a measurement. | line 78 of the saved text | 78 | primary | corrected by the auditor |

| 0 | framing_problem | LLM-based agents act greedily step by step on the current observation without foresight of long-term consequences or alternative paths; in partially observable web environments a single misstep is hard to undo, and existing tree-search methods lack safe backtracking and assume all actions are reversible, which limits their effectiveness on realistic web tasks. | - | Framing statement (how the paper states its problem, challenge, objective, solution or gain); not a measurement. | line 87 of the saved text | 87 | primary | corrected by the auditor |
| 1 | framing_challenge | Five named challenges for tree-search WebAgents: (i) low-quality action generation (invalid actions that reduce search efficiency and waste computation), (ii) redundant candidate actions, (iii) fragile state reversibility in non-deterministic web environments, (iv) destructive actions that permanently alter the environment and invalidate visited states, and (v) computational overhead of exhaustive search such as MCTS rollouts and costly environment resets. | - | Framing statement (how the paper states its problem, challenge, objective, solution or gain); not a measurement. | line 100 of the saved text | 100 | primary | corrected by the auditor |

Candidate actions are scored before execution by a process reward model v_t = f_v(I, {(o_1,a_1),...,(o_t,a_t)}) in [0,1] that predicts the expected utility of executing a_t (appendix A.2.5); following WebShepherd it is a checklist-based process reward r_k(o,a)=(1/L)Σ_l [P(“Yes”/I,C,o,a,F)+0.5×P(“In Progress”/I,C,o,a,F)] (L = number of checklist items, I = instruction, C = checklist, o = observation, a = candidate action, F = generated feedback), with final reward written r(o,a)=Σ_{k=1}^{K} r_k(o,a) (appendix B.4). | 1 | framing_challenge | Standard metrics capture accuracy or other system capabilities but fail to account for cost, and value and cost have been interpreted and reported separately; prior attempts to include cost rely on fixed inference budgets, heuristic performance scores or non-monetary proxies such as conciseness, which tie conclusions to specific constraints or heuristics and limit generality and economic interpretability. LMs act as stochastic producers, and more powerful models, scaffolds or test-time techniques that seek a higher probability of success typically do so at higher computational (and monetary) cost. | - | Framing statement (how the paper states its problem, challenge, objective, solution or gain); not a measurement. | line 82 of the saved text | 82 | primary | corrected by the auditor |
| 2 | framing_objective | Cost-of-pass v(m,p) = C_m(p) / R_m(p) (Eq. 2): R_m(p) is the probability that model m produces a correct answer on problem p; C_m(p) is the expected cost of one inference attempt by m on p (token counts times per-token prices plus extra charges, instantiating w^T x); 1/R_m(p) is the expected number of attempts to the first correct solution assuming independent trials; R_m(p)=0 gives infinite cost-of-pass. Frontier cost-of-pass V_p(M) = min_{m in M} v(m,p) (Eq. 3) and V_p(M ∪ M_0) = min(V_p(M), v(expert,p)) with v(expert,p) ≈ C_expert(p) (Eqs. 4-5); V_p(M_t) over strategies released up to time t (Eq. 6); gain G_p({m_t}, M_{t-1}) = V_p(M_{t-1}) - V_p(M_{t-1} ∪ {m_t}) (Eq. 7); distribution-level versions are averages over problems p ~ P (Eqs. 8-9). Derived analysis metrics: exponential fit V_p(M_t) ≈ a e^{-bt} + c with halving time of the exponential component T_1/2 = ln(2)/b (Eq. 10); counterfactual essentialness of a model family g = G_{p~D}(M_g, M_T \ M_g) / V_{p~D}(M_T \ M_g) (Eq. 11); relative gain of an inference-time technique = G_{p~D}(M_L*, M_L) / V_{p~D}(M_L) over the lightweight+large model set M_L (Eq. 12). | 3 | framing_solution | Adapt Farrell's production-frontier theory (and stochastic frontiers of Aigner et al.) to LMs: treat each LM inference pipeline as a stochastic producer whose unit of output is a correct solution, measure the expected monetary cost per correct output, take the minimum across available models plus an estimated human-expert baseline, and track that frontier over model releases and counterfactual removals of model families. | - | Framing statement (how the paper states its problem, challenge, objective, solution or gain); not a measurement. | line 86 of the saved text | 86 | primary | corrected by the auditor |
| 4 | framing_gain | As an evaluation framework, the headline findings are: frontier cost-of-pass decreased exponentially from May 2024 to February 2025; from a fitted exponential decay (Eq. 10), the exponential component for MATH-500 halved approximately every 2.6 months and for AIME-2024 every 7.1 months. | 1 | framing_challenge | Thought generation consumes the majority of inference compute per step, and in reasoning models thinking may continue well beyond the point where the intended action has converged (prior work shows the committed action is encoded in hidden representations well before the trace ends), implying many post-convergence tokens are waste; excessive thinking may also make the edge model increasingly overconfident in a suboptimal action, which complicates cloud-deferral mechanisms that rely on the edge model's internal uncertainty, while early truncation may raise uncertainty above the model's actual confidence and unduly increase deferral. Even a well-reasoned edge action can be wrong and errors compound over the episode. Related work (Section 2) states that thought calibration, early-exit methods and conformal-prediction wrappers do not jointly calibrate a stopping rule with a deferral mechanism under formal statistical guarantees, that model cascades route single-turn queries without multi-step dependencies, and that ReDAct applies PPL-guided deferral inside an agentic loop but chooses its deferral threshold heuristically. | - | Framing statement (how the paper states its problem, challenge, objective, solution or gain); not a measurement. | line 130 of the saved text | 130 | primary | corrected by the auditor |
| 2 | framing_objective | Eq. (4): min_λ C_L(λ) subject to R(λ) ≥ R^min and C_D(λ) ≤ C_D^max, where λ = (λ_L, λ_D) are the thinking-convergence and deferral thresholds; R(λ) = E[r(λ)] is the expected episode reward (r in [0,1] issued at episode end); C_D(λ) = E[(1/T) Σ_{t=1}^T D_t] is the deferral rate (D_t = 1 if the cloud model is called at step t); C_L(λ) = E[Σ_{t=1}^T L_t] is the thinking cost, L_t being the number of reasoning steps (tokens) before the action at step t, capped at L_max; T is the random number of agent steps. | 3 | framing_solution | A lightweight convergence probe on the edge model's hidden states halts on-device reasoning once the intended action has stabilized, a perplexity-based deferral rule escalates uncertain actions to the cloud model, and the two thresholds are jointly calibrated on end-to-end episode trajectories with multi-objective Learn-Then-Test, giving finite-sample guarantees on expected episode reward and cloud-call rate. The introduction's rationale is that thinking and deferral are intertwined (excessive reasoning can produce overconfident uncertainty signals), so joint calibration has the potential to reduce edge tokens while making cloud deferral more efficient; the conclusion adds, as an insight from the results, that truncated reasoning leads to detecting uncertainty signals at their most meaningful state. | - | Framing statement (how the paper states its problem, challenge, objective, solution or gain); not a measurement. | line 130 of the saved text | 130 | primary | corrected by the auditor |

## f189 — Concurrency without Model Changes: Future-based Asynchronous Function Calling for LLMs

- Source: https://arxiv.org/html/2605.15077v1 · version read: v1 · v1: Thu, 14 May 2026 17:02:28 UTC
- Source class: institutional supplement · no formal publication confirmed
- Audit: None; 6 items kept, 0 dropped

| # | Field | Claim | Figure | Measurement definition | Location | Line | Label | Audit |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 0 | framing_problem | Function calling in LLM agents is typically constrained by synchronous execution semantics: decoding is blocked until each function call completes, which increases end-to-end latency. | - | Framing statement (how the paper states its problem, challenge, objective, solution or gain); not a measurement. | line 54 of the saved text | 54 | primary | corrected by the auditor |
| 1 | framing_challenge | Under the standard synchronous function-calling protocol each call must be immediately followed by its result, and model decoding blocks after each emitted call until the function finishes; this serialization limits concurrency and increases end-to-end latency. Prior approaches that expose in-progress executions to continued generation or shift concurrency management onto the model often alter the function-calling protocol or require model changes. Relaxing strict decode-order execution to gain parallelism introduces correctness risk, since naive parallelization may execute dependent calls prematurely. | - | Framing statement (how the paper states its problem, challenge, objective, solution or gain); not a measurement. | line 58 of the saved text | 58 | primary | corrected by the auditor |
| 2 | framing_objective | Reported target is end-to-end task latency, as speedup of each AsyncFC variant over its corresponding synchronous baseline under the same function-calling API (one-sided paired t-test on per-task log speedups, alternative that the geometric-mean speedup exceeds 1), with accuracy preserved (McNemar test on paired task outcomes). The design-intuition section writes the theoretical maximum speedup ratio R = (T_LLM + T_tool) / max(T_LLM, T_cp) (Eq. 1), where T_tool is the total function execution time summed across all nodes of the task-specific function dependency DAG, T_cp is the sum of function execution times along the critical path, and T_LLM is total decoding time; ideal asynchronous latency is max(T_LLM, T_cp), and large speedups require T_tool >> T_cp and ideally T_LLM ≈ T_cp. | - | Framing statement (how the paper states its problem, challenge, objective, solution or gain); not a measurement. | line 148 of the saved text | 148 | primary | corrected by the auditor |
| 3 | framing_solution | Offload concurrency management from the model to the runtime: automatically transform function schemas to accept and return symbolic futures and add an await_future function; after each decoded call, dispatch the unmodified synchronous function to a background executor and immediately return a future placeholder so decoding continues; integrate resolved results at turn boundaries; and gate execution with a dependency-aware scheduler that serializes all calls in decode order by default (still overlapping decoding with execution) and runs calls in parallel only when optional developer resource annotations show them to be dependency-safe - all without fine-tuning or changes to the standard function-calling protocol. | - | Framing statement (how the paper states its problem, challenge, objective, solution or gain); not a measurement. | line 54 of the saved text | 54 | primary | corrected by the auditor |
| 4 | framing_gain | AsyncFC reduces end-to-end task completion time with no statistically significant accuracy difference from the synchronous baselines: a 1.26x speedup of AsyncFC(S) over Sequential FC on BFCL v4 Web Search composed (paired) workloads with real backend latency (GPT-4o, n=31; accuracy 53.2% vs 54.8%), and a 1.44x speedup over the unmodified SWE-agent baseline on SWE-bench Lite with GPT-5.2 and tool latencies scaled by 2x (n=300; +Par. FC reaches 1.21x; issue-resolution 44.3% vs 47.6%, p_acc > 0.05). | - | Framing statement (how the paper states its problem, challenge, objective, solution or gain); not a measurement. | line 80 of the saved text | 80 | primary | corrected by the auditor |

| 0 | framing_problem | Current LLM function calling is inherently synchronous: each call blocks LLM inference, limiting LLM operation and concurrent function execution, so it is neither resource-efficient nor responsive. | - | Framing statement (how the paper states its problem, challenge, objective, solution or gain); not a measurement. | line 70 of the saved text | 70 | primary | corrected by the auditor |
| 1 | framing_challenge | Each function call blocks LLM inference, one of the most resource-intensive processes, until the function returns, and the executor must finish calls in the order the LLM initiated them; these inefficiencies grow with the number of functions, and prior optimizations (compiled parallel calls, call fusion, concise syntax, serving optimizations) remain limited by the synchronous LLM-waits-for-executor pattern. Making calls asynchronous raises two further challenges: timing interrupt tokens so they do not disrupt ongoing generation, and getting the LLM to handle interrupts that do not follow its training conversations. | - | Framing statement (how the paper states its problem, challenge, objective, solution or gain); not a measurement. | line 76 of the saved text | 76 | primary | corrected by the auditor |
| 2 | framing_objective | Fine-tuning trains the LLM to minimize total task completion time (the makespan) while respecting task dependencies and estimated function execution times. Section 6.3 (proofs in Appendix A) models n independent functions F with token generation latency G(f) and execution time E(f) (averages Ḡ, Ē): L_Sync(F) = Σ_f G(f) + Σ_f E(f) = n(Ḡ + Ē); L_Sync-Parallel(F) = Σ_f G(f) + max_f E(f); L_Async(F) = max_f (E(f) + Σ_{g in pred(f,F)} G(g)) with pred(f,F) = {g in F / E(f) ≤ E(g)} under the Longest-Processing-Time-first order. Theorem 6.1: L_Async ≤ L_Sync-Parallel < L_Sync; Theorem 6.2: L_Sync/L_Async ≈ 1 + Ē/Ḡ (error O((Ē/Ḡ)^2), assuming normally distributed E and large /F/); Theorem 6.3: no deviation from LPT order lowers total latency. Evaluation measures end-to-end task completion latency as the time between the first and last token generation. | - | Framing statement (how the paper states its problem, challenge, objective, solution or gain); not a measurement. | line 125 of the saved text | 125 | primary | corrected by the auditor |
| 3 | framing_solution | Make LLM decoding interruptible: function calls are non-blocking, and when one returns the executor injects interrupt tokens into the token stream; a token-efficient DSL (CML) marks call boundaries so interrupts are deferred safely, fine-tuning teaches the LLM to issue asynchronous calls, handle interrupts and signal when it must wait, and calls are prioritized longest-processing-time first to maximize overlap of generation and execution. | - | Framing statement (how the paper states its problem, challenge, objective, solution or gain); not a measurement. | line 84 of the saved text | 84 | primary | corrected by the auditor |

## f191 — Dynamic Speculative Agent Planning

- Source: https://arxiv.org/html/2509.01920v3 · version read: v3 · v1: Tue, 2 Sep 2025 03:34:36 UTC

| # | Field | Claim | Figure | Measurement definition | Location | Line | Label | Audit |

| 0 | framing_problem | LLM-based agents face critical deployment challenges due to prohibitive latency and inference costs; existing acceleration methods either fail to preserve performance fidelity, require extensive offline training of router modules, or incur excessive operational costs, and give minimal user control over the trade-off between acceleration and other metrics. | - | Framing statement (how the paper states its problem, challenge, objective, solution or gain); not a measurement. | line 67 of the saved text | 67 | primary | corrected by the auditor |
| 1 | framing_challenge | Speculative planning parallelises the inherently autoregressive planning pipeline, but its commonly adopted fixed speculation step k is fundamentally limited: on complex tasks aggressive speculation produces excessive and redundant agent calls (wasted prompt and generation tokens of A, and completed or cancelled T steps after a mismatch), while on simple tasks conservative speculation gives insufficient acceleration; the optimal k is context-dependent, varies even within one task, and is unknown a priori. | - | Framing statement (how the paper states its problem, challenge, objective, solution or gain); not a measurement. | line 74 of the saved text | 74 | primary | corrected by the auditor |
| 2 | framing_objective | The paper states DSP 'explicitly optimizes a joint objective balancing end-to-end latency against dollar cost', steered by a single user parameter, but writes no single latency-plus-cost formula. The learned component is a state-value predictor of the speculative step: minimise the TD loss L_θ = E_{τ∼π}[(G_t^λ − V_θ(s_t))^2] (Eq. 1), where s_t is the state (a token sequence), V_θ a neural (DistilBERT) approximation of V_π(s) = E_π[G_t / s_t = s], the 'expected speculative step of state s', and G_t^λ the λ-return (Eq. 2) interpolating n-step returns G_{t:t+n} (λ ∈ [0,1], γ = 1). The trade-off is exposed by replacing MSE with the expectile loss L_2^τ(u) = /τ − 1(u<0)/ u^2 (τ > 0.5 over-estimates k: faster, costlier; τ < 0.5 cheaper, slower) or by an offset k = max(1, k̂ + β) with user bias β. Reported metrics: ΔTime = (1/N) Σ_i (1 − T_i^SP / T_i^seq) × 100% (N tasks; total task time under speculative vs sequential planning) and ΔCost = (1/N) Σ_i ((PC_i^SP + GC_i^SP)/(PC_i^seq + GC_i^seq) − 1) × 100% (PC, GC = prompt and generation dollar costs, token counts of approximation and target times their per-token API prices), ΔP and ΔG (Eqs. 3-4) are the analogous relative increases in prompt and generation tokens, where the 'seq' baseline is the sum of target and approximation tokens each run sequentially (line 186), plus ratios T(×), P(×), G(×), Cost(×) against fixed k = 2, average peak concurrency MC̄ = (1/N) Σ_i MC_i (Eq. 10) and average speculative step K̄ = (1/M) Σ_i k_i over M planning episodes (Eq. 11). | - | Framing statement (how the paper states its problem, challenge, objective, solution or gain); not a measurement. | line 68 of the saved text | 68 | primary | corrected by the auditor |
| 3 | framing_solution | A lightweight DistilBERT regressor, trained by asynchronous online reinforcement learning (TD learning on (partial trajectory, k) pairs logged while the system runs, with no offline dataset or pre-deployment phase), predicts per state how many steps A will get right before T must intervene, so speculation is suspended before it wastes calls; T still verifies every step, keeping the output lossless, and biased prediction or a biased offset lets practitioners move along the latency-cost continuum. | - | Framing statement (how the paper states its problem, challenge, objective, solution or gain); not a measurement. | line 75 of the saved text | 75 | primary | corrected by the auditor |
| 4 | framing_gain | On two standard agent benchmarks (OpenAGI, TravelPlanner), DSP 'achieves comparable efficiency to the fastest lossless acceleration method while reducing total cost by 30% and unnecessary cost up to 60%' (abstract); the introduction words it as reducing total cost 'by up to 30%', cutting unnecessary cost by 60% and 'preserving comparable acceleration' (line 78). The reference for both figures is the fastest fixed-k speculative-planning configuration (Fix k = 6), not fixed-k planning in general: e.g. Dyn. (offset = 2) gives time reduction comparable to Fix k = 6 with 60.65% less redundant cost (OpenAGI Setting 1, line 1154), and the high-performance mode (tau = 0.99/0.95) gives over 90% of the fastest setting's time savings while saving 30% total cost (line 1167). Against the cheaper Fix k = 2/4 the cost savings are smaller (e.g. 12% and 23.4%, lines 702-703). | - | Framing statement (how the paper states its problem, challenge, objective, solution or gain); not a measurement. | line 69 of the saved text | 69 | primary | corrected by the auditor |
| 5 | framing_classification | Classification by the extractor, checked by the auditor: efficiency in the stated problem = central; efficiency terms = end-to-end latency, inference costs, dollar cost, total cost, unnecessary cost, operational costs, token consumption, prompt tokens, generation tokens, redundant agent calls, Time Decrease (ΔT), Total Cost Increase (ΔCost), Absolute Time Ratio T(×), Absolute Cost Ratio Cost(×), Average Max Concurrent API Calls (MC), Average Speculative Step (K), Prompt Token Increase (ΔP), Generation Token Increase (ΔG), extra cost brought by parallelizing computations, pre-deployment preparation overhead (router training, prompt engineering), API throttling / concurrency limits; agent kind = LLM-based agents doing multi-step agent planning (evaluated on OpenAGI and TravelPlanner); the method (DSP) is a speculative-planning acceleration framework in which a cheaper approximation agent A drafts steps and the original target agent T verifies them in parallel; position = agent loop (steps, calls, context). | - | Reader classification (not a statement of the paper). | whole abstract and introduction |  | secondary | corrected by the auditor |

- Source: https://arxiv.org/html/2601.05777v2 · version read: v2 · v1: Fri, 9 Jan 2026 13:01:49 UTC

| 0 | framing_problem | SE agents powered by LLMs are increasingly adopted in practice but often incur substantial monetary cost; cost efficiency remains a key concern for practical adoption (in a Stack Overflow survey, 53% of software engineers reported agent cost as a barrier), and the monetary cost is also associated with environmental impact through energy consumption. The paper aims to reduce the cost of SE agents while preserving task performance (resolution rate). | - | Framing statement (how the paper states its problem, challenge, objective, solution or gain); not a measurement. | line 79 of the saved text | 79 | primary | corrected by the auditor |
| 1 | framing_challenge | The paper says this cost inefficiency arises largely because SE agents resolve issues through multi-round iterations (e.g. repeated tool invocations) in which the entire conversation history is fed back as context each time, causing computational costs to grow super-linearly ('token snowball'); when stuck on difficult or unsolvable issues, agents often continue consuming iterations that provide little additional benefit (line 84). Existing SE agents typically terminate patch generation and selection only when the backend LLM explicitly signals completion or a predefined iteration budget is exhausted, and the number of generated patches is often fixed by a maximum iteration limit; this coarse-grained control often leads to redundant computation by over-solving simple issues or persisting on difficult ones (lines 114, 122). | - | Framing statement (how the paper states its problem, challenge, objective, solution or gain); not a measurement. | line 84 of the saved text | 84 | primary | corrected by the auditor |
| 2 | framing_objective | No single optimisation formula. The paper evaluates 'both task performance and cost efficiency': performance = % Resolved (percentage of tasks for which the agent produces a patch that passes all tests); cost efficiency = # API Calls (total LLM API invocations across the benchmark), # Input/Output Tokens (total tokens consumed across the benchmark) and Total Cost (total monetary cost across the benchmark in U.S. dollars). Decision rules: patch generation stops early when the LLM's confidence score after a milestone (code modification or test execution) exceeds τ^gen; patch selection stops generating further patches when the confidence score exceeds τ^sel_upper (patch sufficiently reliable) or falls below τ^sel_lower (issue unlikely to be resolved); only the top-1 retrieved experience with TF-IDF similarity above τ_sim is used. | - | Framing statement (how the paper states its problem, challenge, objective, solution or gain); not a measurement. | line 271 of the saved text | 271 | primary | corrected by the auditor |
| 3 | framing_solution | Much like an experienced developer, an agent informed by relevant prior experience can navigate directly to a solution, bypassing costly trial-and-error iterations (line 86). EET abstracts successful, validated past issue-resolution runs into structured experience objects (issue abstraction, key-step execution summary, confidence and confidence reason), retrieves for a new issue the top-1 experience whose TF-IDF similarity exceeds a threshold, conditions patch generation on it, and uses it for LLM confidence-based early-termination checks after milestones in patch generation and after each patch in patch selection (lines 100-124). | - | Framing statement (how the paper states its problem, challenge, objective, solution or gain); not a measurement. | line 86 of the saved text | 86 | primary | corrected by the auditor |
| 4 | framing_gain | On SWE-bench Verified, across three SE agents (Agentless, Mini-SWE-Agent, Trae Agent) and two LLM backends (GPT-5-mini, DeepSeek-V3.2), compared with the same agents without EET, total cost falls by 19.3%-55.1% (31.8% on average) with at most 0.2 percentage points loss in resolution rate (Trae Agent with DeepSeek-V3.2; % Resolved changes are absolute differences, Table 1), via early termination on 8.6%-14.0% of issues (11.3% on average) and average reductions of 20.8% in API calls, 29.9% in input tokens and 25.1% in output tokens. Total cost is the per-benchmark inference cost; the one-time, offline experience-generation cost is excluded from it and reported separately (Appendix J, line 1054). | - | Framing statement (how the paper states its problem, challenge, objective, solution or gain); not a measurement. | line 88 of the saved text | 88 | primary | corrected by the auditor |

| 1 | framing_challenge | The paper attributes the loss of time efficiency to three main reasons: (1) the backbone LLM can be inefficient because of its increasingly large size and high request volume, (2) complex agent structures such as tree-of-thought and ReAct generate prolonged thought before the final answer, extending waiting time and token generation costs, and (3) action steps in a plan are sequential, one must finish before the next can begin; yet not all planning steps need computationally intensive thought, so applying complex agents or advanced backbones to every step is inefficient. | - | Framing statement (how the paper states its problem, challenge, objective, solution or gain); not a measurement. | line 81 of the saved text | 81 | primary | corrected by the auditor |
| 2 | framing_objective | No single optimisation objective. Tokens between breaking points T_{B_i} = tokens of A and T for committed steps + 'wasted tokens' (Eq. 4); rate = maximum concurrent calls, bounded by k+1. Empirically 11 metrics are reported: TT, min-TT, ST, min-ST, TO, min-TO, SO, min-SO, MC, min-MC and average total cost. | - | Framing statement (how the paper states its problem, challenge, objective, solution or gain); not a measurement. | line 273 of the saved text | 273 | primary | corrected by the auditor |

| 0 | framing_problem | GUI agents face an inefficiency challenge: processing long sequences of high-resolution screenshots and solving long-horizon tasks makes inference slow, costly and memory-bound; storing the full KV cache is prohibitive for image-heavy contexts, and existing cache-compression methods are sub-optimal for GUIs. | - | Framing statement (how the paper states its problem, challenge, objective, solution or gain); not a measurement. | line 54 of the saved text | 54 | primary | corrected by the auditor |
| 1 | framing_challenge | Caching all KV states can require extensive GPU memory (UI-TARS-1.5-7B can consume over 80GB GPU memory on a single inference with 5 screenshots and a maximum of 50 steps, which can easily trigger out-of-memory errors on most consumer GPUs), while token-merging or higher-layer pruning alternatives require re-training GUI agents (line 58). The abstract says existing cache-compression methods are sub-optimal because they do not account for the spatial and temporal redundancy of GUIs (line 54); the introduction describes spatial redundancy (large uniform backgrounds, repeated UI elements, static components) and temporal redundancy (consecutive screenshots often share significant visual overlap) and says approaches developed primarily for natural images and documents 'may not be optimal' for GUIs (line 59). In addition, measured on ScreenSpotV2 trajectories with UI-TARS-1.5-7B, GUI attention sparsity averages above 0.99 across all layers (lowest around 0.98, versus natural images averaging 0.92 with minimums around 0.88), so per-layer budget schedules that normalize sparsity (e.g. PyramidKV, VL-Cache) over-amplify tiny differences and misallocate cache (lines 60, 67, 96-97). | - | Framing statement (how the paper states its problem, challenge, objective, solution or gain); not a measurement. | line 54 of the saved text | 54 | primary | corrected by the auditor |
| 2 | framing_objective | No single objective; KV cache selection under a budget γ ∈ (0,1] (fraction of KV states kept, applied uniformly across layers and heads): keep C^h = {i ∈ C : /{j ∈ C : ψ̂_i^h > ψ̂_j^h}/ < ⌈n·γ⌉} (Eq. 10 as printed; the text 'select the top-scoring tokens' (line 145) and Algorithm 1 (line 979) keep the top-⌈n·γ⌉ tokens by ψ̂^h, whereas the printed inequality literally counts lower-scored tokens), where C = {1,...,n} indexes the n input prompt tokens and ψ̂_i^h (Eq. 9) = A_i^h + αS_i for current-frame visual tokens, (A_i^h + αS_i)·1[ρ_i^h ≥ ρ̃^h] for previous-frame visual tokens, and A_i^h for text tokens; A_i^h is the attention a token receives from the last ω observation tokens in head h, S_i the softmax of standardized L2 norms of residual-stream hidden states (temperature τ, Eq. 4), α > 0 balances the two, ρ_i^h = //k_i^h (I − P_t^h)//_2 is the residual of a previous-frame key outside the rank-r QR subspace P_t^h of the current screenshot's keys (Eq. 7), and ρ̃^h the (1−γ) percentile threshold (Eq. 8). Reported targets: click accuracy, step accuracy and success rate at each budget vs full cache, and MFLOPs per token for pre-filling and decoding. | - | Framing statement (how the paper states its problem, challenge, objective, solution or gain); not a measurement. | line 150 of the saved text | 150 | primary | corrected by the auditor |
| 3 | framing_solution | Because GUI attention sparsity is uniformly high across layers, GUI-KV assigns a uniform budget to each layer and ranks tokens by attention augmented with a softmax-normalised residual-stream L2-norm saliency (spatial saliency guidance), while zeroing the scores of previous-frame visual tokens whose keys lie largely in the rank-r QR subspace of the current frame's keys, i.e. whose residual falls below the per-head (1-γ) percentile (temporal redundancy scoring); it thus retains tokens that are both intrinsically important and temporally unique, plug-and-play without retraining. | - | Framing statement (how the paper states its problem, challenge, objective, solution or gain); not a measurement. | line 151 of the saved text | 151 | primary | corrected by the auditor |
| 4 | framing_gain | The abstract claims that across standard GUI agent benchmarks and models GUI-KV outperforms competitive KV compression baselines and closely matches full-cache accuracy at modest budgets (line 54). The results section (six benchmarks, UI-TARS-1.5-7B and OpenCUA-7B, baselines SnapKV, PyramidKV, VL-Cache) words it as 'consistently matches or surpasses the best competing compression schemes' across budgets 1%-80%, with positive average absolute gains over the best baseline on four of six benchmarks (+0.7 to +3.6) and a baseline sometimes ahead at 1-3% budgets (lines 685, 688); the introduction's 'typically 10-20%' budget for near-full-cache accuracy is qualified to UI-TARS-1.5-7B (lines 63, 688, 736). In a 5-screenshot AgentNetBench setting at 40% budget on UI-TARS-1.5-7B, GUI-KV reduces MFLOPs per decoded token by 38.9% (290.4 -> 177.4, Table 2) while raising step accuracy by 4.1 points (absolute) over the full-cache baseline, with pre-filling overhead reported as <0.29% across all settings; the decoding savings grow with more screenshots (lines 714, 729). These are computed FLOP counts, not measured wall-clock time, memory or dollar cost. | - | Framing statement (how the paper states its problem, challenge, objective, solution or gain); not a measurement. | line 54 of the saved text | 54 | primary | corrected by the auditor |
