| 0 | framing_problem | A major bottleneck in current LLM agent frameworks is the high inference cost of tool selection, especially in ReAct-style agents that repeatedly invoke the LLM to decide which tool to use at each step, which limits use in resource-constrained or real-time scenarios. | - | Framing statement (how the paper states its problem, challenge, objective, solution or gain); not a measurement. | line 75 of the saved text | 75 | primary | corrected by the auditor |
| 1 | framing_challenge | Agents repeatedly infer the next tool (and its parameters) with a complete LLM inference at every step, even though not all decision steps are equally complex: many tool invocations occur in highly patterned or repetitive contexts that do not need the LLM's full reasoning, so universal use of the LLM over-utilises it and creates unnecessary computational overhead. | - | Framing statement (how the paper states its problem, challenge, objective, solution or gain); not a measurement. | line 82 of the saved text | 82 | primary | corrected by the auditor |
| 2 | framing_objective | Given historical trajectories D_hist = {tau_1, ..., tau_N}, each tau_i = (o_0, a_0, o_1, a_1, ...) of observations o and actions a, where an action a_t = (tool_{t+1}, params_{t+1}) is chosen at timestep t from observation o_t, task goal G and tool set T (ReAct infers a_t ~ p_LLM(a / o_t, G, T) via a complete LLM inference), construct M_AutoTool, a training-free decision-making algorithm based on the Tool Inertia Graph that selectively bypasses the LLM for predictable actions to improve efficiency. Tool choice uses CIPS = (1 - alpha) * Score_freq + alpha * Score_ctx (Score_freq from Tool Inertia Graph edge weights; Score_ctx the semantic alignment of the agent's current intuition with the candidate tool's description); the highest-CIPS tool v* goes to parameter filling only if CIPS(v*) > theta_inertial, and the inertial call is executed only if all required parameters are filled, otherwise the LLM is called (experiments: theta_inertial = 0.1, alpha = 0.5, inertial calls capped at 30% of operations, line 408-409). Evaluation target: reduce computational overhead measured by number of LLM calls and token consumption while maintaining comparable task performance measured by AgentBoard progress rate (line 406). | - | Framing statement (how the paper states its problem, challenge, objective, solution or gain); not a measurement. | line 253 of the saved text | 253 | primary | corrected by the auditor |
| 3 | framing_solution | Exploiting 'tool usage inertia' (tool invocations follow predictable sequential patterns), AutoTool builds a directed graph from agent trajectories, with tools as nodes, edges capturing transition probabilities, and parameter-dependency edges; before each LLM call it attempts an 'inertial' call: choose the next tool by a score combining historical frequency and contextual relevance (CIPS), then fill its parameters non-LLM (dependency backtracking, then environmental state matching, then heuristic filling), falling back to the LLM whenever either stage fails. | - | Framing statement (how the paper states its problem, challenge, objective, solution or gain); not a measurement. | line 75 of the saved text | 75 | primary | corrected by the auditor |

| 1 | framing_challenge | The components schedule and allocate resources separately per request without end-to-end knowledge of the workflow, which causes (1) KV cache thrashing (caches of programs waiting on tools are evicted and must be re-prefilled, raising end-to-end latency by up to 7.14x), (2) cross-node memory imbalance from pinning a workflow to one node, and (3) tool lifecycle obliviousness (unreclaimed sandboxes and ports, long environment setup before reasoning). | - | Framing statement (how the paper states its problem, challenge, objective, solution or gain); not a measurement. | line 114 of the saved text | 114 | primary | corrected by the auditor |

The scheduling target is to minimise Cost_recompute, Cost_unused and Cost_caching, thereby maximising throughput, subject to GPU memory capacity (line 147). A program is P = <ID, c, T, L, tau, s>: identifier, context token count, tool environments, node placement, execution phase (reasoning/acting), scheduling status. | - | Framing statement (how the paper states its problem, challenge, objective, solution or gain); not a measurement. | line 249 of the saved text | 249 | primary | corrected by the auditor |

- Source: https://arxiv.org/html/2604.24039v1 · version read: v1 · v1: Mon, 27 Apr 2026 04:51:15 UTC

| 0 | framing_problem | Embodied AI agents increasingly rely on LLMs for planning, yet per-step LLM calls impose severe latency and cost; under the standard synchronous setup the agent must wait for each plan before acting, stalling real-time execution. | - | Framing statement (how the paper states its problem, challenge, objective, solution or gain); not a measurement. | line 124 of the saved text | 124 | primary | corrected by the auditor |
| 1 | framing_challenge | Over 70% of runtime across benchmarks is spent on LLM planning queries in a synchronous plan-act loop; existing asynchronous strategies (parallelized planning-acting, speculative planning) still rely on repeated LLM queries, so LLM cost scales linearly with trajectory length and every step is treated as a fresh decision even when plans follow a predictable pattern; existing caches (KV, context, template) reduce redundant computation inside the model but, the paper says, not repeated LLM invocations during execution. Plan locality alone is insufficient because environmental changes can invalidate cached plans, while always consulting the LLM reintroduces the latency caching is meant to avoid. | - | Framing statement (how the paper states its problem, challenge, objective, solution or gain); not a measurement. | line 164 of the saved text | 164 | primary | corrected by the auditor |
| 2 | framing_objective | No single optimisation objective; reported metrics are success rate SR, latency L (hours), token usage T and cost C (USD, measured input/output token counts multiplied by OpenAI list prices, October 2025). The cache's plan-selection rule is P* = argmax_{P_j in F(P_i)} S(P_i -> P_j) with S(P_i -> P_j) = C(P_i -> P_j) * I(P_j), where F(P_i) is the feasible set of successor plans whose stored metadata ranges contain the current task state, C(P_i -> P_j) is the transition count (how often P_j was observed immediately after P_i), and I(P_j) = N^conf(P_j)/N^cand(P_j) is the importance factor (times the background LLM confirmed P_j divided by times P_j appeared as a feasible candidate). | - | Framing statement (how the paper states its problem, challenge, objective, solution or gain); not a measurement. | line 295 of the saved text | 295 | primary | corrected by the auditor |
| 3 | framing_solution | Because embodied tasks exhibit plan locality (the next plan is largely predictable from the current one), each agent queries a runtime cache of frequent 2-gram plan transitions instead of calling the LLM every step, while a background Cache Updater asynchronously queries the LLM to confirm or correct cached entries without blocking execution, with query suppression and optional offline prefilling for warm start. | - | Framing statement (how the paper states its problem, challenge, objective, solution or gain); not a measurement. | line 136 of the saved text | 136 | primary | corrected by the auditor |
| 4 | framing_gain | Across 12 configurations (four multi-agent embodied benchmarks x GPT-5, GPT-5-mini, GPT-5-nano), AgenticCache improves task success rate by 22% on average, reduces simulation latency by 65% and lowers token usage by 50%; the text does not name the comparator for these averages (calc. from Table 2: they match the synchronous Baseline row, mean +22.2 SR points, -64.5% latency, -50.6% tokens, not the parallelized or speculative planners); e.g. on TDW-COOK with GPT-5, versus the synchronous baseline, latency drops from 12.86 h to 1.75 h (7.4x) and cost from $21.0 to $4.4 (4.8x). | - | Framing statement (how the paper states its problem, challenge, objective, solution or gain); not a measurement. | line 124 of the saved text | 124 | primary | corrected by the auditor |

| # | Field | Claim | Figure | Measurement definition | Location | Line | Label | Audit |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 0 | framing_problem | Inference engines evict a finished request's KV cache when new requests are waiting (end-of-turn eviction); this breaks for agentic workloads that interleave LLM calls with tools, because the tool calls introduce pauses that prevent effective KV reuse across turns, and the paper aims to optimize job completion time for multi-turn agent workloads. | - | Framing statement (how the paper states its problem, challenge, objective, solution or gain); not a measurement. | line 95 of the saved text | 95 | primary | corrected by the auditor |
| 1 | framing_challenge | After eviction the engine must recompute the prefix (prefill) or reload the KV cache from CPU when the tool returns, and, even with CPU offloading, the returning request suffers a per-turn queueing delay waiting for GPU memory, which accumulates over turns and is not measurable by offline profiling; at the same time tool-call durations are variable (some extremely long-tailed), so a retention time must be bounded, since a pinned KV cache can occupy GPU memory for a long time and even cause deadlocks, yet a TTL that expires just before the tool returns wastes the waiting time. Prior work falls short: InferCept decides only on reload cost and does not model per-turn queueing delay or handle variable tool durations, Autellix uses end-of-turn eviction, Pie provides no retention policy, and Ayo/Alto/Parrot assume static workflows. | - | Framing statement (how the paper states its problem, challenge, objective, solution or gain); not a measurement. | line 98 of the saved text | 98 | primary | corrected by the auditor |
| 2 | framing_objective | TTL choice maximizes expected net benefit in units of time (total job completion latency): τ* = argmax_τ P(τ,f) × Benefit(r) − Cost(τ,r) (Eq. 1), with Cost(τ,r) = MemUsage(r)/M × τ; Benefit(r) = CacheMissCost(r) + OutofOrderCost(r); CacheMissCost(r) = MemUsage(r) × Prefill-Reload(r) / M; OutofOrderCost(r) = T/M × MemUsage(r) × η; η = −Corr(k, N−k); P(τ,f) = (1//S[f]/) Σ_{t∈S[f]} I[t ≤ τ]; after cancelling MemUsage(r)/M this becomes argmax_τ P(τ,f) × (T·η + Prefill-Reload(r)) − τ (Eq. 2). Symbols: r a request that generates tool call f; τ the TTL (seconds); MemUsage(r) GPU memory of r's KV cache; M average GPU memory footprint of active requests; Prefill-Reload(r) time to reconstruct the KV cache by prefill or CPU reload (from offline profiling); T average queueing delay of evicted requests (sliding-window average); η memoryfulness factor of the workload, with N the total requests in a program and k those already served; S[f] historical durations of tool f; I the indicator function. Reported end-to-end targets are average job completion time / delay and throughput. | - | Framing statement (how the paper states its problem, challenge, objective, solution or gain); not a measurement. | line 479 of the saved text | 479 | primary | corrected by the auditor |
| 3 | framing_solution | For requests that generate tool calls, Continnum pins the KV cache in GPU memory for a time-to-live set by weighing reload/prefill cost and the queueing delay that eviction would cause against the memory it occupies, using the empirical distribution of that tool's durations; when the TTL expires the cache is evicted automatically, which keeps it robust to unexpectedly long tool calls, and a TTL-aware program-level first-come-first-serve priority preserves multi-turn continuity. | - | Framing statement (how the paper states its problem, challenge, objective, solution or gain); not a measurement. | line 103 of the saved text | 103 | primary | corrected by the auditor |
| 4 | framing_gain | Delay (job completion time) and throughput on multi-turn agentic workloads: across three hardware and model setups Continnum reduces delay by 1.12x to 3.66x and improves throughput by 1.10x to 3.22x (the sentence does not name the baseline; the evaluated baselines are vanilla vLLM, vLLM+LMCache CPU offloading, Autellix/Autellix+ and InferCept); on Company A's internal H100 testbed it reduces delay for real SWE-agent workloads by up to 8.18x, where the comparison is against distributed inference solutions (SGLang, Dynamo); the abstract states 'improves the average job completion times by over 8x while improving throughput'. | - | Framing statement (how the paper states its problem, challenge, objective, solution or gain); not a measurement. | line 166 of the saved text | 166 | primary | corrected by the auditor |

|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 0 | framing_problem | LLM-brained web agents face a critical cost-performance trade-off: upgrading to a more powerful model often yields only marginal accuracy gains while substantially increasing operational costs, e.g., price, which makes it impractical to use a single 'best model' in real-world web agents; the paper therefore argues it is important to develop a dynamic router that matches each web query to the most cost-effective LLM capable of resolving it. | - | Framing statement (how the paper states its problem, challenge, objective, solution or gain); not a measurement. | line 40 of the saved text | 40 | primary | corrected by the auditor |
| 1 | framing_challenge | Web-agent prompts are verbose and complex, concatenating user goals, action histories (memory) and detailed environmental states (perception); the paper says this informational redundancy can degrade the performance of conventional routing mechanisms such as ZOOTER and RouterDC (line 60). As a task progresses the growing action history makes prompts increasingly verbose and noisy, with a significant portion of queries exceeding thousands of tokens (Fig. 3), and the paper posits that this noise challenges traditional routers that rely on direct semantic embeddings (lines 101-103); the abstract states that the complex prompts lead to degraded LLM ensemble performance (line 41). | - | Framing statement (how the paper states its problem, challenge, objective, solution or gain); not a measurement. | line 60 of the saved text | 60 | primary | corrected by the auditor |
| 2 | framing_objective | Learn a router psi that takes a query q_i and outputs a probability distribution p_i = psi(q_i) in R^T over T candidate LLMs (line 83), by minimising the cost-aware VIB loss (Eq. 6): L_ca-VIB = (1/N) sum_{i=1..N} ( E_{p_theta(z_i/q_i)}[-log p_phi(y_i/z_i)] + beta * KL[p_theta(m_i/q_i) // r(m_i)] + lambda * E_{p_theta(z_i/q_i)}[ sum_{t=1..T} p_phi(y_t/z_i) * C(M_t) ] ). N = training samples; q_i = query (user's high-level goal, agent's action history, current web representation); z_i = m (.) h_q, the input feature representation h_q masked element-wise by a stochastic binary mask m; p_theta = stochastic encoder; p_phi = decoder predicting the target model distribution; r = the reference distribution in the KL (compression) term, not defined further in the text; y_i = the ground-truth outcome in the problem formulation (line 83); in the prediction term the cross-entropy target is a distribution derived from a softmax over the score vector s_i (line 135); beta = weight of the compression term; lambda = hyperparameter controlling cost-sensitivity; C(M_t) = pre-defined, query-agnostic unit cost of invoking model M_t (e.g. c_p^(t)+c_c^(t) for a single token). Experiments set beta = 0.3, lambda = 0.2 (line 267). Supervision score (Eq. 3): s_i^(t) = P(q_i,M_t) x S_cost(C_i^(t)), with P a binary task-success indicator and S_cost the min-max-normalised exponential utility U(c) = exp(-c) of the operational cost (Eq. 2) C(q_i,M_t) = n_p*c_p^(t) + n_c*c_c^(t) (n_p, n_c = prompt and completion tokens; c_p^(t), c_c^(t) = per-token costs of model M_t). Reported metrics (Table 1): task accuracy (acc., %), average price ($), average number of steps; running time is reported in Fig. 5(b). | - | Framing statement (how the paper states its problem, challenge, objective, solution or gain); not a measurement. | line 120 of the saved text | 120 | primary | corrected by the auditor |
| 3 | framing_solution | Train the router under the Variational Information Bottleneck principle so it learns a compressed representation of the input prompt that filters out irrelevant information and keeps only the features critical for the routing decision, implemented by a learned stochastic binary mask on the input's feature representation to address token-level redundancy; add an explicit expected-operational-cost regularisation term so the router is trained to favour less expensive models; the supervision score is non-zero only when the model successfully completes the overall task and its magnitude is inversely related to the operational cost. | - | Framing statement (how the paper states its problem, challenge, objective, solution or gain); not a measurement. | line 61 of the saved text | 61 | primary | corrected by the auditor |
| 4 | framing_gain | On five WebVoyager websites (Apple, Arxiv, Coursera, Google, Huggingface), against browser-use with GPT-4o WebRouter reduces the average price from $0.98 to $0.12 (the paper's 87.8% reduction) with the paper's 3.8% accuracy drop (Table 1 averages 86.1% vs 82.3%); against the RouterDC router it has higher accuracy (82.3% vs 67.8%) and fewer steps (8.38 vs 9.40). Running time is about 14% higher than the GPT-4o baseline (line 274). | - | Framing statement (how the paper states its problem, challenge, objective, solution or gain); not a measurement. | line 270 of the saved text | 270 | primary | corrected by the auditor |

| 1 | framing_challenge | Because the service does not understand how requests are correlated, it cannot exploit three opportunities: dependent consecutive requests go back and forth to the client, adding network latency and queuing delays; scheduling optimizes per-request latency rather than end-to-end latency; and common prompt prefixes (e.g. long system prompts, over 94% of tokens repeated in a production search engine) are provided repeatedly in each request, wasting storage, computation and memory bandwidth. The paper adds that without knowledge of the prompt structure, token-by-token matching of every request is expensive at the cluster level, so a public service can hardly detect and co-locate prompt-sharing requests and engine-level redundancy avoidance is hard to bring into effect (line 146). | - | Framing statement (how the paper states its problem, challenge, objective, solution or gain); not a measurement. | line 90 of the saved text | 90 | primary | corrected by the auditor |

Requests generating a throughput-annotated variable are marked throughput-preferred when scheduling (line 200); for latency-critical outputs, parallel requests at the same stage form a task group whose latency as a whole the scheduler should minimise, often with a higher batch capacity (line 201); to meet latency targets an engine must keep its token count below a threshold set by the request with the strictest latency constraint (line 208). No formula is given; the scheduling policy is Algorithm 1. Evaluation reports mean and P90 end-to-end latency, latency per output token (TPOT), normalized latency (request latency per number of output tokens), token generation speed, sustainable request rate and GPU memory of KV cache. | - | Framing statement (how the paper states its problem, challenge, objective, solution or gain); not a measurement. | line 208 of the saved text | 208 | primary | corrected by the auditor |

Observation Masking f_mask(tau_{t-1}, M) replaces o_i by a placeholder p_i if i < t-M and keeps o_i if i >= t-M (M = window size). ## f213 — DroidSpeak: KV Cache Sharing for Cross-LLM Communication and Multi-LLM Serving

- Source: https://arxiv.org/html/2411.02820v4 · version read: v4 · v1: Tue, 5 Nov 2024 05:41:41 UTC
- Source class: top venue · formal venue (confirmed at the official source): 23rd USENIX Symposium on Networked Systems Design and Implementation (NSDI 26)
- Audit: None; 6 items kept, 0 dropped

| # | Field | Claim | Figure | Measurement definition | Location | Line | Label | Audit |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 0 | framing_problem | In compound AI systems, different LLMs often process inputs that share the same context prefix; prefix KV cache reuse has been enabled across inputs for a single model, but how to enable one model to reuse the prefix KV cache of a different model remains an open question. | - | Framing statement (how the paper states its problem, challenge, objective, solution or gain); not a measurement. | line 72 of the saved text | 72 | primary | corrected by the auditor |
| 1 | framing_challenge | Standard prefix-caching techniques work only when the KV cache is reused by the same LLM, and naively sharing the KV cache across different LLMs causes generation quality to drop greatly (reusing the whole KV cache loses more than 50% of accuracy points on HotpotQA for most model pairs); the challenge is to figure out which part to re-compute or re-use without incurring much delay overhead or degradation of quality. Recomputing only the scattered critical layers is inefficient, because every transition layer from reuse to recompute needs the sender model's E cache (up to 2x the KV cache size for Mistral-7B/Llama-3-8B, up to 4x for Llama-3.1-70B) stored in GPU memory and loaded from remote nodes, and inaccurate, because the E-cache deviation at each transition layer propagates to later layers. As background motivation, lengthy prefill reduces goodput because TTFT grows super-linearly with input length. | - | Framing statement (how the paper states its problem, challenge, objective, solution or gain); not a measurement. | line 100 of the saved text | 100 | primary | corrected by the auditor |
| 2 | framing_objective | No explicit formula. The central design question is how to determine the layers to re-compute to reduce latency while keeping the quality loss minimal. Offline profiling on a held-out 'training' set (50 HotpotQA contexts) builds a Pareto frontier of quality (F1) versus number of re-computed contiguous layers; the configuration chosen keeps the F1 drop within 5% of the receiver model's original quality while minimizing the number of re-computed layers (lines 344, 417-418). Online, the point on the frontier is chosen based on the latency SLO (line 355); Appendix B (line 945) gives the rule: if requests are queuing, choose the configuration with the lowest number of re-computed layers above an accuracy target; otherwise estimate prefill latency from the request's token count and select the highest recomputation ratio that satisfies the latency SLO, to maximize accuracy. Evaluation reports quality (F1, Rouge-L, code similarity) and system metrics TTFT, TBT, E2E, prefill latency (GPU prefill time plus KV/E-cache loading delay over InfiniBand, line 422) and throughput; goodput is defined as the number of queries processed per second within a latency SLO (line 190); Appendix B reports SLO violation rate (line 944). | - | Framing statement (how the paper states its problem, challenge, objective, solution or gain); not a measurement. | line 306 of the saved text | 306 | primary | corrected by the auditor |
| 3 | framing_solution | Because only a small subset (often around 10%) of layers are sensitive to KV cache differences and these are largely consistent across inputs for a model pair, DroidSpeak recomputes a contiguous group of critical layers identified by offline profiling and reuses the other model's KV cache for the remaining layers, and pipelines layer-wise recomputation with loading of reused KV cache from remote nodes to hide the loading delay. | - | Framing statement (how the paper states its problem, challenge, objective, solution or gain); not a measurement. | line 75 of the saved text | 75 | primary | corrected by the auditor |
| 4 | framing_gain | Up to 4x throughput improvement and about 3.1x faster prefill (time to first token), with negligible quality loss in F1, Rouge-L or code similarity, compared with a baseline that allows no KV cache sharing across models (prefill speedup 1.7-3.1x, average 2.1x). | - | Framing statement (how the paper states its problem, challenge, objective, solution or gain); not a measurement. | line 77 of the saved text | 77 | primary | corrected by the auditor |
| 5 | framing_classification | Classification by the extractor, checked by the auditor: efficiency in the stated problem = central; efficiency terms = latency, prefill latency / prefill delay, time to first token (TTFT), time between tokens (TBT), end-to-end latency (E2E), throughput, goodput, latency SLO, computation demand, re-computation, KV cache loading delay, GPU memory, profiling overhead, SLO violation rate, E cache size / storage; agent kind = distributed multi-LLM inference (serving) system for compound AI systems such as agentic / multi-agent workflows, multi-LoRA or multiple fine-tuned model serving, and personalized assistants, where different fine-tuned LLMs of the same architecture share a context prefix; position = model inference/serving. | - | Reader classification (not a statement of the paper). | whole abstract and introduction |  | secondary | corrected by the auditor |

| 1 | framing_challenge | First, high latency and long response time: each individual UI interaction step requires one LLM call to reason which UI to interact with, so a task involving multiple UI interaction steps can incur considerable time and monetary costs; LLM call latency is also positively correlated with the number of processed tokens, and to get high-quality outputs the UI agent must pass a large volume of UI information to describe the current state, which also increases latency in each call (lines 51-72). Second, reliability: during long sequential calls the chance of selecting a wrong UI control or hallucinating a non-existent UI increases with each reasoning step, resulting in compounding errors and task failure (lines 73-84). Third, UI generalization: how UI agents handle applications whose UIs are not included in LLM pretraining remains a critical obstacle without good solutions (lines 84-91). | - | Framing statement (how the paper states its problem, challenge, objective, solution or gain); not a measurement. | line 53 of the saved text | 53 | primary | corrected by the auditor |

The authors state that, compared to UI agents, API-first agents require fewer tokens and can obtain more accurate, code-formatted responses from LLMs with low latency and high reliability (lines 82-86). | - | Framing statement (how the paper states its problem, challenge, objective, solution or gain); not a measurement. | line 78 of the saved text | 78 | primary | corrected by the auditor |

| 0 | framing_problem | LLM-based agents in complex embodied environments often suffer from inefficiencies in multi-turn interactions, frequently trapped in repetitive loops or issuing ineffective commands, leading to redundant computational overhead (abstract, line 110); the paper explores early-exit behavior so that an agent can terminate its interaction when appropriate (lines 110, 140). | - | Framing statement (how the paper states its problem, challenge, objective, solution or gain); not a measurement. | line 110 of the saved text | 110 | primary | corrected by the auditor |
| 1 | framing_challenge | A key underexplored limitation is that agents often fail to recognize when a goal is too difficult or when they are stuck; prior work shows they may repeat the same errors in unproductive loops without meaningful actions or self-correction, leading to unnecessary computational overhead, and in real-world settings repeated mistakes can waste energy, cause wear-and-tear or damage objects (line 116). Without early exit, an agent keeps exploring until the task is completed or a predefined maximum number of steps is reached (line 138; 'continue until the step limit, often wasting valuable interactions', line 769). Existing trajectory-training and prompt-design methods 'often neglect efficiency, especially in failure cases', and post-hoc strategies (self-reflection, trajectory revision, experience extraction) help only after trials conclude (Related Work, line 814). | - | Framing statement (how the paper states its problem, challenge, objective, solution or gain); not a measurement. | line 116 of the saved text | 116 | primary | corrected by the auditor |
| 2 | framing_objective | A trade-off between two new metrics, reported with Success Rate (SR) and Progress Rate (PR): Redundant Steps RS = n_total - n_subgoal, where n_total is the total number of steps in the trajectory and n_subgoal the index of the last step that achieves a new subgoal (RS = n_total if PR = 0; RS = 0 if the task is completed); Progress Degradation PD = max(PR_ref - PR_exit, 0), where PR_ref is the progress rate without exit and PR_exit the progress rate with early exit. PR at step t is r_t = max_{0<=i<=t} (1/K) sum_{k=1..K} f(s_i, g_k), with subgoals g_1..g_K and f a binary indicator that state s_i satisfies subgoal g_k. Strategy selection follows the principle of minimizing progress degradation while reducing redundant steps (line 807). | - | Framing statement (how the paper states its problem, challenge, objective, solution or gain); not a measurement. | line 180 of the saved text | 180 | primary | corrected by the auditor |
| 3 | framing_solution | Give the agent a way to stop: Intrinsic Early Exit appends an exit instruction to the agent's prompt so it can emit an EXIT action itself; Extrinsic Early Exit adds a verification module sharing the same LLM backbone that, every k steps (k=1 in experiments), outputs YES/NO on whether to exit; a hybrid combines both. A practical variant hands control after exit to a stronger agent within the remaining step budget. | - | Framing statement (how the paper states its problem, challenge, objective, solution or gain); not a measurement. | line 117 of the saved text | 117 | primary | corrected by the auditor |
| 4 | framing_gain | In the three embodied environments, almost all early-exit mechanisms reduce redundant steps (RS) relative to the baseline by approximately 50% to 70%, with average steps falling alongside (line 739), at the cost of slight drops in success and progress rates; e.g., the extrinsic method on Llama3.1-70B-Instruct lowers progress rate by under 2%, 3% and 4% on ALFWorld, BabyAI and ScienceWorld (line 741). | 0 | framing_problem | Although major LLM providers offer prompt caching to reduce cost and latency, its benefits for agentic workloads remain underexplored in the research literature; to the authors' knowledge, no prior work quantifies these cost savings or compares caching strategies for multi-turn agentic tasks (abstract, line 70; intro, line 81). | - | Framing statement (how the paper states its problem, challenge, objective, solution or gain); not a measurement. | line 70 of the saved text | 70 | primary | corrected by the auditor |
| 1 | framing_challenge | As agentic workloads grow in complexity, conversations can span dozens of API calls with context windows accumulating tens of thousands of tokens, leading to significant costs and latency overhead (line 75). For caching, agentic workloads feature dynamic, session-specific content that accumulates unpredictably; tool results often contain user-specific data that will not benefit other sessions, and the interleaving of static system prompts with dynamic tool outputs complicates cache reuse (line 97). Naive full-context caching can paradoxically increase latency because dynamic tool calls and results may trigger cache writes for content that will not be reused across sessions (line 86). The Discussion adds that dynamic values in the system prompt (timestamps, session identifiers, user information) and changing tool definitions break the cached prefix (lines 217-218). | - | Framing statement (how the paper states its problem, challenge, objective, solution or gain); not a measurement. | line 75 of the saved text | 75 | primary | corrected by the auditor |
| 2 | framing_objective | Two primary metrics measured against a no-cache baseline: API cost per session, computed from token counts in API responses (standard input tokens, cached input tokens, cache creation tokens) each multiplied by the provider's price and summed over all API calls in the session; and TTFT, the time from request initiation to receipt of the first streamed response chunk. Reported as percentage improvement over the baseline with independent-samples t-tests (alpha = 0.05, n = 40 per condition). No optimization formula. | - | Framing statement (how the paper states its problem, challenge, objective, solution or gain); not a measurement. | line 115 of the saved text | 115 | primary | corrected by the auditor |
| 3 | framing_solution | Prompt caching reuses previously computed KV tensors to avoid redundant computation on repeated prompt prefixes (line 75); the paper compares full-context, system-prompt-only and exclude-tool-results caching against a no-cache baseline, forcing cache boundaries with UUIDs (lines 109-113), and concludes that strategic control of cache boundaries - such as caching only the system prompt or explicitly excluding tool results, so that only stable, reusable content is cached - beats naive full-context caching, with system-prompt-only caching giving the most consistent benefits across cost and latency (line 86). The abstract's guidance also names placing dynamic content at the end of the system prompt and avoiding dynamic traditional function calling (line 70). | - | Framing statement (how the paper states its problem, challenge, objective, solution or gain); not a measurement. | line 86 of the saved text | 86 | primary | corrected by the auditor |
| 4 | framing_gain | Against the no-cache baseline, prompt caching reduces API costs by 41-80% and improves time to first token by 13-31% across providers (abstract, line 70). Section 4.1 gives the TTFT range as 6% to 31% (line 123). | - | Framing statement (how the paper states its problem, challenge, objective, solution or gain); not a measurement. | line 70 of the saved text | 70 | primary | corrected by the auditor |

## f218 — Autellix: An Efficient Serving Engine for LLM Agents as General Programs

- Source: https://arxiv.org/html/2502.13965v1 · version read: v1 · v1: Wed, 19 Feb 2025 18:59:30 UTC
- Source class: top venue · formal venue (confirmed at the official source): 23rd USENIX Symposium on Networked Systems Design and Implementation (NSDI 26)
- Audit: None; 6 items kept, 0 dropped

| # | Field | Claim | Figure | Measurement definition | Location | Line | Label | Audit |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 0 | framing_problem | Agentic programs scale LLM calls and output tokens, but existing LLM serving systems ignore dependencies between programs and calls, missing significant opportunities for optimization (abstract, line 53); because they optimize individual LLM calls without program-level context, they often suffer from suboptimal end-to-end performance for complex programs, in particular programs' end-to-end latencies (line 90). The authors' analysis shows programs submitted to LLM serving engines experience long cumulative wait times, primarily due to head-of-line blocking (line 54). | - | Framing statement (how the paper states its problem, challenge, objective, solution or gain); not a measurement. | line 53 of the saved text | 53 | primary | corrected by the auditor |
| 1 | framing_challenge | Head-of-line blocking at two levels: call-level, where LLM calls with long decodes delay shorter ones (line 132), and program-level, where program-agnostic schedulers let longer programs with many LLM requests delay shorter programs - without program-level context even preemptive MLFQ blindly prioritizes new LLM requests, leading to starvation of shorter programs when long programs' new calls are prioritized (lines 134-135). LLM calls within a program often share common prefixes and cumulative conversation states, while calls across programs typically share only the system prompt (line 96); within a program cache-hit rates remain above 90% across all input lengths, whereas across programs the cache-hit rate decays exponentially with input length, so serving systems across engines should consider a program's data locality to avoid recomputing its KV cache (lines 96, 141). The authors assume a program's LLM invocation pattern emerges only at runtime, making it difficult to fully know or predict the entire graph in advance (line 88). | - | Framing statement (how the paper states its problem, challenge, objective, solution or gain); not a measurement. | line 54 of the saved text | 54 | primary | corrected by the auditor |
| 2 | framing_objective | Minimize programs' end-to-end latency (response time), which for a single-threaded program comprises (1) waiting time (total queuing time of its LLM calls on the engine), (2) execution time (cumulative feedforward time of its LLM calls) and (3) interceptions (time waiting for external interrupts such as tool calls or human input); Autellix targets (1) and (2) because (3) is unrelated to LLM serving (line 124). Priority formulas: PLAS, Eq. 1, p(c_j) = sum of runtimes t_k of all prior LLM calls k<j with the same program ID (larger value = lower priority, lines 254-260); ATLAS, Eq. 2, p(c_j) = 0 if c_j is a root, otherwise max over parents c_k of (p(c_k) + t_k), an estimate of the critical path (lines 262-268). Anti-starvation promotes a call to Q_1 when W_total / T_total >= beta (line 276-278). Stated system objectives: (1) program end-to-end latency for users, (2) maximizing GPU utilization for providers, (3) mitigating starvation / fairness measured via P95 and P99 latencies (line 147). Evaluation metric: program-level token latency = total program response time / number of tokens generated (critical-path response time / total tokens across threads for multi-threaded programs), with throughput compared at equal latency (lines 353-355). | - | Framing statement (how the paper states its problem, challenge, objective, solution or gain); not a measurement. | line 124 of the saved text | 124 | primary | corrected by the auditor |
| 3 | framing_solution | Treat programs as first-class citizens: intercept LLM calls through a stateful session API, keep a global process table, and, inspired by OS schedulers, prioritize LLM calls by program-level attained service with preemption into discretized queues and anti-starvation - PLAS for single-threaded programs uses the total execution time of the program's previously completed calls (lines 93-94, 254-260), and ATLAS for multi-threaded DAG programs uses the maximum cumulative service time across threads, i.e. an estimate of the program's critical path (lines 95, 262-269) - so LLM calls from long programs, which are unlikely to complete soon, are deprioritized, allowing shorter programs to complete first; a data-locality-aware load balancer routes long calls to their programs' engines and load-balances shorter calls to other engines to avoid recomputing the programs' KV cache (line 96). | - | Framing statement (how the paper states its problem, challenge, objective, solution or gain); not a measurement. | line 93 of the saved text | 93 | primary | corrected by the auditor |
| 4 | framing_gain | Across diverse LLMs and agentic workloads, Autellix improves throughput of programs by 4-15x at the same latency compared to state-of-the-art systems such as vLLM (abstract, line 55); across engines, up to 1.5x over standard load balancers (intro, line 97). Per-workload single-engine results (Sec. 6.3, lines 365-367): ShareGPT/BFCL up to 8x vLLM, 2x vLLM-opt and 1.5x MLFQ; LATS up to 5x vLLM, 2x vLLM-opt and 2.5x MLFQ; Mixed up to 15x vLLM, 4x vLLM-opt and 5.5x MLFQ. Sec. 6.4 reports up to 1.4x higher throughput than round-robin and least-used load balancers (line 377). | - | Framing statement (how the paper states its problem, challenge, objective, solution or gain); not a measurement. | line 55 of the saved text | 55 | primary | corrected by the auditor |
| 5 | framing_classification | Classification by the extractor, checked by the auditor: efficiency in the stated problem = central; efficiency terms = end-to-end latency, waiting time, execution time, throughput of programs, program-level token latency, P95/P99 tail latency, makespan, GPU utilization, prefix cache hit rate / KV-cache recomputation, number of LLM calls and output tokens, KV-cache swap overhead (GPU-CPU swaps); agent kind = LLM serving system (serving engine) for agentic programs: dynamic, non-deterministic DAGs of LLM calls from one or more agents plus external interrupts (tool calls, code execution, human input), e.g. chatbots, ReAct agents, Map-Reduce and MCTS programs; position = model inference/serving. | - | Reader classification (not a statement of the paper). | whole abstract and introduction |  | secondary | corrected by the auditor |

| 0 | framing_problem | Speculative tool execution, used to hide latency, dispatches calls before the agent commits to a branch; those calls leak agent-inferred user intent (topics, entities, destinations, follow-up actions) to external observers such as providers, and abandoned 'ghost tool calls' cannot be retracted once an observer has recorded them. | - | Framing statement (how the paper states its problem, challenge, objective, solution or gain); not a measurement. | line 120 of the saved text | 120 | primary | corrected by the auditor |
| 1 | framing_challenge | Timing, not authorization, is the issue: existing safety abstractions reason about state mutation (read/write, reversible/irreversible) or about which committed calls a policy allows, and none models the observer state created by issuing a call before commitment, so commit-time cleanup, read-only restrictions and access-control allow-lists cannot unsend what an observer already holds. | - | Framing statement (how the paper states its problem, challenge, objective, solution or gain); not a measurement. | line 128 of the saved text | 128 | primary | corrected by the auditor |
| 2 | framing_objective | The measured target is privacy leakage, not final-answer correctness (line 233): the marginal exposure \Delta_{i}=O_{i}(S)\setminus O_{i}(C), the ordered multiset of (arguments, destination, metadata) tuples and field deltas observer i sees in S but not in C, where S is the issued trace (ordered log of every dispatched tool event), C\subseteq S is the committed trace (the ordered subsequence whose results or side effects the runtime ultimately uses), and O_{i}(\cdot) is the projection of a trace into the channels observer class i can recover (O_{i}(S) = what i actually records; O_{i}(C) = the committed-only counterfactual, the projection i would have seen had the runtime issued only C from the start); at the semantic level the paper measures inference advantage, the increase in an adversary's probability of recovering a sensitive label given O_{i}(S) versus O_{i}(C), operationalised as closed-set adversarial recovery of a hidden sensitive label from observer projections (line 235). Task success (Haiku-4.5 LLM-as-judge rubric on final answers, 30-task subset) is reported as the utility axis (line 301); provider calls/task and wall-clock are reported under 'Cost and Gate calibration' (line 299) and async wall-clock savings at p50 under RQ4 (line 261). | - | Framing statement (how the paper states its problem, challenge, objective, solution or gain); not a measurement. | line 151 of the saved text | 151 | primary | corrected by the auditor |

## f221 — Optimizing Agentic Language Model Inference via Speculative Tool Calls

- Source: https://arxiv.org/html/2512.15834v1 · version read: v1 · v1: Wed, 17 Dec 2025 18:22:44 UTC
- Source class: institutional supplement · no formal publication confirmed

| # | Field | Claim | Figure | Measurement definition | Location | Line | Label | Audit |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 0 | framing_problem | Tools improve LM capabilities but introduce performance bottlenecks during inference: the model alternates between generation and tool invocation, leaving gaps while waiting on tool completion, and the overhead of tool-centric agents is increasingly dominated by the time spent waiting on tools. | - | Framing statement (how the paper states its problem, challenge, objective, solution or gain); not a measurement. | line 86 of the saved text | 86 | primary | corrected by the auditor |
| 1 | framing_challenge | Each tool call forces generation to stop and return to the user, an interrupt-driven process with a strict sequential dependency in which tool latencies accumulate; evicted sequences and tool output must be rescheduled back into the engine (and the history prefilled again), and prefix caching does not remove the overheads of removing, processing and rescheduling sequences, which worsen in multi-tenant settings; breaking this is non-trivial because tool latencies span orders of magnitude and are hard to predict or bound, long tools dominate end-to-end latency while for short tools eviction and re-entry overheads can outweigh latency hiding, running tools early or out of order risks wasted computation or outputs inconsistent with the model's eventual decisions, and existing in-engine optimizations (speculative decoding, KV-cache management) treat tools as opaque interruptions. | - | Framing statement (how the paper states its problem, challenge, objective, solution or gain); not a measurement. | line 86 of the saved text | 86 | primary | corrected by the auditor |
| 2 | framing_objective | Reported metrics: Time Saved = 100\times\frac{T_{\text{base}}-T_{\text{spec}}}{T_{\text{base}}}\,\%, where T_base and T_spec are the agent's start-to-finish times without and with speculation for the same prompt(s) (mean over async agents), and throughput = tokens generated per second averaged per agent; for commercial models, the additional cost of speculation per 100 agent turns. Walltime is deliberately not used because response lengths vary. Analytic model (client side): S_{\mathrm{spec}}(\alpha)=\frac{G+T}{\alpha\,\max\{G,\,g+T\}+(1-\alpha)(G+T)}, where alpha is the acceptance rate of the speculative model S, G and g the generation times of the main and speculative models, and T the tool call time, with S_max < 2. Engine side: T^{\ast}_{\textrm{spec}}=(1-\alpha)2Ko+\varphi(X_{1}+\sum_{i=1}^{K}(t_{i}+t_{o,i}))+\delta(\alpha K+\sum_{i=1}^{K}R_{i}+(1-\alpha)\sum_{i=1}^{K}t_{i})+(1-\alpha)\sum_{i=1}^{K}T_{i} over K consecutive agent turns, where X_i are prefilled tokens, R_i reasoning tokens decoded, t_i tool-call tokens decoded, t_{o,i} tool-output tokens, T_i tool seconds and o the HTTP/batch-loading overhead per pass; varphi and delta multiply prefill and decode token counts but are not defined in the readable prose of the saved text. Prefix-cached baseline (Eq. 5, line 1762): T_{\textrm{cached}}=2Ko+\varphi(X_{1}+\sum_{i=1}^{K}(t_{i}+t_{o,i}))+\delta\sum_{i=1}^{K}(R_{i}+t_{i})+\sum_{i=1}^{K}T_{i}; Eq. 6 equals T_cached at alpha=0, and at alpha=1 saves 2Ko+\delta(\sum t_{i}-K)+\sum T_{i} over prefix-cached inference (line 1779). | - | Framing statement (how the paper states its problem, challenge, objective, solution or gain); not a measurement. | line 1839 of the saved text | 1839 | primary | corrected by the auditor |
| 3 | framing_solution | Speculative tool execution: a client-side strategy sends the prompt to a small speculative model alongside the main model, launches its predicted (stateless, cheap) tool calls asynchronously and reuses the cached result if the main model emits the same call, breaking the sequential dependency without engine changes; an engine-side variant posts speculated tool outputs to a tool cache in the inference engine, validates tool-call tokens by speculative sampling and ingests tool outputs directly so the sequence stays resident and avoids eviction and re-prefill. | - | Framing statement (how the paper states its problem, challenge, objective, solution or gain); not a measurement. | line 97 of the saved text | 97 | primary | corrected by the auditor |
| 4 | framing_gain | Against non-speculative tool calling, client-side speculation (1x speculation, gpt-oss-120b on BFCL prompts with configured tool latencies) can save between 6-21% end-to-end time per agent at average tool latencies of 0.5-3 s (up to 6% for ~0.5 s tools, up to 21% for ~2.0-2.5 s tools); engine-side speculation gives 2-3% better time savings than client-side when tools finish before the main model is done reasoning (tool latencies ~0-1 s, one async agent only); Figure 1 reports up to 196 tokens/s throughput improvement with 32 agents (the abstract says 'several hundred tokens per second'); and with gpt-5 plus one gpt-5-nano speculation nearly 10% time is saved per agent turn for about a 4% price increase (cost shown per 100 agent turns), while nine speculations add only marginal time saving at around 25-30% of the main generation's cost (Figure 7, lines 1867-1872). | - | Framing statement (how the paper states its problem, challenge, objective, solution or gain); not a measurement. | line 1861 of the saved text | 1861 | primary | corrected by the auditor |

| 1 | framing_challenge | The paper calls optimal routing (maximizing quality within a cost constraint or minimizing cost for a target quality) challenging and lists what an ideal router must do: (1) optimize response quality while invoking a single LLM per query, minimizing cost and latency compared with multi-LLM approaches; (2) generalize to out-of-domain queries without separate per-domain routers; (3) work across a broad range of LLMs without retraining. A further stated challenge is label sparsity in the raw Chatbot Arena preference data (on average under 0.1% comparison labels between any two models, line 147). | - | Framing statement (how the paper states its problem, challenge, objective, solution or gain); not a measurement. | line 64 of the saved text | 64 | primary | corrected by the auditor |
| 2 | framing_objective | Minimize cost while achieving a specific performance target (e.g. 90% of the strong model). Routing rule R^{\alpha}(q) = M_weak if P(win_s/q) < alpha, M_strong if P(win_s/q) >= alpha, where P_theta(win_s/q) is the learned probability that the strong model beats the weak model on query q (trained by \max_{\theta}\sum\log P_{\theta}(l_{s,w}\mid q) over preference data with labels l_{s,w} in {win_s, tie, win_w}) and alpha in [0,1] is the cost threshold. Metrics: c(M_{R^{\alpha}}) = (1//Q/) sum_q I{R^alpha(q) = M_strong} (percentage of strong-model calls, the cost measure); r(M_{R^{\alpha}}) = (1//Q/) sum_q s(M_{R^alpha}(q)) (average response quality score s); PGR = (r(M_{R^alpha}) - r(M_w)) / (r(M_s) - r(M_w)); APGR = \int_{0}^{1}PGR(M_{R^{\alpha}})\;d(c(M_{R^{\alpha}})), approximated by the mean PGR over 10 call-percentage bins; CPT(x%) = the minimum percentage of strong-model calls needed to reach PGR x%. | - | Framing statement (how the paper states its problem, challenge, objective, solution or gain); not a measurement. | line 69 of the saved text | 69 | primary | corrected by the auditor |
| 3 | framing_solution | Learn a win-prediction model from human preference data (Chatbot Arena, with golden-label and GPT-4-judge augmentation) and threshold it, so that simpler queries go to the weak model and more complex ones are reserved for the strong model, with only one LLM invoked per query. | - | Framing statement (how the paper states its problem, challenge, objective, solution or gain); not a measurement. | line 69 of the saved text | 69 | primary | corrected by the auditor |

| # | Field | Claim | Figure | Measurement definition | Location | Line | Label | Audit |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 0 | framing_problem | Agentic workflows incur high inference latency because LLMs are invoked repeatedly for each agent; prefix caching of the agents' fixed prompts reduces this, but prefix caching alone is insufficient under limited GPU memory, where the LRU eviction of existing serving systems leads to suboptimal performance in agentic workflows. | - | Framing statement (how the paper states its problem, challenge, objective, solution or gain); not a measurement. | line 77 of the saved text | 77 | primary | corrected by the auditor |
| 1 | framing_challenge | LRU eviction fails to anticipate future agent usage and often discards KV caches shortly before their reuse (an agent about to run may have been idle a long time), causing frequent cache misses and recomputation or swapping overhead; memory runs out with many concurrent workflows or very large agent prompts on limited hardware, and reactive CPU-to-GPU loading of offloaded prefixes still adds noticeable transfer latency. | - | Framing statement (how the paper states its problem, challenge, objective, solution or gain); not a measurement. | line 70 of the saved text | 70 | primary | corrected by the auditor |
| 2 | framing_objective | No formal objective function. The evaluation asks (1) whether KVFlow reduces end-to-end latency for individual workflows with large prompt prefixes and limited GPU memory and (2) how it performs under high concurrency with multiple parallel workflows. Single-workflow latency is measured at batch size 1 for a 10-agent sequential workflow executed ten times (latency averaged over all runs) and reported as speedup over SGLang (GPU-only radix cache), with SGLang w/ HiCache also compared; the high-concurrency results are reported as speedup / 'performance' over SGLang and HiCache without a further metric definition in the saved text. The paper states the evaluation focuses exclusively on system performance metrics like latency because output semantics are unchanged. The design quantity is each agent's steps-to-execution (how soon the agent is expected to run), computed on the Agent Step Graph by step aggregation functions, e.g. \max(E1,E2)+1 when an agent needs both upstream executors E1 and E2 to finish and \min(E1,E2)+1 when either suffices. | - | Framing statement (how the paper states its problem, challenge, objective, solution or gain); not a measurement. | line 149 of the saved text | 149 | primary | corrected by the auditor |
| 3 | framing_solution | Because the workflow structure predicts which agents run next, KVFlow replaces LRU with a workflow-aware eviction policy that evicts KV cache nodes of agents with large steps-to-execution first (priorities set per cache-tree node so shared prefixes are kept, varying suffixes evicted first), and prefetches the KV tensors of next-scheduled agents from CPU to GPU in background threads with status-aware scheduling so transfers overlap with computation. | - | Framing statement (how the paper states its problem, challenge, objective, solution or gain); not a measurement. | line 82 of the saved text | 82 | primary | corrected by the auditor |
| 4 | framing_gain | Speedup: up to 1.83x over SGLang with hierarchical radix cache (HiCache) for single workflows with large prompts (single-workflow latency, batch size 1) and up to 2.19x for scenarios with many concurrent workflows; in the body also 2.91x over GPU-only SGLang (8192/32/32 on A10G, where the 1.83x over HiCache is also measured), an 'up to 1.25x speedup' in the high-concurrency settings where KVFlow outperforms both SGLang and HiCache (the sentence does not name the baseline of the 1.25x), and up to 1.12x / 1.08x over SGLang / HiCache in a PEER-style realistic workflow simulation. | - | Framing statement (how the paper states its problem, challenge, objective, solution or gain); not a measurement. | line 73 of the saved text | 73 | primary | corrected by the auditor |

| 0 | framing_problem | Current test-time scaling makes agents 'think' longer before acting, which does not allow them to acquire new information from the environment or adapt their behavior over time; post-trained agents are reactive and often suboptimal in partially observable or non-stationary settings where information-seeking behavior is needed. | - | Framing statement (how the paper states its problem, challenge, objective, solution or gain); not a measurement. | line 84 of the saved text | 84 | primary | corrected by the auditor |
| 1 | framing_challenge | Teaching agents to scale interaction autonomously presents key challenges: without appropriate training signals agents may overfit to exploratory behaviors like blindly clicking links without progress toward the task, wasting the additional steps; prompting alone ('check-again') only lets the agent revisit its behavior upon task completion and cannot produce mid-rollout switching between exploration and exploitation; and RL with a fixed horizon either overfits and terminates prematurely (short h) or learns slowly because of higher loss variance and noisy credit assignment (long h). | - | Framing statement (how the paper states its problem, challenge, objective, solution or gain); not a measurement. | line 95 of the saved text | 95 | primary | corrected by the auditor |

Training objective (Eq. 5.1, online filtered BC): \argmax_{\theta} E_{\mathcal{T}~tasks}[ E_{o_{0:h},a_{0:h-1}~\pi(./\mathcal{T})}[ (\sum_{t=0}^{h-1} \log \pi_{\theta}(a_t / o_{\leq t}, \mathcal{T})) · 1[R(o_{0:h},\mathcal{T})=1] ] ], where \theta are the policy parameters, \mathcal{T} a task, o_t the observation and a_t the action at step t, h the maximum interaction horizon, and R the binary task reward, so only successful trajectories are imitated. TTI sets the horizon per iteration i by a curriculum: additive h_i := clip(h_min + i, h_max) or multiplicative h_i := clip(h_min · i, h_max) (default, h_min = 10, h_max = 30). | - | Framing statement (how the paper states its problem, challenge, objective, solution or gain); not a measurement. | line 160 of the saved text | 160 | primary | corrected by the auditor |
| 3 | framing_solution | Scale test-time interaction (more interaction steps within one rollout) as an axis complementary to per-step reasoning, because each extra step of interaction provides new information from the environment whereas thinking longer only reorganizes information the agent already has; to learn this, combine online RL with a curriculum over the interaction horizon that trains on short trajectories first and gradually exposes the agent to longer ones, so it learns effective exploitation before extending its horizon to explore. | - | Framing statement (how the paper states its problem, challenge, objective, solution or gain); not a measurement. | line 95 of the saved text | 95 | primary | corrected by the auditor |

## f225 — Multi-Segment Attention: Enabling Efficient KV-Cache Management for Faster Large Language Model Serving

- Source: https://arxiv.org/html/2606.02964v1 · version read: v1 · v1: Mon, 1 Jun 2026 23:51:37 UTC
- Source class: institutional supplement · no formal publication confirmed
- Audit: None; 6 items kept, 0 dropped

| # | Field | Claim | Figure | Measurement definition | Location | Line | Label | Audit |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 0 | framing_problem | Within lossless KV cache management under GPU memory pressure (long contexts, concurrent sessions, multi-turn workloads), decide which KV cache blocks should remain resident in GPU memory, with the goal of improving serving efficiency without sacrificing output correctness. | - | Framing statement (how the paper states its problem, challenge, objective, solution or gain); not a measurement. | line 112 of the saved text | 112 | primary | corrected by the auditor |
| 1 | framing_challenge | Existing lossless systems base eviction decisions on access frequency or positional heuristics without considering how different KV cache blocks affect the execution efficiency of GPU attention kernels; their policies do not explicitly model each block's future reuse likelihood and marginal impact on attention-kernel latency, although recomputation cost is asymmetric (later positions cost more because attention is quadratic) while shared prefixes carry hit rate. Supporting non-contiguous cached segments needs an attention kernel that handles disjoint KV regions, and dispatching each segment to a separate kernel call adds kernel launch and host synchronization overheads; and the straightforward frequency-value definitions of existing cost-aware policies cause linear-time eviction, which is highly inefficient compared to LRU's O(1). | - | Framing statement (how the paper states its problem, challenge, objective, solution or gain); not a measurement. | line 92 of the saved text | 92 | primary | corrected by the auditor |
| 2 | framing_objective | Eviction criterion (Eq. 3): block_id <- \argmin_{B} E(B,t) = \argmin_{B} f_{B}(t) · \Delta T_{B}, i.e. evict the block with the lowest expected recomputation cost. f_B(t) is the frequency value of KV block B at time t (historical access frequency with decay, taken as a proxy for reuse probability), defined in Eq. 9 as f_B(t) := min(exp(-\tau_B(t)/\alpha), exp(-(\tau_B(t)-\tau_0)/\beta)), where \alpha and \beta set the decay rates of the two exponential pieces and \tau_0 shifts the second piece (\tau_B(t) itself is not defined in words in the saved text). \Delta T_B is the block's cost, the additional prefilling time if it is evicted, approximated from a fitted linear latency model T(l_1,q_1,l_2,q_2) as \Delta T_B = 2k_5·(l_1+q_1)+(k_2-k_3+k_5), where (l_1+q_1) is the block's positional index (number of preceding blocks) and the k's are coefficients fitted on about 1.1K profiling instances (l_1,q_1,l_2,q_2 refer to Figure 6 and are not defined in words in the text). In the implementation (Algorithm 1) the two exponential pieces are kept in two balanced trees and the evicted block is \argmin\{B_1.w_1, \lambda × B_2.w_2\}, where \lambda (initially 1) is adjusted online from the average lifespan \tau of cache blocks in a sliding window as \lambda_{new} <- \exp((\tau-\tau_0)/\beta - \tau/\alpha) (Eq. 10). Reported metrics are average TTFT and TPOT plus request- and block-level hit rates; for agent workloads, average and P90 job latency. | - | Framing statement (how the paper states its problem, challenge, objective, solution or gain); not a measurement. | line 202 of the saved text | 202 | primary | corrected by the auditor |
| 3 | framing_solution | AsymCache aligns KV cache residency decisions with GPU attention-kernel performance: the evictor ranks blocks by frequency times position-dependent recomputation cost (keeping both shared prefixes and costly later blocks, dropping less useful middle segments) with a piecewise exponential frequency function that allows logarithmic-time eviction; a Multi-Segment Attention kernel computes attention over non-contiguous cached segments in one kernel call; and a chunking scheduler adapts prefill chunk sizes. ## f229 — Preble: Efficient Distributed Prompt Scheduling for LLM Serving

- Source: https://arxiv.org/html/2407.00023v2 · version read: v2 · v1: Wed, 8 May 2024 06:30:58 UTC
- Source class: top venue · formal venue (confirmed at the official source): The Thirteenth International Conference on Learning Representations (ICLR 2025)
- Audit: None; 6 items kept, 0 dropped

| # | Field | Claim | Figure | Measurement definition | Location | Line | Label | Audit |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 0 | framing_problem | Prompts are long and partially shared across requests, and existing KV-cache reuse is confined to a single-GPU optimization, while production LLM serving systems are distributed; current distributed serving systems are not prompt-cache-aware and distribute computation load equally across GPUs, which could send requests with shared prefixes to different GPUs, causing KV computation at all of them that could otherwise be avoided if prefixes were cached and reused on the same GPU. | - | Framing statement (how the paper states its problem, challenge, objective, solution or gain); not a measurement. | line 64 of the saved text | 64 | primary | corrected by the auditor |
| 1 | framing_challenge | Load balancing and prefix reuse conflict: equal load distribution could send shared-prefix requests to different GPUs and cause avoidable KV computation there (line 64), while a naive solution that always sends shared-prefix requests to the same GPU would result in imbalanced loads and low overall GPU utilization, because the GPU first serving a popular prefix accumulates a huge load of new requests (line 65); in addition, the variations in prompt-sharing features and request arrival patterns make it challenging to build an efficient distributed serving system (line 95), and the Azure trace shows requests arriving at varying speeds over time and across LLM usages (line 68). Prompts are 37x to 2494x longer than generated sequences in the five studied workloads (line 67), and long prompts with short generations imply that the prefill phase significantly outweighs decoding (line 60). | - | Framing statement (how the paper states its problem, challenge, objective, solution or gain); not a measurement. | line 65 of the saved text | 65 | primary | corrected by the auditor |
| 2 | framing_objective | The system aims at high serving throughput and low average and tail request latency (line 78). The E2 scheduler, when exploring and all GPUs have relatively balanced prefill-decoding loads, assigns request R_k to the GPU with the lowest total cost L_{i}+M_{i}+P_{i}, all expressed as GPU computation time: L_{i}=\sum_{r\in W}(PT_{r}+DT_{r}) is GPU_i's load over the requests W in a recent window H (default 3 minutes), with PT_r the prefill time estimated by regression from the tokens of R_r not matching prefixes on GPU_i and DT_r the decoding time estimated from the average output length in H; M_{i}=\sum_{j\in E}PT_{j}\times N_{j} is the eviction cost, with E the set of tree nodes to evict, PT_j the prefill time for node j's length and N_j the number of requests sharing node j in H over the total requests on GPU_i in H; P_i is the prefill time of the missed tokens of R_k. E2 exploits (sends to the GPU caching the longest matched prefix, with ties broken by the lightest load) when matched prefix tokens exceed the remaining tokens (lines 115-116). Before the load-cost comparison, a request to be explored is sent to a GPU heavily loaded with decoding-phase units (requests whose prompts are fully cached); this prefill-decoding balancing rule is prioritised over the load-cost comparison (line 144). Post-assignment rules: if the most heavily loaded GPU's load exceeds Th_{bal} times the lightest GPU's load, requests that would exploit the heavy GPU are redirected to the light one until the difference is below Th_{bal} (lines 139-140); a prefix is autoscaled (replicated, subtree split by load) when its average queueing time doubles over H after rebalancing (line 141). Local wait queue: P priority groups by cached-token percentage, with more requests selected per batch from higher-priority groups (lines 155-156). Evaluation metrics: requests per second (serving capacity), average end-to-end request latency (scheduling, queueing, prefill and decoding time) and p99 request latency (line 173). | - | Framing statement (how the paper states its problem, challenge, objective, solution or gain); not a measurement. | line 134 of the saved text | 134 | primary | corrected by the auditor |
| 3 | framing_solution | A distributed scheduling algorithm, E2 (Exploitation + Exploration), co-designs computation load-balancing and prefix-cache sharing: requests reuse cached prefixes on the same GPU when the saved recomputation exceeds the new computation, and otherwise explore the GPU with the lowest prompt-aware load; this is complemented by load rebalancing and prefix autoscaling, prefill-decoding mixing based on cache hits, and fairness-aware local scheduling. | - | Framing statement (how the paper states its problem, challenge, objective, solution or gain); not a measurement. | line 69 of the saved text | 69 | primary | corrected by the auditor |
| 4 | framing_gain | Preble reports 1.5x to 14.5x lower average latency and 2x to 10x lower p99 latency than the SOTA serving systems (abstract, line 56); in the body the ranges are over data-parallel (round-robin) SGLang on the five workloads with Poisson arrivals, Mistral 7B on two/four A6000 GPUs and Llama-3 70B on eight H100 GPUs (Figure 3; lines 165, 176, 181, 188). The introduction says results are similar against vLLM (line 85), while Appendix C reports less relative improvement with vLLM as the backend (line 611). The Azure-trace experiment (mixed tool-use and video QA on four A6000 GPUs) is described only as significant improvements in average and p99 latency, TTFT and TPOT, with no range (lines 189-193). | - | Framing statement (how the paper states its problem, challenge, objective, solution or gain); not a measurement. | line 56 of the saved text | 56 | primary | corrected by the auditor |
| 5 | framing_classification | Classification by the extractor, checked by the auditor: efficiency in the stated problem = central; efficiency terms = average latency, p99 latency, tail latency, end-to-end request latency, queueing time, serving throughput, serving speed, requests per second (RPS), TTFT, TPOT, prefill computation, KV recomputation, GPU computation time, load, GPU utilization, system overhead; agent kind = LLM serving system: Preble, a distributed GPU-based LLM serving platform with a global request-level scheduler and per-GPU local schedulers; agents (tool use, embodied agents) appear only as studied workloads.; position = model inference/serving. | - | Reader classification (not a statement of the paper). | whole abstract and introduction |  | secondary | corrected by the auditor |

## f231 — Efficient LLM Serving for Agentic Workflows: A Data Systems Perspective

- Source: https://arxiv.org/html/2603.16104v1 · version read: v1 · v1: Tue, 17 Mar 2026 04:03:18 UTC
- Source class: top venue · formal venue (confirmed at the official source): Proceedings of the ACM on Management of Data, 4
- Audit: None; 6 items kept, 0 dropped

| # | Field | Claim | Figure | Measurement definition | Location | Line | Label | Audit |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 0 | framing_problem | Agentic workflows issue a large volume of interdependent LLM calls with extensive redundancy from overlapping prompts and intermediate results (speculative and parallel exploration), but existing LLM serving systems such as vLLM optimize individual inference calls and overlook cross-call dependencies, leading to significant inefficiencies and leaving performance optimizations unexplored for batch agentic workflows. | - | Framing statement (how the paper states its problem, challenge, objective, solution or gain); not a measurement. | line 48 of the saved text | 48 | primary | corrected by the auditor |
| 1 | framing_challenge | Serving engines work at the granularity of single calls with no visibility into the workflow DAG ('operator-level myopia'), so their prefix caching is local, passive and reactive and cannot guarantee KV reuse for related calls separated by unrelated requests; orchestration frameworks and data systems treat LLM calls as black-box UDFs, hiding the stateful KV cache and prefill/decode cost structure from the optimizer; and in multi-turn patterns such as debate the shared context is reprocessed on every turn. | - | Framing statement (how the paper states its problem, challenge, objective, solution or gain); not a measurement. | line 84 of the saved text | 84 | primary | corrected by the auditor |
| 2 | framing_objective | Scheduling is formulated as a multi-worker makespan problem: Minimize T(sigma) = max_{i=1../W/, j=1../L_i/} c(i,j) such that b(i,j) >= c(i',j') + d(i',j') for all (l^{i'}_{j'}, l^i_j) in E', and c(i,j) = b(i,j) + u(i,j). Here sigma = (sigma_1,...,sigma_/W/) assigns and orders LLM calls (leaves l of the call-level templated radix tree T=(V,E,E')) on workers W; b(i,j) and c(i,j) are the start and completion token steps of the j-th call on worker i; token usage u(i,j) = alpha_i (lenOut(l^i_j) x u_p(i,j) + u_d(i,j)), where u_p is the prefill usage (sum of node weights omega(v), i.e. prompt-segment token counts, on the path from the root for the first call, otherwise from the lowest common ancestor with the previous call on that worker, so shared prefixes are not counted), u_d = 1/2 lenOut(lenOut+1) is the cumulative decode token count, lenOut is the estimated number of output tokens, and alpha_i is a worker normalization constant (1/M_i for identical workers, M_i = KV cache capacity in tokens); d(i,j) = alpha_i M_i x lenOut(l^i_j) is a precedence delay that models batching; T(sigma) is the total token step, analogous to makespan; the problem is NP-hard. | 1 | framing_challenge | Three limitations of prior approaches: a static tool set of primitive actions (the minimum spanning set to reach any browser state) that costs longer execution times and higher error rates; sequential execution that does not explore the space of schedules such as task parallelism and request hedging; and non-determinism post-plan, where the standard agent loop calls the LM at each step even when no LM call is needed between tool calls; in addition, prior code-action work ignores that many valid code plans exist with different latency. | - | Framing statement (how the paper states its problem, challenge, objective, solution or gain); not a measurement. | line 109 of the saved text | 109 | primary | corrected by the auditor |
| 2 | framing_objective | Two argmin objectives. Planner (Algorithm 1): among k = 32 valid candidate plans, return argmin over (pi, c) of c, where c is a unitless weighted call count that accumulates C_tool * gamma^d for each tool call and C_eval * gamma^d for each ai_eval (LLM) call at CFG depth d (base weights C_tool = 0.1, C_eval = 10.0; gamma = 10 is a loop-nesting penalty), and a plan is invalid if the tracked state s does not contain a tool's precondition (s is updated with the tool's postconditions); the paper states this cost only ranks plans by expected latency (by number of LLM calls and nesting depth) and does not predict absolute latency. Scheduler (Algorithm 2): minimizes estimated latency. Scheduler (Algorithm 2): return argmin over sigma in {Ser, Par, Hed} of mean latency L-bar_sigma over N_MC Monte Carlo trials, with serial latency S(U_sigma), hedge latency min_{w=1..n} S(U_sigma) + delta_h, and parallel latency S(U_sigma^seq) + max_{w=1..n} S_w(U_sigma,w) + delta_p, where S(U) = sum_{e in U} sum_{i=1}^{count(e)} sample(D_e), U_sigma is the LLM-predicted element usage, count(e) the predicted number of interactions with element e, D_e its learned latency distribution, n the workers (vCPU budget, n = 4 in experiments), N_MC = 1000, and delta_h (5-15 s), delta_p (20-30 s) overheads. | 0 | framing_problem | As AI agents move toward persistent, stateful execution, checkpoint and rollback are becoming essential for recovery, yet their security implications remain largely unexplored: correct rollback does not imply secure recovery, since a faithfully restored checkpoint may resume an execution whose states, assumptions and external effects never coexisted in any valid history. | - | Framing statement (how the paper states its problem, challenge, objective, solution or gain); not a measurement. | line 65 of the saved text | 65 | primary | corrected by the auditor |
| 1 | framing_challenge | Recovery carries forward security-relevant facts (an artifact validated, an operation authorized, an external effect not yet occurred) whose validity depends on state spread across framework components, files and runtimes, nondeterministic decisions and external services, which do not necessarily share the same recovery scope, so a checkpoint's recovery boundary may not cover the full set of security dependencies on which the restored state relies. | - | Framing statement (how the paper states its problem, challenge, objective, solution or gain); not a measurement. | line 99 of the saved text | 99 | primary | corrected by the auditor |
| 2 | framing_objective | Prevalence of each of five security failures (SF1-SF5) at the execution level: for each task execution, whether a given SF is observed at least once during its execution and rollback, validated by restoring a random checkpoint with the framework's native mechanism and re-executing (for SF4 candidates the post-checkpoint execution is re-executed independently three times, and SF4 is validated when the replay produces a different security-relevant execution path). The formal model writes the recovered configuration as X̂ = ((s_i^{k_i})_{P_i∈K} ⊕ (ρ_j)_{P_j∉K}, W^{t_r}), where P_i are logical processes, s_i^{k_i} their checkpointed local states, K the set of processes covered by checkpoint C_K (its recovery boundary), ρ_j the recovered state of an uncovered process, and W^{t_r} the outside world at rollback time t_r; execution continuity requires security-relevant states, decisions, assumptions and effects to stay jointly consistent with a valid continuous execution history. | - | Framing statement (how the paper states its problem, challenge, objective, solution or gain); not a measurement. | line 1041 of the saved text | 1041 | primary | corrected by the auditor |
| 3 | framing_solution | Characterize existing C/R designs by recovery boundary (framework, workspace, OS/VM state), build a general execution model with partial recovery boundaries and a non-rolling-back outside world, derive five failure modes from it, and detect them with a multi-agent pipeline (collector, analyzer, checker, validator) that reconstructs execution semantics from traces and validates candidates through actual rollback. | - | Framing statement (how the paper states its problem, challenge, objective, solution or gain); not a measurement. | line 67 of the saved text | 67 | primary | corrected by the auditor |
| 4 | framing_gain | No efficiency gain is claimed; the paper reports that failures are common across 1,735 framework-task executions (347 TerminalBench and AgentBench traces, five frameworks), with SF1 and SF4 in 67.2% and 67.7% of executions and SF5 in 2.3%, and demonstrates three end-to-end attacks (malware-verification bypass, unauthorized mail forwarding, double payment); the detection pipeline reaches 98.7% precision and 99.9% recall under manual validation. | - | Framing statement (how the paper states its problem, challenge, objective, solution or gain); not a measurement. | line 1141 of the saved text | 1141 | primary | corrected by the auditor |

Prior acceleration work (DAG-based parallel tool execution, overlapping tool execution with decoding) targets tool execution rather than generation, and because tool-calling generation can be formulated as constrained decoding under predefined schemas, acceleration methods designed for general text generation may be suboptimal for tool calling (§3.2). | - | Framing statement (how the paper states its problem, challenge, objective, solution or gain); not a measurement. | line 84 of the saved text | 84 | primary | corrected by the auditor |

## f238 — Reducing Cost of LLM Agents with Trajectory Reduction

- Source: https://arxiv.org/html/2509.23586v2 · version read: v2 · v1: Sun, 28 Sep 2025 02:43:41 UTC
- Source class: top venue · formal venue (confirmed at the official source): Proceedings of the ACM on Software Engineering, 3
