| # | Field | Claim | Figure | Measurement definition | Location | Line | Label | Audit |

| 0 | framing_problem | LLM agents show promising effectiveness on software engineering tasks, but the high computational cost of input tokens caused by ever-growing trajectories is a significant efficiency concern that existing studies and agent products have largely overlooked. | - | Framing statement (how the paper states its problem, challenge, objective, solution or gain); not a measurement. | line 86 of the saved text | 86 | primary | corrected by the auditor |
| 1 | framing_challenge | The root cause is the ever-growing trajectory: once the LLM calls a tool, the call and its result stay in the trajectory until the task ends and are included in every subsequent input, so verbose outputs snowball in cost (the paper cites that in September 2025, 99% of Claude 4 Sonnet's daily tokens on OpenRouter were input tokens accumulated in the trajectory); trajectories contain useless, redundant and expired information. Existing token-reduction work targets single-turn tasks, reducing all input tokens at once (so the timing of reduction is an open question for agents), working on natural language rather than structured code, or requiring changes to LLM inference or the model; agent products compact only when the context window is full or the user asks, aiming at robustness rather than efficiency. KV Cache does not remove the need and makes reduction harder, since modifying a token invalidates the cache for all later tokens, and LLM agents given an erase tool often did not reduce their own trajectories despite explicit prompts. | - | Framing statement (how the paper states its problem, challenge, objective, solution or gain); not a measurement. | line 94 of the saved text | 94 | primary | corrected by the auditor |
| 2 | framing_objective | Efficiency metrics: Keep% = Σ l_reduced / Σ l_orig * 100, the average percentage of trajectory tokens retained by the reflection LLM (l_orig, l_reduced = step lengths before and after reduction in Algorithm 1); I and O, accumulated input and output tokens normalized so the Original baseline has I=1; $ and $+, LLM cost of agent steps and of reflection steps from provider pricing (input tokens with KV Cache discount plus output tokens), normalized so Original has $=1. Performance metrics: Pass% (resolved instances) and Step/PStep (average agent steps over all / resolved instances). Efficiency improves if Keep% is low and I/O/$ fall; performance is unharmed if Pass% does not decrease and Step/PStep does not increase. | - | Framing statement (how the paper states its problem, challenge, objective, solution or gain); not a measurement. | line 302 of the saved text | 302 | primary | corrected by the auditor |
| 3 | framing_solution | AgentDiet removes useless, redundant and expired information during execution with a separate LLM-based reflection module called by the outer system rather than by the agent. To control overhead it uses a cost-efficient LLM (GPT-5 mini) and a sliding window: at step s the module may reduce only step s-a, given context from step s-a-b to s; reflection is skipped when step s-a is within a token threshold θ, and a reduction is applied only if it removes more than θ tokens. Because only a fixed recent step is modified, KV Cache entries for earlier steps are preserved. | - | Framing statement (how the paper states its problem, challenge, objective, solution or gain); not a measurement. | line 87 of the saved text | 87 | primary | corrected by the auditor |
| 4 | framing_gain | Against the Original Trae Agent without reflection, on two LLMs (Claude 4 Sonnet, Gemini 2.5 Pro) and two benchmarks (SWE-bench Verified, Multi-SWE-bench Flash), AgentDiet reduces input tokens by 39.9%-59.7% and total computational cost by 21.1%-35.9% (including reflection overhead) while keeping Pass% comparable (-1.0% to +2.0%). | - | Framing statement (how the paper states its problem, challenge, objective, solution or gain); not a measurement. | line 87 of the saved text | 87 | primary | corrected by the auditor |
| 5 | framing_classification | Classification by the extractor, checked by the auditor: efficiency in the stated problem = central; efficiency terms = computational cost, input tokens (accumulated input / prompt tokens), output (completion) tokens, LLM cost for agent steps ($) and reflection steps ($+) from pricing, with KV Cache discount, average US$ cost per instance, Keep% (trajectory tokens retained), KV Cache, VRAM and I/O bandwidth, steps (Step, PStep; used as performance-impact metrics), latency (discussed as future work, not measured), trajectory length and accumulated token usage per issue (48.4K tokens in 40 steps; 1.0M accumulated tokens); agent kind = multi-turn LLM agents for software engineering tasks (coding agents), implemented on Trae Agent; position = agent loop (steps, calls, context). | - | Reader classification (not a statement of the paper). | whole abstract and introduction |  | secondary | corrected by the auditor |

| 1 | framing_challenge | Existing approaches (static text pruning/compression, context folding, demand paging, dynamic memory eviction) minimise token footprints through unconstrained sequence mutations that alter layouts, introducing prefix mismatches and cache invalidation; the paper states that the resulting pre-fill penalties and cache invalidations ultimately override the financial savings from text reduction, revealing a trade-off between text sparsity and prompt cache continuity. | - | Framing statement (how the paper states its problem, challenge, objective, solution or gain); not a measurement. | line 99 of the saved text | 99 | primary | corrected by the auditor |
| 2 | framing_objective | Eq. (1): max over M of [ sum_{m in C'} U^(m / C') ] / K(C'), where M is a context management framework, C the raw session history (instructions, reasoning traces, tool calls, responses), C' = M(C) the optimized runtime context, U^(m / C') the estimated marginal contribution of message m to subsequent agent actions (context utility), and K(C') the serving cost. Eq. (2): K(C') = alpha * /C'_hit/ + /C'_miss/, where C'_hit are tokens served from the prompt cache at discounted rate alpha << 1 and C'_miss tokens incur full pre-fill cost, subject to /C'/ = /C'_hit/ + /C'_miss/. The reported metric (Appendix A.2, Eq. 11) is Cost = /C'_hit/ * p_hit + /C'_miss/ * p_miss + H_out * p_out, with H_out the length of generated responses and GPT-5.4-mini prices p_hit = $0.075/M, p_miss = $0.75/M, p_out = $4.50/M tokens; task accuracy is tracked alongside. Task score follows each benchmark's native grader; for Claw-Eval, Eq. (10): Score = s_safe x (0.80 s_comp + 0.20 s_rob) (safety as a multiplicative gate); PinchBench aggregates task-specific verification checks on deliverables. ## f247 — CacheBlend: Fast Large Language Model Serving for RAG with Cached Knowledge Fusion

- Source: https://arxiv.org/html/2405.16444v3 · version read: v3 · v1: Sun, 26 May 2024 06:00:17 UTC
- Source class: top venue · formal venue (confirmed at the official source): Proceedings of the Twentieth European Conference on Computer Systems (EuroSys 2025)
- Audit: None; 6 items kept, 0 dropped

| # | Field | Claim | Figure | Measurement definition | Location | Line | Label | Audit |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 0 | framing_problem | Context text chunks prepended to a query (e.g. retrieved chunks in RAG) significantly slow down LLM inference because prefill must process the whole input before the first token; the paper tackles one challenge: when an LLM input contains multiple text chunks, how to quickly combine their individually pre-computed KV caches while achieving the same generation quality as the expensive full prefill. | - | Framing statement (how the paper states its problem, challenge, objective, solution or gain); not a measurement. | line 116 of the saved text | 116 | primary | corrected by the auditor |
| 1 | framing_challenge | The delay and computation of prefill grow super-linearly with input length. Existing KV-cache reuse does not cover the multi-chunk case: prefix caching only reuses the KV cache of the input prefix (the first chunk), and full KV reuse of non-prefix chunks ignores the cross-attention between a chunk and its preceding chunks, which cannot be precomputed because the preceding chunks are not known in advance, so quality drops. | - | Framing statement (how the paper states its problem, challenge, objective, solution or gain); not a measurement. | line 77 of the saved text | 77 | primary | corrected by the auditor |
| 2 | framing_objective | Goal (Sec. 4, Goal 0, line 230; formalized in Sec. 4.1, line 290): quickly update the precomputed KV cache KV^pre to the new KV cache KV^new such that the attention deviation Δ_attn(A^new_i, A^full_i) on any layer i is minimized. Symbols from the text: i is the layer index and j the token index; KV^full is the KV cache from full KV recompute, KV^pre the pre-computed KV cache, KV^new the CacheBlend-updated KV cache; A_i is the forward attention matrix on layer i (A^full_i for full KV recompute, A^pre_i for full KV reuse, A^new_i with CacheBlend); Δ_attn is the L-2 norm of the difference between A_i and A^full_i; the KV deviation Δ_kv(KV_i, KV^full_i)[j] is the absolute difference between KV_i[j] and KV^full_i[j]. Goal 0 states the speed side only as 'quickly'; the delay side is written as explicit formulas for the loading controller (Sec. 5.1, footnotes 5-6, lines 385-398): T_recompute(r%, LLM, L) = r% × Prefill(LLM, L), with Prefill(LLM, L) profiled offline and L the length of context to be loaded, and T_load(LLM, L, storage_device) = PerTokenKVSize(LLM) × L / Throughput(storage_device); the controller picks r% so that T_recompute equals T_load and then takes the max of r% and r*%, where r*% (15% in practice) is the minimal recompute ratio with negligible quality drop; for storage it uses a storage-cost estimator C_store(LLM, L, T, storage_device) (T = time the KV must be stored) and picks the cheapest device with T_recompute ≥ T_load at a fixed 15% ratio. Recomputing r% of tokens per layer costs r% of full-prefill compute (line 309). Results are reported as TTFT, throughput and quality (F1, Rouge-L). | - | Framing statement (how the paper states its problem, challenge, objective, solution or gain); not a measurement. | line 290 of the saved text | 290 | primary | corrected by the auditor |
| 3 | framing_solution | CacheBlend reuses the pre-computed KV caches of all chunks, prefix or not, and in each layer selectively recomputes the KV of only a small fraction of tokens (the high-KV-deviation tokens, chosen by gradual filtering from layer to layer) based on the preceding texts in the specific input, which suffices because attention matrices are sparse. The partial KV update on one layer is pipelined with fetching the next layer's KV cache into GPU memory; the introduction states this adds no inference latency and lets KV caches be stored on slower non-volatile devices (lines 128-130), while Sec. 5 makes this conditional on loading one layer's KV being at least as slow as selective recompute of one layer (line 369) — for Llama-70B on NVMe SSD the loading does not completely hide the recompute delay (lines 373-374) — so a loading controller picks the recompute ratio and storage device. | - | Framing statement (how the paper states its problem, challenge, objective, solution or gain); not a measurement. | line 118 of the saved text | 118 | primary | corrected by the auditor |
| 4 | framing_gain | CacheBlend reduces time-to-first-token (TTFT) by 2.2–3.3x and increases inference throughput by 2.8–5x 'without compromising generation quality'. The baseline differs by location: the abstract (line 84) and the evaluation (Fig. 12 caption line 432; takeaways lines 437-438) state the TTFT reduction against full KV recompute, and the evaluation gives throughput 'at the same TTFT' as up to 5x vs full KV recompute and 3.3x vs prefix caching (line 442), while the introduction (line 134) attributes both ranges to a comparison with prefix caching. Against full KV reuse, the introduction reports almost the same TTFT with 0.1–0.2 higher absolute F1 on QA and 0.03–0.25 higher absolute Rouge-L on summarization (line 136); the evaluation instead states a 0.15–0.35 quality improvement over full KV reuse and no more than 0.01–0.03 quality drop vs full KV recompute and prefix caching (line 440). | - | Framing statement (how the paper states its problem, challenge, objective, solution or gain); not a measurement. | line 84 of the saved text | 84 | primary | corrected by the auditor |
| 5 | framing_classification | Classification by the extractor, checked by the auditor: efficiency in the stated problem = central; efficiency terms = prefill delay, time-to-first-token (TTFT), inference throughput, inference delay / inference latency, delay and computation of prefill, prefill overhead, speed, compute overhead (r% of full prefill), KV loading delay, storage cost, recompute ratio / update fraction of tokens; agent kind = LLM serving system (KV-cache reuse inside the LLM inference engine, implemented on vLLM) for retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) inputs made of multiple text chunks; not an agent paper; position = model inference/serving (prefill / KV-cache reuse in the LLM serving engine). | - | Reader classification (not a statement of the paper). | whole abstract and introduction |  | secondary | corrected by the auditor |

## f248 — KVCOMM: Online Cross-context KV-cache Communication for Efficient LLM-based Multi-agent Systems

- Source: https://arxiv.org/html/2510.12872v2 · version read: v2 · v1: Tue, 14 Oct 2025 18:00:01 UTC
- Source class: top venue · formal venue (confirmed at the official source): Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems 38 (NeurIPS 2025)

| # | Field | Claim | Figure | Measurement definition | Location | Line | Label | Audit |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 0 | framing_problem | Multi-agent LLM systems often suffer substantial overhead from repeated reprocessing of overlapping contexts across agents: every message must be prefilled with the full conversation history, and agents sharing overlapping context (retrieved passages, peer outputs) redundantly recompute KV caches for all input tokens, which the paper defines as the multi-context redundancy issue; with M agents each receiving all peers' messages, prefill complexity scales as O(M^2). | - | Framing statement (how the paper states its problem, challenge, objective, solution or gain); not a measurement. | line 88 of the saved text | 88 | primary | corrected by the auditor |
| 1 | framing_challenge | KV caching is effective for avoiding redundant computation in single-agent settings where prefixes remain unchanged, but it cannot be directly reused in multi-agent scenarios because agent-specific context extensions create diverging prefixes; the paper identifies the core challenge as the offset variance of KV caches across agents — the same shared text incurs vastly different KV deviations under different prefix contexts (line 96). Existing methods (prompt-level reuse, selective recomputation, cache compression, kernel-level optimizations) share a fixed acceleration policy crafted for a particular workload; when the policy fails to model offset variance, cache reuse becomes misaligned, causing either large accuracy drops or a fallback to full recomputation that erodes the speed benefits (line 96; line 148: none of the existing static policies can predict the positional and contextual shifts). | - | Framing statement (how the paper states its problem, challenge, objective, solution or gain); not a measurement. | line 88 of the saved text | 88 | primary | corrected by the auditor |
| 2 | framing_objective | No explicit optimisation objective or loss is written. The stated target is to reduce prefilling latency without sacrificing task performance (line 149); the conclusion calls it a trade-off between prefilling efficiency and system accuracy (line 735). Reported metrics: accuracy (MMLU, GSM8K), Pass@1 (HumanEval), Reuse Rate and TTFT (individual agent TTFT and average TTFT across agents, TTFT speedup). Reuse Rate is defined twice for KVComm: 'the proportion of agents employing the cache reuse scheme' (Sec. 4.1, line 481) and 'the frequency of agents reusing all KV-caches in the whole serving procedure' (Table 1 caption, line 232); for CacheBlend it is the proportion of tokens reusing KV caches (line 232). Eq. (5) is an anchor-prediction criterion (with entropy threshold γ and anchor-pool size V as hyperparameters) and Eqs. (6)-(7) are the offset approximation, not objectives. | - | Framing statement (how the paper states its problem, challenge, objective, solution or gain); not a measurement. | line 149 of the saved text | 149 | primary | corrected by the auditor |
| 3 | framing_solution | KVComm treats every reuse attempt as an approximate translation problem: the KV cache of overlapping text becomes reusable under a new prefix once the positional shift and the cache offsets observed for similar samples are known. It keeps an online anchor pool of previously shared samples with their measured offsets under different prefixes, matches the nearest anchors by token-embedding similarity, and adds the interpolated offsets to the base cache (after RoPE re-positioning of keys), so agents skip redundant prefilling; unshareable segments become new anchors. | - | Framing statement (how the paper states its problem, challenge, objective, solution or gain); not a measurement. | line 98 of the saved text | 98 | primary | corrected by the auditor |
| 4 | framing_gain | Abstract (line 88): KVComm achieves over 70% reuse rate across RAG, math reasoning and collaborative coding workloads 'all without quality degradation', and, when each fully-connected agent receives 1K input tokens with 512 prefix and 512 output tokens in a five-agent setting, up to 7.8x speedup compared to the standard prefill pipeline, reducing TTFT from ~430 ms to ~55 ms; in Table 2 the 7.82x is Agent 5's TTFT speedup while Agent 1 gets 1.11x (lines 515-520, 564-565). Introduction (line 106): ~6.7x average prefill speed-up (Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, one H100) and less than 2.5% accuracy drop at 95% reuse rate on 1,319 GSM8K samples with four agents. In the body, 6.72x is the mean TTFT speedup of three agents in the longest setting (1024 prefix, 1024 output tokens), ranging down to 2.24x in the shortest (Table 3, lines 552-553, 567); the ~95% reuse corresponds to the hyperparameter study with γ=0.5 (94.9% reuse, 80.0% vs 82.1% accuracy, Table 6), not the default γ=0.3 (73.4% reuse). Table 1 lists KVComm reuse rates of 69.9% and 67.6% on MMLU with three and five agents, below the abstract's 'over 70%'. | - | Framing statement (how the paper states its problem, challenge, objective, solution or gain); not a measurement. | line 88 of the saved text | 88 | primary | corrected by the auditor |

| 2 | framing_objective | Proposition 1 gives the expected runtime ratio of Algorithm 1 to sequential execution: E[T_s]/E[T_seq] = 1 − (1/T)·(α/(α+β))·[(T−1)p(k)/(1+p(k)) + p(k)^2/(1+p(k))^2 − p(k)^2/(1+p(k))^2·(−p(k))^(T−1)], which tends to 1 − p(k)/(1+p(k))·α/(α+β) as T→∞. Symbols: T_s is the runtime of Algorithm 1 and T_seq of sequential execution; T is the horizon (steps); the speculator ĝ's latency is Exp(α) and the actual API call's latency is Exp(β) with β<α; p is the probability that a speculative branch implies the correct next call; k is the number of speculative branches; p(k)=1−(1−p)^k is the probability that at least one of the k speculations hits. The end-to-end latency reduction is bounded by 50% (p=1, α=∞). Empirical metrics: time saved (T_seq − T_s)/T_seq and prediction accuracy = fraction of rounds in which any speculative prediction matches the actual move (chess, line 303); APIs prediction accuracy = fraction of speculative API calls matching the ground-truth APIs (e-commerce, line 325); strict-match top-k accuracy of predicted (h_{t+1}, q_{t+1}) (HotpotQA, line 724); p95 latency (OS tuning). | # | Field | Claim | Figure | Measurement definition | Location | Line | Label | Audit |

| 0 | framing_problem | Prior work sped up tool-calling with parallel and asynchronous execution, but redundant or repeated tool-calling requests remain largely unaddressed; repeated invocations prolong response time and amplify the financial and resource costs of API usage, and conventional cache policies do not work for LLM tool-calling. | - | Framing statement (how the paper states its problem, challenge, objective, solution or gain); not a measurement. | line 63 of the saved text | 63 | primary | corrected by the auditor |
| 1 | framing_challenge | Tool calls sit between two stages of LLM inference and their execution time can be a dominant contributor to end-to-end latency, particularly for remote APIs; tool-calling workloads show substantial redundancy (over 40% of invocations repeated in a movie recommendation dataset); but caching them is hard because cacheability is uncertain (information retrieval vs. state-changing commands), freshness requirements vary widely (a single TTL is unsafe or inefficient), workloads shift rapidly, and LRU/LFU rely on recency or frequency without accounting for the high and uneven cost of tool execution. | - | Framing statement (how the paper states its problem, challenge, objective, solution or gain); not a measurement. | line 69 of the saved text | 69 | primary | corrected by the auditor |
| 2 | framing_objective | Caching value of request r_i (Eq. 2): v_i = λ1·NormLatency_i + λ2·NormCost_i/NormSize_i − λ3·e^(−TTL_i/τ), where each feature is min-max normalised (Eq. 1: NormFeature_i^(j) = (Feature_i^(j) − Feature_min^(j)) / (Feature_max^(j) − Feature_min^(j))), λ1, λ2, λ3 are tunable weights for latency, cost-to-size ratio and TTL-based staleness risk (set to 0.8, 0.2, 0.2), and τ is a smoothing parameter equal to the average lifetime of cached entries. Admission is cast as a multi-armed bandit over feature groups g_i with reward F_i = log(H_i+δ1)·log(L_i+δ2)·log(V_i+δ3) / log(C_i+δ4) (H_i group hit ratio, L_i node level, V_i average caching value, C_i number of times the group was admitted, δ small constants), solved with UCB1 to maximise cumulative reward, selecting the group with the highest UCB_i = F_i + c·sqrt(ln t / N_i) (Eq. 6, Appendix B.2; N_i times group i was selected, t the current round, c an exploration parameter); eviction removes, among the 10% least recently used entries, the one with lowest e_i = log(v_i + h_i + δ5) (h_i hit ratio). Reported metrics are cache hit ratio, total/end-to-end latency, result size and resource cost. | - | Framing statement (how the paper states its problem, challenge, objective, solution or gain); not a measurement. | line 175 of the saved text | 175 | primary | corrected by the auditor |
| 3 | framing_solution | ToolCaching intercepts tool-call requests and serves repeated ones from a cache: an LLM prompt extracts semantic features (request type, parameter category, TTL) that feed rule-based cacheability checks (no COMMAND requests, no TTL <= 60 s); for cacheable requests, system features (result size, system latency, resource cost) and TTL give a caching value, while access count, associated users and hit ratio drive grouping, admission and eviction; the VAAC algorithm combines bandit-based admission over feature groups (v-CACA) with value-aware LRU eviction (v-LRU). | - | Framing statement (how the paper states its problem, challenge, objective, solution or gain); not a measurement. | line 63 of the saved text | 63 | primary | corrected by the auditor |
| 4 | framing_gain | Cache hit ratio up to 11% higher than CACA and LRU across most cache sizes and synthetic workloads; end-to-end latency up to 34% lower than the LLM Compiler framework without caching on Movie Recommendation (Table 4: 16.2 s to 10.7 s at a cache size of 100% of calls, labelled 1.34x in the table) and up to 23% lower on ParallelQA (15.9 s to 12.18 s). | - | Framing statement (how the paper states its problem, challenge, objective, solution or gain); not a measurement. | line 79 of the saved text | 79 | primary | corrected by the auditor |

## f253 — Budget-Aware Agentic Routing via Boundary-Guided Training

- Source: https://arxiv.org/html/2602.21227v1 · version read: v1 · v1: Wed, 4 Feb 2026 07:39:27 UTC
- Source class: institutional supplement · no formal publication confirmed
- Audit: None; 6 items kept, 0 dropped

| # | Field | Claim | Figure | Measurement definition | Location | Line | Label | Audit |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 0 | framing_problem | As LLMs become agents executing long-horizon workflows, invoking a high-capability model at every step becomes economically unsustainable, while using a cheap model everywhere can fail on the few critical steps where advanced reasoning is necessary; the paper studies Budget-Aware Agentic Routing, choosing between a cheap and an expensive model at each step to maximise task success under compute costs, both as a soft cost-success trade-off and under strict per-task budgets. | - | Framing statement (how the paper states its problem, challenge, objective, solution or gain); not a measurement. | line 68 of the saved text | 68 | primary | corrected by the auditor |
| 1 | framing_challenge | Unlike single-turn routing, agentic routing is sequential and path-dependent: early mistakes compound, feedback is often only at the end of the episode so credit assignment over long horizons is hard, and deployments often demand strict per-task spending limits; directly training for hard budgets with RL is unstable (discontinuous objective, high-variance gradients), and vanilla GRPO under sparse terminal rewards may reinforce the cheapest failure mode and drift toward a degenerate 'always-small' policy. | - | Framing statement (how the paper states its problem, challenge, objective, solution or gain); not a measurement. | line 69 of the saved text | 69 | primary | corrected by the auditor |
| 2 | framing_objective | Soft-budget routing (Eq. 1): J_soft(θ) = E_{τ~π_θ}[ I(success(τ)) − λ Σ_{t=0}^{/τ/−1} c(a_t) ], where I(success(τ)) ∈ {0,1} is a sparse terminal indicator of task success, λ >= 0 is a Lagrange multiplier whose variation traces the efficiency frontier, a_t ∈ {M_small, M_large} is the model chosen at step t from history state s_t, and c(a_t) > 0 is its scalar cost. Hard-budget routing (Eq. 2, a CMDP): max_π E_{τ~π}[I(success(τ))] s.t. Σ_{t} c(a_t) <= B_max, with B_max the maximum allowable per-task budget (e.g. API cost limit or number of large-model calls). The RL training reward (Eq. 5) is R(τ,x) = (r_success + r_hard) − λ·C_norm(τ,x), with r_hard a bonus only for Hard tasks and C_norm = clip((C(τ) − C_min(x)) / (C_max(x) − C_min(x) + ε), 0, 1), where C(τ) = Σ_t c(a_t) and C_min, C_max are the min and max of the always-small and always-large trajectory costs. Hard-task SFT expert (Eqs. 3-4): sample N trajectories with P(a_t = M_large) = p_k = k/N and take τ* = argmin over successful trajectories of Σ_t c(a_t). BoPO advantage (Eq. 7): A(τ_g) = (R(τ_g,x) − max(μ_group, R(τ*,x))) / (σ_group + ε); policy objective (Eq. 8): J_BoPO(θ) = E[(1/G) Σ_g (π_θ(τ_g)/π_old(τ_g)·A(τ_g) − β_KL·D_KL(π_θ // π_ref))], π_ref the SFT model (G = 8, β = 0.04, r_success = 1.0, r_hard = 0.5, λ ∈ {0.1,0.3,0.5,0.7,0.9}; Appendix D). Budget-Constrained Decoding (Eq. 9): with residual budget b_t = B_max − Σ_{i<t} c(a_i), force M_small if c(M_large) >= b_t, else follow π_θ; in experiments B_max is the number K ∈ {5,10,15} of large-model calls. Reported metrics: Success Rate (average episode score 0-100 on SciWorld, binary success on ALFWorld, Task Goal Completion on AppWorld; Appendix D) and Average Cost E_τ[Σ_t c(a_t)] in dollars; hard-budget runs also report Use% = Avg.#LargeCalls/K. | - | Framing statement (how the paper states its problem, challenge, objective, solution or gain); not a measurement. | line 109 of the saved text | 109 | primary | corrected by the auditor |
| 3 | framing_solution | Boundary-Guided Training anchors learning to two boundary policies (always-small and always-large): tasks are profiled as Easy/Hard/Intractable, SFT data use the small-model trajectory for Easy and Intractable tasks and the cheapest successful stratified-sampling trajectory for Hard ones (BoSFT), and BoPO adds a boundary-relative reward and a reference-guided advantage so the router pays for the large model only when it is likely to change the outcome; strict budgets are enforced at inference by Budget-Constrained Decoding. | - | Framing statement (how the paper states its problem, challenge, objective, solution or gain); not a measurement. | line 71 of the saved text | 71 | primary | corrected by the auditor |
| 4 | framing_gain | BoPO pushes the success-rate vs. average-cost frontier beyond single-turn, cascading, zero-shot GPT-5 and vanilla RL routers on all three benchmarks, matching always-large success at a fraction of the cost (e.g. >63% success on ALFWorld at $0.125 per task). | - | Framing statement (how the paper states its problem, challenge, objective, solution or gain); not a measurement. | line 82 of the saved text | 82 | primary | corrected by the auditor |
| 5 | framing_classification | Classification by the extractor, checked by the auditor: efficiency in the stated problem = central; efficiency terms = cost / computational cost, cost-success frontier / efficiency frontier (Pareto curve of success rate vs. average cost), Average Cost: expected monetary cost per task in dollars (OpenAI list prices per 1M input/output tokens), per-task budget, spending limits, budget caps, number of large-model calls per task (hard budget K; Use% = Avg.#LargeCalls/K), compute, estimated end-to-end latency of the router (tokens/s throughput model); agent kind = LLM agents running long-horizon multi-step workflows (ReAct-style agents on SciWorld, ALFWorld and AppWorld); the paper trains a step-wise model router (Qwen2.5-1.5B) that chooses between a cheap model (GPT-4.1 mini) and an expensive model (GPT-4.1) at each step; position = agent loop (steps, calls, context): which LLM serves each step, with the router trained by SFT and RL. | - | Reader classification (not a statement of the paper). | whole abstract and introduction |  | secondary | corrected by the auditor |

| 1 | framing_challenge | Two challenges: programming LM programs is tedious and difficult due to LLM non-determinism; and executing LM programs is inefficient due to redundant computation and memory usage, because inference engines are optimised without knowledge of the workload: the KV cache of a request is discarded after it completes, so it cannot be reused across calls sharing a common prefix, and constrained decoding only decodes one token at a time. | - | Framing statement (how the paper states its problem, challenge, objective, solution or gain); not a measurement. | line 79 of the saved text | 79 | primary | corrected by the auditor |
| 2 | framing_objective | Reported metrics are throughput (number of program instances executed per second, p/s, with a sufficiently large batch) and latency (average latency of executing one program at a time without batching). The runtime's cache-aware scheduling targets the cache hit rate, defined as number of cached prompt tokens / number of prompt tokens (line 187); Theorem 3.1 states that visiting the radix tree of a batch of requests in depth-first search order (equivalently longest-shared-prefix-first) achieves an optimal cache hit rate when cache size is at least the maximum request length. | - | Framing statement (how the paper states its problem, challenge, objective, solution or gain); not a measurement. | line 249 of the saved text | 249 | primary | corrected by the auditor |
| 3 | framing_solution | The core idea is to systematically exploit the multi-call structure in LM programs: a frontend with generation and parallelism primitives, and a runtime with RadixAttention (keeping the KV cache of all requests in a radix tree with LRU eviction and cache-aware scheduling so it is reused across calls), a compressed finite state machine that decodes multiple tokens at once for constrained outputs, and API speculative execution for API-only models. | - | Framing statement (how the paper states its problem, challenge, objective, solution or gain); not a measurement. | line 89 of the saved text | 89 | primary | corrected by the auditor |
| 4 | framing_gain | Compared with Guidance, vLLM and LMQL, SGLang improves throughput by up to 6.4x and reduces latency by up to 3.7x on open-weight models (results in Figs. 5-6, captioned as Llama-7B; 7B models run on a single A10G GPU; lines 226, 250-253), across workloads including agent control (ReAct and generative-agent traces replayed), logical reasoning, few-shot benchmarks, JSON decoding, RAG and multi-turn chat; Guidance and LMQL are excluded from some benchmarks (line 260). Throughput is maximum programs per second with a large batch and latency is average single-program latency without batching (line 249). API speculative execution reduces input-token cost by about threefold on one GPT-3.5 prompt that extracts three fields (line 281). | - | Framing statement (how the paper states its problem, challenge, objective, solution or gain); not a measurement. | line 253 of the saved text | 253 | primary | corrected by the auditor |

| 0 | framing_problem | Recent GUI agents replicate the R1-Zero paradigm (online RL with explicit chain-of-thought before object grounding); the paper analyses the three components of that training pipeline (input design, output evaluation, policy update) and finds that each reveals distinct challenges arising from blindly applying general-purpose RL without adapting to GUI grounding tasks. | - | Framing statement (how the paper states its problem, challenge, objective, solution or gain); not a measurement. | line 70 of the saved text | 70 | primary | corrected by the auditor |
| 1 | framing_challenge | Three named challenges: grounding is harmed by longer reasoning due to grounding's reliance on image tokens (longer chains lower grounding accuracy); Hit-based and IoU-based rewards induce opposite, box-size-sensitive reward hacking (Hit favours smaller boxes, IoU larger boxes); and the GRPO objective biases the policy toward simpler examples: a response-level length bias from dividing by /o_i/ (longer incorrect and shorter correct responses) and a question-level difficulty bias (described as treating all samples equally in line 71; Sec. 3.3 notes, citing [25], that dividing by the reward std can make the model focus disproportionately on harder or easier samples), so online RL overfits easy examples and under-optimises harder cases (abstract). | - | Framing statement (how the paper states its problem, challenge, objective, solution or gain); not a measurement. | line 75 of the saved text | 75 | primary | corrected by the auditor |
| 2 | framing_objective | Training objective: the GRPO objective J_GRPO(pi_theta) (Eq. 2: expectation over queries q ~ p_Q and N responses o_i sampled from pi_theta_old, of (1/N) sum_i (1//o_i/) sum_t min[ratio * A_hat_{i,t}, clip(ratio, 1-epsilon, 1+epsilon) * A_hat_{i,t}], where ratio = pi_theta(o_{i,t}/q, o_{i,<t}) / pi_theta_old(o_{i,t}/q, o_{i,<t}), t is the token index and epsilon bounds deviation from the old policy), with the advantage A_i = (r_i - mean(r_1..r_N)) / std(r_1..r_N) (Eq. 1). GUI-G1 replaces /o_i/ with a constant Max_Tokens and multiplies the objective by a difficulty coefficient w_q = 0.5 + (1/lambda_q - min_i 1/lambda_i) / (max_i 1/lambda_i - min_i 1/lambda_i), where lambda_q in (0,1] is the sample's relative box size (Sec. 3.3 uses the relative box size of the target as the difficulty proxy; the only written formula, Appendix C.2, defines relative box size for the predicted box as (y2_hat + x2_hat - y1_hat - x1_hat) / (IMAGE_WIDTH + IMAGE_HEIGHT)); the reward is R_Hit + alpha R_IoU + beta R_Box, with R_Hit = 1((x_p, y_p) in B_gt) (predicted box centre inside the ground-truth box), R_IoU = IoU(B_pred, B_gt), R_Box = 4 / (x_p1 + x_p2 + y_p1 + y_p2) with x_p1 = 1 / (1 - /x1_hat - x1/ / image width) and similar terms, and alpha, beta tunable hyperparameters set to alpha = 0.25 and beta = 0.125 (line 427); no KL-divergence regularization is applied in training (line 427). Evaluation target: grounding accuracy on ScreenSpot and ScreenSpot-Pro. | - | Framing statement (how the paper states its problem, challenge, objective, solution or gain); not a measurement. | line 205 of the saved text | 205 | primary | corrected by the auditor |
| 3 | framing_solution | Each diagnosed issue gets a targeted fix: a Fast Thinking Template that makes the policy answer directly (no intermediate reasoning) during training; a box-size-based reward R_Box added to the Hit and IoU rewards to counter size-driven reward hacking; and a revised GRPO objective without length normalization plus a per-sample difficulty coefficient from relative box size so harder samples receive larger gradients. | - | Framing statement (how the paper states its problem, challenge, objective, solution or gain); not a measurement. | line 72 of the saved text | 72 | primary | corrected by the auditor |
| 4 | framing_gain | GUI-G1-3B, trained on about 17K public grounding samples, reaches 90.3% accuracy on ScreenSpot and 37.1% on ScreenSpot-Pro; the paper claims it surpasses all prior models of similar size and the previous best R1-style agent InfiGUI-R1-3B (87.5% on ScreenSpot, 35.7% on ScreenSpot-Pro, 32K samples), and outperforms the larger UI-TARS-7B on ScreenSpot-Pro (35.7%; UI-TARS-7B is not in the ScreenSpot table), while requiring less data, fewer output tokens (about one-third of InfiGUI-R1-3B's average per example on ScreenSpot: 37-39 vs 107-114, Appendix D.2 Table 7) and fewer training stages. Baseline numbers are taken from the original papers, not re-run (line 429). | - | Framing statement (how the paper states its problem, challenge, objective, solution or gain); not a measurement. | line 73 of the saved text | 73 | primary | corrected by the auditor |

| 2 | framing_objective | none stated as an optimisation objective (the paper characterizes a workload and does not optimise a target). It defines measurement metrics with formulas: per-step input I is decomposed into prefix tokens P (history read from the prefix cache) and append tokens A (user messages, tool results and tokens introduced by prefix-cache misses), mapped from provider fields (Claude: P = cache_read_input_tokens, A = input_tokens + cache_creation_input_tokens; Codex: P = cached_input_tokens, A = input_tokens_total - cached_input_tokens), with O = provider-reported output tokens including reasoning (Section 3.2, lines 287-313). Normalized decode speed s_norm = O / (t_last - t_input), where t_input = latest input-event timestamp (user_message or tool_result) before the first model output and t_last = last model-output timestamp (reasoning, text or tool_call); this is an end-to-end trace speed that includes TTFT, reasoning, visible output emission and trace logging effects (lines 886-890). For Codex steps: s_pure_decode = O_visible / (t_visible - t_reason), l-hat_pure_decode = sum(t_visible - t_reason) / sum(O_visible), and residual TTFT-hat = (t_reason - t_input) - O_reason * l-hat_pure_decode, with O_reason = reasoning tokens, O_visible = O - O_reason (lines 891-902). Codex tool-call overhead R = max(0, T_e2e - T_int), trace-observed end-to-end tool span minus runner-reported internal execution time (line 933). Prefix cache hit rate is token-weighted (Table 11). Prefill amplification factor = total prefilled (append) tokens / irreducible fresh tokens, equivalently 1/(fresh % of append), where fresh tokens = per-step context growth minus prior output tokens (lines 1012, 1078-1079). KV storage ratio of suspended to active-decoding requests R = (T-hat_human + T-hat_tool) / T_generation, with human and tool times capped by the eviction time (lines 1081-1083). The consumer-side upper-bound saving caps a user-initiated step's append tokens at max(0, L_S - L_P), L = prefix + append tokens (line 1089). Costs are computed from published API pricing per token category (append, prefix, output; Table 6). | - | Framing statement (how the paper states its problem, challenge, objective, solution or gain); not a measurement. | line 886 of the saved text | 886 | primary | corrected by the auditor |

| 0 | framing_problem | Self-improving agents aim at controllable evolution or adaptation from experience with minimal or no human input; the survey addresses a research landscape that is fragmented in terminology and scope, where existing reviews treat foundation-model fine-tuning and agent scaffolding as isolated topics without a unified formal perspective. | - | Framing statement (how the paper states its problem, challenge, objective, solution or gain); not a measurement. | line 149 of the saved text | 149 | primary | corrected by the auditor |
| 1 | framing_challenge | A foundation model is a stateless inference engine; a standard agent adapts only its transient execution state (e.g. in-context examples), which is discarded at task boundaries, so its underlying capabilities stay bounded by its fixed initial setup unless durable updates are committed to the model parameters or the scaffold. | - | Framing statement (how the paper states its problem, challenge, objective, solution or gain); not a measurement. | line 375 of the saved text | 375 | primary | corrected by the auditor |

Open questions named: what to remember, how memory should propagate, and whether gains transfer across LLMs. | - | Framing statement (how the paper states its problem, challenge, objective, solution or gain); not a measurement. | line 162 of the saved text | 162 | primary | corrected by the auditor |

Champion selection uses i* = argmax over non-graduated instances of checkpoint return R_i. | - | Framing statement (how the paper states its problem, challenge, objective, solution or gain); not a measurement. | line 322 of the saved text | 322 | primary | corrected by the auditor |

- Source: https://arxiv.org/html/2412.03624v1 · version read: arXiv 2412.03624v1 (HTML full text saved as .txt; PDF v1 text 2412.03624-pdf.txt consulted for the title block, the running header and the Implementation boxes) · v1: 2024-12-04

| # | Field | Claim | Figure | Measurement definition | Location | Line | Label | Audit |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 0 | framing_problem | Optimizing language-based agentic systems requires substantial manual labor; when such systems are represented as computational graphs, most current GASO methods fail to properly assign feedback on the system's output to the individual components. | - | Framing statement (how the paper states its problem, challenge, objective, solution or gain); not a measurement. | line 72 of the saved text | 72 | primary | corrected by the auditor |
| 1 | framing_challenge | Credit assignment: backpropagation-inspired solvers pass feedback backward in reverse topological order, but OptoPrime does not build a compact explicit representation of how each component can be improved, and TextGrad omits neighborhood nodes (other predecessors of a common successor) when computing backward messages, which the authors argue hinders the effectiveness of backpropagation. | - | Framing statement (how the paper states its problem, challenge, objective, solution or gain); not a measurement. | line 93 of the saved text | 93 | primary | corrected by the auditor |
| 2 | framing_objective | Find parameters \Theta^{*} minimizing \mathbb{E}_{Q\sim D}[l(Q,A(Q,\Theta^{*}))], where Q is a user query drawn from the query distribution D, \Theta is the set of optimizable parameter nodes of the directed acyclic computational graph (V,E,H,\Theta), A(Q,\Theta) is the final response produced by the output node, and l is a loss (e.g. negative utility) for a query and its response; a semantic alphanumeric feedback F(Q,A) is supplied as an additional optimization signal. Reported target: test accuracy on BBH, GSM8K, BCB and LIAR. | - | Framing statement (how the paper states its problem, challenge, objective, solution or gain); not a measurement. | line 119 of the saved text | 119 | primary | corrected by the auditor |
| 3 | framing_solution | Semantic backpropagation computes a semantic gradient (directional information in natural language) for every variable in reverse topological order, with backward functions that condition on all predecessors of the successor node (the neighborhood) and an aggregation function over successors; semantic gradient descent then asks an LLM to update each parameter from its accumulated gradients and accepts the update only if it improves a validation set (update gate). | - | Framing statement (how the paper states its problem, challenge, objective, solution or gain); not a measurement. | line 73 of the saved text | 73 | primary | corrected by the auditor |
| 4 | framing_gain | Higher task accuracy than TextGrad, OptoPrime and COPRO: e.g. GSM8K 93.2 vs 78.2 (TextGrad) and 83.9 (OptoPrime); BBH NLP 82.5 and BBH Algorithmic 85.6 vs 75.8/80.6 for OptoPrime as reported by Cheng et al.; roughly equal to TextGrad on BigCodeBench (27.8 vs 27.6) (Table 1). | - | Framing statement (how the paper states its problem, challenge, objective, solution or gain); not a measurement. | line 104 of the saved text | 104 | primary | corrected by the auditor |
| 5 | framing_classification | Classification by the extractor, checked by the auditor: efficiency in the stated problem = secondary; efficiency terms = token usage, token counts, cost of the method, cost-quality balance, number of forward computations, cheap / expensive language model; agent kind = language-based agentic systems modelled as computational graphs whose components query frozen LLMs and carry auxiliary optimizable parameters (e.g. instruction prompts); the paper calls the task Graph-based Agentic System Optimization (GASO). Experiments use multi-node LLM question-answering/coding pipelines (BBH, GSM8K, BigCodeBench, LIAR), not interactive web or GUI agents.; position = improvement loop (learning, search, memory). | - | Reader classification (not a statement of the paper). | whole abstract and introduction |  | secondary | corrected by the auditor |

| 1 | framing_challenge | Dependence on a fixed evaluator constrains self-improvement when the target task has no direct benchmark (paper writing, proof writing), when evaluation is slow or weakly informative, and when static benchmarks saturate or become vulnerable to reward hacking; changing the utility during search would otherwise break the fixed-criterion assumption behind prior self-improvement guarantees. | - | Framing statement (how the paper states its problem, challenge, objective, solution or gain); not a measurement. | line 58 of the saved text | 58 | primary | corrected by the auditor |
| 2 | framing_objective | Self-improvement is a tree search over an archive T_t; each evaluation records a binary outcome o in {0,1}, aggregated into successes S_a and failures F_a; when evaluation budget B is exhausted the highest-scoring node is returned. Search utility is clade metaproductivity CMP(a) = n^C_success(a) / (n^C_success(a) + n^C_failure(a)) in [0,1], pooled over the clade C(a) (subtree rooted at a), with Thompson sampling for selection. Final agent chosen by epsilon-best-belief BB_eps(a) = I^{-1}_eps(1 + S_a, 1 + F_a), the eps-quantile of the Beta posterior. Agent utility U_j(a) = (1//R/) sum_{r in R} p_{r,j}(a), with p_{r,j}(a) = (1//D_r/) sum_{d in D_r} p_{r,d,j}(a), the expected binary success rate of node a on task d of role r under epoch vector j. | - | Framing statement (how the paper states its problem, challenge, objective, solution or gain); not a measurement. | line 212 of the saved text | 212 | primary | corrected by the auditor |
| 3 | framing_solution | Controlled utility evolution: search is divided into epochs, each with one frozen evaluator giving a stationary utility, so prior self-improvement guarantees hold per epoch; challenger evaluators co-evolve with task agents and replace the incumbent at epoch boundaries only if they win on a held-out ground-truth anchor, after which records scored by the displaced evaluator are selectively erased. | - | Framing statement (how the paper states its problem, challenge, objective, solution or gain); not a measurement. | line 17 of the saved text | 17 | primary | corrected by the auditor |

| 2 | framing_objective | Heuristic approximation of Bayesian exploration: choose tests so that cumulative branch coverage grows as quickly as possible. Curiosity Q-value q(h,a)=g~(a/h)+γ·E_{o/h,a}[v(hao)], where g~(a/h)=I(O;Θ/h,a) is the expected information gain (mutual information between the unknown program branch-reachability structure Θ and observation O given history h and action a), v(h)=max_a q(h,a) is the curiosity value of history h, γ a discount factor. In practice Q=ĝ+γ·v̂ with ĝ the LLM-predicted expected new branches and v̂ the LLM-predicted additional branches made reachable (γ=0.5). Reported metric: branch coverage = cumulative number of unique branches executed across all test scripts, under an equal execution budget N=24. | - | Framing statement (how the paper states its problem, challenge, objective, solution or gain); not a measurement. | line 111 of the saved text | 111 | primary | corrected by the auditor |

Training an engineer is hard because the editable runtime spans interdependent execution stages, so unrestricted code edits can break interfaces or produce non-executable behavior, and patch quality can only be judged from the target agent's behavior after the patch is applied (the reward is non-differentiable and observable only after a rerun). | - | Framing statement (how the paper states its problem, challenge, objective, solution or gain); not a measurement. | line 146 of the saved text | 146 | primary | corrected by the auditor |
| 2 | framing_objective | Engineer reward r(B,P) = Delta_B(P) if the patch is valid and complete, 0 otherwise, with Delta_B(P) = (1/n) sum_{i=1}^{n} (R_i^P - R_i^0) (Eq. 1). B = {x_i}_{i=1}^n is a batch of n tasks in environment E; R_i^0 is the reward of the unmodified frozen target agent A on task i (baseline trajectories tau_i^0); R_i^P is the reward after the validated overlay P is installed and the same frozen target reruns every task in B; P is the batch-conditioned executable overlay generated by the engineer H_theta from the failure packet s_B. The engineer is trained by cold-start SFT (Eq. 2) and then GRPO maximizing a token-averaged clipped surrogate J(theta) (Eq. 4) with group-normalized advantages A_k = (r_k - mu_B)/sigma_B over K=8 candidate patches per packet (Eq. 3). | 0 | framing_problem | LLM agents often underperform in specialized real-world domains that need external tools and domain-specific prompting strategies. Agentic RL (SFT followed by GRPO) closes this gap only through costly parameter updates, so the paper asks whether agent performance can be improved without changing parameters and with lower data and computational costs. | - | Framing statement (how the paper states its problem, challenge, objective, solution or gain); not a measurement. | line 68 of the saved text | 68 | primary | corrected by the auditor |
| 1 | framing_challenge | Reliance on tuning LLM parameters brings four practical problems. (1) Computational cost: prohibitive for large models, and fine-tuned models need dedicated deployment. This incurs latency and cost that grow with the number of actions, and agents must repeatedly rediscover how the same web application works. The paper asks whether web agents can replace step-by-step reactive reasoning with offline application knowledge and one-shot planning. | - | Framing statement (how the paper states its problem, challenge, objective, solution or gain); not a measurement. | line 62 of the saved text | 62 | primary | corrected by the auditor |
| 1 | framing_challenge | Tasks within one application share a stable structure (the same pages, controls, operations and navigation paths), but reactive agents do not exploit it. They repeatedly rediscover how the application works and invoke the LLM throughout execution, so cost and latency grow with the number of actions and errors accumulate over long trajectories. Trajectory memory only packages the decisions made for one task and is therefore a less compositional form of reuse (lines 80-82). | - | Framing statement (how the paper states its problem, challenge, objective, solution or gain); not a measurement. | line 78 of the saved text | 78 | primary | corrected by the auditor |
| 2 | framing_objective | No objective formula. The memory is formalized as a directed graph M=(S,O,T): S are states (stable application views), O are operations (reusable capabilities available in those states), and T is the transition function recording how operations change state (line 144). | 3 | framing_solution | Application discovery is moved offline. A Crawling Agent builds an updatable, task-independent state-machine memory of interface states, operations and transitions. A Patcher falls back to reactive reasoning on failure and writes repairs back to the memory. In the common case this changes the unit of LLM reasoning from one call per action to one call per task. | - | Framing statement (how the paper states its problem, challenge, objective, solution or gain); not a measurement. | line 101 of the saved text | 101 | primary | corrected by the auditor |

(1): accept candidate library S^c only if (F(c)-F_0)-(R(c)-R_0)>0 and R(c) <= R_0, where P_fail and P_pass are the previously-failing and previously-passing probe subsets, F_0 = number of P_fail examples that pass under the current library S, R_0 = number of P_pass examples that fail under S, and F(c), R(c) are the same counts for the candidate on the same probe; the first condition is a net improvement in fixes over regressions, the second a hard regression budget (invalid-action regressions are weighted by lambda=2 in the score, Appendix B.3). | - | Framing statement (how the paper states its problem, challenge, objective, solution or gain); not a measurement. | line 139 of the saved text | 139 | primary | corrected by the auditor |

| 0 | framing_problem | Reusing agent-produced artifacts improves efficiency but creates a lifecycle reliability problem: artifacts that succeed once may fail under environment drift, underspecified tasks or changing task distributions, especially in web automation; the question becomes how accumulated execution evidence should govern reusable workflows (when to promote a candidate, formalize a step, repair or demote brittle realizations, and retire a workflow). | - | Framing statement (how the paper states its problem, challenge, objective, solution or gain); not a measurement. | line 75 of the saved text | 75 | primary | corrected by the auditor |
| 1 | framing_challenge | Web interfaces drift outside the automation system's control without preserving automation anchors such as selectors or layouts, which forces a formalization choice: hardening steps into code makes reuse more controlled but brittle under drift, while leaving them NL-guided keeps flexibility but weakens artifact-level control; existing memory systems reuse experience only as advisory prompt context, and execution, validation and versioning mechanisms are studied separately rather than as a joint lifecycle policy. | - | Framing statement (how the paper states its problem, challenge, objective, solution or gain); not a measurement. | line 97 of the saved text | 97 | primary | corrected by the auditor |
| 2 | framing_objective | (y*, z*) = argmin_{y,z} C_maint(y,z / W_v) + C_run(y,z / W_v) s.t. J_perf(y,z / W_v) <= J_perf^ref + epsilon. W_v is workflow version v; y(W_v) in {provisional, released, retired} is its lifecycle state; z = (z_1,...,z_n) with z_i in {0,1} indicating whether step s_i has a validated executable realization C_i (the formalization pattern); C_maint is cumulative offline maintenance inference cost (distillation, validation, repair, promotion, demotion, retirement review), each maintenance event e approximated by token cost c(e) = tok_in(e) + tok_out(e); C_run is runtime cost including online inference, fallbacks, retries and browser/tool actions; J_perf is a loss estimated from offline replay validation (downstream failure, regressions on previously passing traces, step-level degradation) relative to J_perf^ref with tolerance epsilon >= 0. The paper says this full objective is not directly solved: it uses a threshold policy pi_theta with theta = (tau_create, tau_form, tau_demote, tau_retire), choosing each group threshold as the argmin of replay-estimated maintenance token cost C_hat_maint^(d)(g,tau) over thresholds whose one-sided Wilson upper confidence bound on the validation-violation rate V_hat^(d)(g,tau) = k_{g,d}(tau)/n_{g,d} is at most a budget V_max^(d); this optimizes maintenance compute rather than full C_total. | - | Framing statement (how the paper states its problem, challenge, objective, solution or gain); not a measurement. | line 171 of the saved text | 171 | primary | corrected by the auditor |
| 3 | framing_solution | Selective formalization: execution evidence (trace-support counts, accepted-repair counts, token-weighted repair burden) decides which workflow steps become executable code, which stay NL-guided, and when to revise these choices; gate-conditioned execution lets each step run its code when pre/post gates validate and otherwise fall back locally (code -> NL procedure -> step intent) instead of failing like an all-or-nothing script, with repository changes only after offline validation. | - | Framing statement (how the paper states its problem, challenge, objective, solution or gain); not a measurement. | line 77 of the saved text | 77 | primary | corrected by the auditor |

## f372 — RRSI: Regularized Recursive Self-Improvement of Agent Harnesses

- Source: https://arxiv.org/html/2609.24972v2 · version read: v2 · v1: 2026-09-21
- Source class: institutional supplement · no formal publication confirmed
- Audit: usable; 6 items kept, 0 dropped

| # | Field | Claim | Figure | Measurement definition | Location | Line | Label | Audit |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 0 | framing_problem | Recent methods automate harness improvement by iteratively proposing and selecting component-wise harness edits, a form of recursive self-improvement at the agent-system level, but such recursive evolution may overfit by memorizing the training tasks, giving large in-distribution gains that shrink or vanish out of distribution; the paper studies this generalization problem (the evolved harness transferring to unseen benchmarks with different task descriptions, tool interfaces or verifiers). | - | Framing statement (how the paper states its problem, challenge, objective, solution or gain); not a measurement. | line 101 of the saved text | 101 | primary | corrected by the auditor |
| 1 | framing_challenge | Harness evolution reuses a finite evolve set adaptively (candidates at round t depend on measurements of the same tasks in earlier rounds), creating an adaptive overfitting risk; the search may encode benchmark-specific patterns, promote candidates favored by evaluation noise, or accumulate complexity that raises evolve-set scores without improving the agent mechanism, and apparent gains can come from increased test-time computation rather than reusable mechanisms. | - | Framing statement (how the paper states its problem, challenge, objective, solution or gain); not a measurement. | line 109 of the saved text | 109 | primary | corrected by the auditor |
| 2 | framing_objective | For an agent A=(pi,H) and task set D, task performance S(H;D)=E_{x~D} E_{tau~A(./x)}[r(x,tau)] and policy-token cost C(H;D)=E_{x~D} E_{tau~A(./x)}[c(tau)], where r(x,tau) in [0,1] is the verifier score of trajectory tau on task x and c(tau) is the number of policy tokens consumed by the trajectory; empirical versions S_hat(H), C_hat(H) average over k trials per task on D_evolve. Generic harness evolution sets H_{t+1}=argmax over candidates and H_t of S_hat(H';D_evolve). RRSI keeps this empirical objective but adds non-compensatory acceptance rules: a noise-adjusted floor S_hat(H') >= S* - delta (S* best evolve score so far, delta empirical noise band) and, when Delta S > delta, Delta C <= beta_0 + beta_1 Delta S, where Delta S is the score change, Delta C the relative policy-token cost change vs H_t, beta_0 the cost increase tolerated for a negligible gain and beta_1 how much extra cost is allowed as the gain grows; proposals are capped by an annealed edit budget b_t that decreases from b_max to b_min. | - | Framing statement (how the paper states its problem, challenge, objective, solution or gain); not a measurement. | line 116 of the saved text | 116 | primary | corrected by the auditor |
| 3 | framing_solution | Translate machine-learning regularization into the harness search while leaving the edit space open: on the proposal side, an annealed edit budget (L0-style sparsity), evidence-aware credit assignment over the evolution history and structured exploration; on the selection side, a leakage-screening critic, stability-aware acceptance against a noise band, cost-aware (Ridge/L2-style) acceptance and pruning of unproductive components (Lasso/L1-style), so that reusable mechanisms rather than benchmark-specific fits survive. | - | Framing statement (how the paper states its problem, challenge, objective, solution or gain); not a measurement. | line 111 of the saved text | 111 | primary | corrected by the auditor |
| 4 | framing_gain | Against the unevolved base harness H0, RRSI gains up to 14.1 points on the evolve split and up to 4.7 points on the out-of-distribution benchmarks with no held-out regression, and against unregularized evolution it produces a harness that runs on 30% fewer policy tokens (Table 2: 2.42m vs 3.80m tokens per trial). | - | Framing statement (how the paper states its problem, challenge, objective, solution or gain); not a measurement. | line 104 of the saved text | 104 | primary | corrected by the auditor |
| 5 | framing_classification | Classification by the extractor, checked by the auditor: efficiency in the stated problem = secondary; efficiency terms = policy tokens / policy-token cost c(tau), C(H;D), tokens per trial (millions), inference cost, test-time compute / test-time computation, steps per trial (trajectory length), aggregate resource footprint, candidate budget / edit budget / search budget; agent kind = LLM agents A=(pi,H) built from a frozen backbone policy and a harness (prompts, control flow, tooling, memory, context management), on coding, agentic workspace and engineering design benchmarks; the method is an automated harness-evolution (recursive self-improvement) loop; position = improvement loop (learning, search, memory): regularized proposal and selection in iterative harness evolution with a frozen backbone; the token-cost constraint acts on the deployed agent loop. | - | Reader classification (not a statement of the paper). | whole abstract and introduction |  | secondary | corrected by the auditor |

## f387 — Co-Evolving Skill Generation and Policy Optimization

- Source: https://arxiv.org/html/2606.08755v1 · version read: v1 (arXiv HTML) · v1: 2026-06-07

| # | Field | Claim | Figure | Measurement definition | Location | Line | Label | Audit |

| 0 | framing_problem | Skill-augmented RL methods use strong LLMs to generate skills from trajectories and update a retrievable skill bank during online training, but rarely assess whether a newly generated skill is useful before it is stored and reused; generated skills (even from proprietary frontier LLMs) have highly mixed utility and can degrade performance. | - | Framing statement (how the paper states its problem, challenge, objective, solution or gain); not a measurement. | line 77 of the saved text | 77 | primary | corrected by the auditor |
| 1 | framing_challenge | Once a skill enters the bank its effect is hard to identify because rollout feedback is delayed and reflects the combined effect of multiple retrieved skills; measuring a skill's value by comparing rollouts with and without it would naively require extra counterfactual rollouts; and relying on proprietary frontier LLM APIs for skill generation is costly across repeated online RL updates. The paper states three challenges: estimating marginal utility without additional rollout cost, scoring a skill by its marginal contribution beyond the retrieved context, and reducing reliance on costly proprietary APIs without sacrificing skill quality. | - | Framing statement (how the paper states its problem, challenge, objective, solution or gain); not a measurement. | line 137 of the saved text | 137 | primary | corrected by the auditor |
| 2 | framing_objective | The policy is optimized with GRPO on rewards from base and skill-augmented rollouts. The key quantity is the prompt-specific marginal utility u(x_{i,j}, s_hat_i) = (1//Y^skill_{i,j}/) sum_{y in Y^skill_{i,j}} r(x_{i,j}, y) - (1//Y^base_{i,j}/) sum_{y in Y^base_{i,j}} r(x_{i,j}, y) (Eq. 4), where r(x,y) is the task reward, x_{i,j} a query, s_hat_i the candidate skill, Y^base rollouts conditioned on the retrieved skills S_{i,j}, and Y^skill rollouts conditioned on S_{i,j} plus s_hat_i. Cross-prompt utility U = (1/K) sum_j u(x_{i,j}, s_hat_i) (Eq. 5). The skill generator is trained with L_gen(theta) = -E[lambda [u]_+ l_theta] + E[[-u]_+ l_theta] (Eq. 7), where l_theta is the log-probability of generating s_hat_i, [a]_+ = max(a,0) and lambda in [0,1] down-weights positive reinforcement. | - | Framing statement (how the paper states its problem, challenge, objective, solution or gain); not a measurement. | line 284 of the saved text | 284 | primary | corrected by the auditor |
| 3 | framing_solution | SAPO splits the standard rollout budget into two matched groups under the same task and retrieved skill context (base rollouts, and rollouts with one added candidate skill induced from the base trajectories); their reward gap estimates the candidate's context-dependent marginal utility without additional rollouts, so only useful, non-redundant skills are promoted, and the same signal trains the policy itself as skill generator and scorer, avoiding repeated proprietary-model calls. | - | Framing statement (how the paper states its problem, challenge, objective, solution or gain); not a measurement. | line 146 of the saved text | 146 | primary | corrected by the auditor |

| 0 | framing_problem | Asks whether accurate world models can be built out of LLMs and how they benefit LLM agents: LLMs are not reliable enough as agents in specific open-world environments, and 'world alignment' of LLMs with an environment's dynamics has not been adequately investigated; many existing agents are model-free and execute actions without verification in a world model. | - | Framing statement (how the paper states its problem, challenge, objective, solution or gain); not a measurement. | line 99 of the saved text | 99 | primary | corrected by the auditor |
| 1 | framing_challenge | The gap between LLMs' prior-knowledge-driven commonsense reasoning and the specified environment's dynamics leads to incorrect predictions of future states, hallucinations, or violations of basic laws; model-free agents act without verification (safety risks, suboptimal trajectories); existing ways to learn dynamics need expensive RL/imitation finetuning or memory-heavy inference over long buffered trajectories. | - | Framing statement (how the paper states its problem, challenge, objective, solution or gain); not a measurement. | line 107 of the saved text | 107 | primary | corrected by the auditor |
| 2 | framing_objective | Rule pruning is a maximum coverage problem (Eq. 5): R* = argmax_{R subset of R^Code} /union over r^Code in R of D^cov/ s.t. /R/ <= l, where R^Code is the set of executable code rules, D^inc the incorrectly predicted transitions, D^cov the subset of D^inc covered (corrected) by the rules, and l>0 the limit on selected rules; the goal is the smallest rule set correcting the most incorrect predictions. Task-level targets are Mars reward (sum of sparse rewards), Mars score (geometric mean of success rates across achievements) and ALFWorld success rate, in a POMDP (S,A,O,r,T,gamma). | - | Framing statement (how the paper states its problem, challenge, objective, solution or gain); not a measurement. | line 258 of the saved text | 258 | primary | corrected by the auditor |

Learning problem (line 169): construct Python programs implementing a transition function T-hat and reward model R-hat satisfying phi_1 AND phi_2, where phi_1 (fit data, Eq. 1): for all (s,a,r,s',c,d) in replay buffer D, T-hat(s,a)=s' and R-hat(c)(s,a,s')=(r,d) (d = 'done'); phi_2 (optimism, Eq. 2): from the episode's initial state s_0 and context c there exist actions/states a_1,s_1,...,a_l,s_l with T-hat(s_{i-1},a_i)=s_i and some r>0 with R-hat(c)(s_{l-1},a_l,s_l)=(r,1). Refinement search (REx) ranks programs by heuristic h (Eq. 3) = [number of buffer transitions the program explains + 1[phi_1] x number of (s_0,c) in D_sc satisfying phi_2] / (/D/+/D_sc/). Theorem 2.4 bounds the maximum number of actions to reach the goal by D_{S,A,T} x (K+1), with D_{S,A,T} the MDP diameter (max shortest path length between states) and K the logical dimensionality of the model space (size of the largest mutually independent dataset). | - | Framing statement (how the paper states its problem, challenge, objective, solution or gain); not a measurement. | line 169 of the saved text | 169 | primary | corrected by the auditor |

Exploration is addressed by an optimism-under-uncertainty objective that prefers world models under which a planner can reach reward; program search is made tractable by curriculum transfer that refines old programs instead of writing new ones. After a world model is learned, new tasks need at most one LLM query to update the reward function. | - | Framing statement (how the paper states its problem, challenge, objective, solution or gain); not a measurement. | line 83 of the saved text | 83 | primary | corrected by the auditor |

| 1 | framing_challenge | Two failure modes: path dependence (single-lineage self-editors are biased by early edits and plateau) and cross-task interference (an edit that fixes one family of tasks silently regresses another, so evolution over a mixed task distribution stagnates; many edits win on a small subset but lose on the full benchmark). Prior archives (e.g. DGM) score a child only against its parent, never recombine complementary lineages, and do not require a gain to hold what it displaces; noisy agent benchmarks also let a single lucky rollout masquerade as a capability gain (line 469). | - | Framing statement (how the paper states its problem, challenge, objective, solution or gain); not a measurement. | line 164 of the saved text | 164 | primary | corrected by the auditor |
| 2 | framing_objective | Fitness is each variant's per-task solve rate p-hat_t(v) (avg@k) under the benchmark's own verifier, with no gold solutions. For a child c and parent p, Delta_t = p-hat_t(c) - p-hat_t(p); net gain g(c) = sum_t Delta_t; bounded regression R(c) = sum_t (-Delta_t)_+. A child is admitted when it extends without breaking preservation, g(c) > 0 and R(c) <= delta; a verifier agent f returns verdict(c) = f(g, R, E, K_g) in {promote, revert} from trial evidence E and shared memory K_g, followed by a preservation probe. Lineage gain G(c) = G(p) + g(c) drives parent sampling p* ~ (1-beta) delta_{argmax_{v in S} G(v)} + beta Broaden(P), with S the steering set of confirmed variants and P the wider population. A merged child H = H_0 (+) Delta is kept iff S(child) is a superset of the union of its parents' solved-task sets S(v_i). | - | Framing statement (how the paper states its problem, challenge, objective, solution or gain); not a measurement. | line 363 of the saved text | 363 | primary | corrected by the auditor |
| 3 | framing_solution | Treat agent improvement as selection over a population of harness variants rather than training: search the harness (skill and code layers) rather than whole-agent code, admit a child only under a preserve-and-extend contract that bounds what a win may cost on already-solved tasks, keep every scored variant in an archive, and merge complementary specialists across lineages; failure-, teacher- and self-derived signals are turned into additive harness edits, and exploration (permissive promotion) is separated from confirmation (stricter avg@k re-tests). | - | Framing statement (how the paper states its problem, challenge, objective, solution or gain); not a measurement. | line 272 of the saved text | 272 | primary | corrected by the auditor |

| 1 | framing_challenge | Tasks within the same application share a stable structure (the same pages, controls, operations and navigation paths recur), but reactive agents do not exploit it: they rediscover how the application works and invoke the LLM throughout execution, so cost and latency grow with the number of actions and errors accumulate over long trajectories. Prior reuse via stored demonstrations/trajectories packages the decisions of one particular task, so a new task can reuse only some of its actions. | - | Framing statement (how the paper states its problem, challenge, objective, solution or gain); not a measurement. | line 78 of the saved text | 78 | primary | corrected by the auditor |

| 1 | framing_challenge | Harness evolution repeatedly proposes and selects edits using feedback from a finite evolve set (adaptive reuse), so overfitting arises through coupled behaviours: encoding benchmark-specific patterns, promoting candidates favoured by evaluation noise, and accumulating complexity that raises evolve-set scores without improving the underlying mechanism. | - | Framing statement (how the paper states its problem, challenge, objective, solution or gain); not a measurement. | line 109 of the saved text | 109 | primary | corrected by the auditor |
| 2 | framing_objective | Task performance S(H;D)=E_{x~D} E_{tau~A(./x)}[r(x,tau)] and policy-token cost C(H;D)=E_{x~D} E_{tau~A(./x)}[c(tau)], where A=(pi,H) is the agent with backbone policy pi and harness H, x a task from task set D, tau a trajectory, r(x,tau) in [0,1] the verifier score, and c(tau) the number of policy tokens consumed. Generic evolution selects H_{t+1}=argmax over candidates of the empirical score S-hat on D_evolve (k trials per task). RRSI keeps this empirical objective but adds non-compensatory acceptance rules: noise floor S-hat(H') >= S* - delta, and for gains Delta S > delta the relative cost increase Delta C = (C-hat(H') - C-hat(H_t))/C-hat(H_t) must satisfy Delta C <= beta_0 + beta_1 Delta S (beta_0: cost tolerated for negligible gain; beta_1: extra cost allowed per unit gain). | - | Framing statement (how the paper states its problem, challenge, objective, solution or gain); not a measurement. | line 121 of the saved text | 121 | primary | corrected by the auditor |
| 3 | framing_solution | Translate machine-learning regularization into harness search: on the proposal side an annealed edit budget (L0-style), evidence-aware credit assignment and structured exploration; on the selection side leakage screening by a critic, stability-aware acceptance against a noise band, complexity-aware acceptance that requires extra inference cost to be justified by measured gain (Ridge/L2-style), and structural pruning of unproductive components (Lasso/L1-style), so that reusable mechanisms rather than benchmark-specific ones survive. | - | Framing statement (how the paper states its problem, challenge, objective, solution or gain); not a measurement. | line 135 of the saved text | 135 | primary | corrected by the auditor |

| 1 | framing_challenge | Fully automated synthesis of compliance test cases faces three gaps: the Ambiguity Gap (regulations are unstructured natural language lacking the determinism needed for automated verification), the Validity Gap (LLM-generated traces contain hallucinated API calls or invalid arguments), and the Inference Gap (stating rules in the instruction is trivial, so tests must require inferring implicit constraints). The introduction adds that static, manually curated test sets are expensive to scale and mainly check functional correctness. | - | Framing statement (how the paper states its problem, challenge, objective, solution or gain); not a measurement. | line 93 of the saved text | 93 | primary | corrected by the auditor |
| 2 | framing_objective | Primary metric is Pass@1 (Safe Success Rate): a test case T=(I, S*, Phi_task) passes iff the LLM achieves the functional goal and satisfies all hidden LTL constraints. Functional Oracle: S_mut ≡ S*, where S_mut is the final state reached by the LLM and S* the target state derived from the ground-truth trace; Safety Oracle: ∀φ∈Φ_task, τ_mut ⊨ φ, where τ_mut is the LLM's execution trace and Φ_task the task's regulatory LTL constraints; I is the user instruction. Failures are split into Benign Failure, Unsafe Failure and Unsafe Success. For the generator itself, diversity is measured by Safety Critical API Coverage and ATC = /{(a_i,a_{i+1}) / 1≤i<N}/ / /A/^2, with τ=[a_1,...,a_N] a trace and A the set of unique APIs (line 213). | - | Framing statement (how the paper states its problem, challenge, objective, solution or gain); not a measurement. | line 258 of the saved text | 258 | primary | corrected by the auditor |
